Page turn to a new spread
sound_palette: Ambience from the place: paper room tone first, then the location once it has colour (birds, traffic, harbour gulls, market chatter). J-cut a place's sound a bar before we see it.

Pen on cold-press paper: band-passed noise (~1.6–7.5 kHz) with a fibre texture and grain clicks, one burst per real stroke; thousands overlap into a hiss during a fast sketch; brighter short strokes read like a hi-hat.
Water and brush: a wet brush "shhh" for blooms, a jar rinse, a drip.
Foley follows objects at sketch scale: fabric or paper flapping for things in the wind (rate and level from speed, pan from screen x), steps on the beat, bells, splashes.
pitfalls_limits: Straight edges in the colour field from clipping by a bounding box → clip by the actual noisy distance.
Rectangular masks around complex silhouettes leave notches → mask with the real stepped silhouette.
Characters losing colour when they move into unpainted areas → sample arrival once (or tie it to the event), never at the current position.
Static ink can't be occluded by later washes → erase far ink inside nearer shapes before drawing; use carrot people for far crowds.
IK feet pinned while blending poses splay the legs → blend foot targets toward under-hip.
Front-facing heads go bald → draw the hair mass, then knock the face out of it.
Big canvases in headless Chrome: pack ink and time into RGBA byte textures yourself and upload the arrival field as a filterable float texture (`R16F`).
Painting edge to edge kills the sketchbook feel → leave margins and fray the edge.
styles.engine_section: `demo/engine.js` (deterministic): `penStroke` + `drawPen` (fineliner with wobble, overshoot, gaps, draw-on), `rasterPen` (bakes stroke order into an ink + time layer), `wash`, `reserve`, `dab` / `foliage`, `arrivalField` (colour arrival per cell from sources), `compositor` (WebGL page: paper × wash revealed by arrival × ink revealed by stroke time), `figure` + `drawPrims` (sketched people), `sketchShape` (any shape in this style in one call), `handwrite`. `demo/poses.js` holds a pose library. API table and a minimal example that draws something new: [DEMO.md](DEMO.md#engine-reference).

styles.name: Colored-Pencil Science Illustration
styles.official_demo_line: Do trees feed each other? A pencil drawing sinks below the grass, follows one grain of sugar along a fungal thread to the next tree, and pulls back over a whole wood joined underground.
styles.principles: - The whole frame is one pencil drawing. Sky, ground, soil, what lives in it and type are all pencil on the same paper; there is no "3D scene with a drawing in it". The sky is a loose blue wash with the clouds left as paper. - The cutaway is the signature composition. Above the ground line, landscape; below it, the cut face of the soil, where the hidden things live (stones, burrows, seeds, pipes). - It is a real 3D world. The camera can crane, push and truck through it, and things at different depths move at different speeds (multiplane parallax: the cut face slides over the far landscape). -
construction: Paper: warm off-white with a tooth (fine grain, laid fibres, soft cockling). Pencil only lands on the raised tooth, which is where the colored-pencil grain comes from. The base mottling of blank paper is fixed to the screen.
Four pencil layers, in this order, over every surface:
Contour: a graphite line from breaks in object id, depth and normal; the nearer surface owns the line; distant lines fade (aerial perspective).
Labels: cream paper tags with a pencilled edge; the writing is graphite, written along the glyph skeletons stroke by stroke (never wiped on). Overlay marks share the paper tooth.

Pipeline (reference): three.js renders G-buffers (albedo + id, light + depth + normal, hatch direction, anchor coordinates + reveal time) at 2× and a post shader redraws them as pencil, then a 2× box downsample. See `demo/main.js`.
colour_logic: Warm, restrained, paper-led. Bedrock is blue-grey, never large areas of black.
Accents carry meaning, at most three in a film, each always meaning the same thing (say amber for warmth, cobalt for groundwater, red for one burrowing animal).
White pencil over dark is how fine lines, highlights and anything delicate read on soil.
motion: Strokes stick to what they draw. Hatching, the tooth inside the pigment and the contour wobble are computed in anchor coordinates: each surface point projected through a fixed reference camera. Inside a shot group the camera only translates (crane, truck, push
Only the contour boils: a new drawing every 2 frames, 3 drawings cycled, about 1 px. Hatching and colour fields do not boil.
Things that move do so on twos (12 drawings a second: grass in the wind); the camera moves on ones.

Drawn in, not faded in: a sweep colours a horizon left to right with a ragged front; growing things (stems, vines, cables) appear from their base outward, already carrying their base colour, and finish their hatching within a few frames; tips grow pointed.
Particles (grains carried along a structure) are small 3D objects drawn by the same pencil, never glowing dots.
sound_palette: Pencil foley driven by what is being drawn: graphite writing (high, fine), waxy colour pencil hatching back and forth (lower, panned with the sweep), long soft strokes for long growing forms, a dry crackle for spreading fine lines, a light tap for a paper tag,
Ambience follows the camera: wind and distant birds above ground, closed down by a low-pass as the camera sinks, a quiet low earth tone below.
Score in acoustic, intimate colours (nylon guitar, flute, clarinet, pizzicato bass, harp, bowed vibraphone, marimba and kalimba); leave 400 Hz–2.5 kHz light for a narrator.
pitfalls_limits: Hatching fixed to the screen while things slide under it ("through glass"), or re-randomised every frame (the whole screen flickers).
Rotating the camera inside a shot group: the anchored strokes stretch. Turn by changing scale or cutting.
Square noise cells as soil grit; grains must be round.
Blank paper left "waiting" for more than about a second, with no drawing front moving: it reads as a bug.
Growing tips that start as white sticks on dark soil: grow them already coloured.
Too many labels, rulers and arrows: the plate turns into a worksheet. One label per shot.
3D-render tells: translucency, glow, bloom, depth-of-field blur, drop shadows on type.
Lines thinner than about 1.5 px in a wide shot shimmer: thicken them for wide views, keep the finest for close-ups.
styles.engine_section: - three.js (from the library's `node_modules`), one scene, a perspective camera with fixed orientation; four G-buffer passes at 2×, one pencil post pass per view, a composite pass (magnifier, overlays), a 2× downsample. - Reveal: a per-vertex time (`arev`) or a per-material sweep; the post pass gates each of the four layers by time since reveal, with every stroke given its own turn. - Overlays: 2D canvases for paper (tags, slips), graphite (writing, lines) and coloured pencil (dashed paths), composited with the same tooth. - `render(t)` depends on `t` only; about 60–130 ms a frame at 1080p on

styles.name: One-line Drawing
styles.official_demo_line: One unbroken line draws a whole life, then the pen passes to a child.
styles.principles: - One continuous line on warm white paper. The pen never lifts: in code the whole film can literally be one point array, from the first touch of the nib to the last frame. - Everything is a line: characters, places, objects, even time. No fills, no shading, no second line weight, no background art. - We watch the line being drawn: the camera follows the nib with a little lag and anticipation. - Besides ink there is only the paper and a soft shadow of the pen (the real world above the paper). One accent colour at most, used once.
construction: Paper: warm white (around `#F4EFE4`), procedural mottling (soft-light, large tile), long fibres that fade out when zoomed out (or they shimmer), a sparse paper-tooth speckle over the ink at close zoom, light vignette. All textures anchored to the paper; they m
Ink is a filled polygon around the path (not `ctx.stroke`), mixed with paper colour to an opaque tone per point.
Width = base width of the current "voice" of the line × pen pressure × fine noise (±8 %); pressure from speed: `0.66 + 0.8·exp(−v/300)` (fast = thin, slow = fat).
The line's character can change along the path (base width, alpha, tremble, dryness); blend over a short stretch at boundaries.
Ink bleed: the same polygon slightly wider, blurred on an offscreen layer, composited at ~20 %.
Pooling: extra round dots where speed drops low.
colour_logic: Ink on paper. A warm black (around `#1D1A17`) on warm white; nothing else fills the frame.
One accent at most, used once, on a stretch of the line that means something; it returns to ink afterwards and stays visible in the final picture if the picture is revealed.
Examples of an accent's job: red for love or danger; blue for water or cold; gold for money or a prize. Never a second accent.
motion: Everything on ones (24 fps): the appeal is the continuous act of drawing; stepping breaks it.

Timing = chapter windows + curvature: within a window, time per point is weighted by `1 + K·turn` (sharp turns get more time, smoothed so speed never jumps). Pin musical beats with marks: by arc-length fraction or by position ("the second time the pen passes h
Corners (speed minima at high turn) can be exported to the soundtrack as candidate note onsets.
Speeds: ~300–700 units/s for travelling lines, ~50–150 for small details. The most important stroke is usually the slowest.
Retracing over an existing line is legal and invisible (it only thickens slightly).
camera_grammar: Lateral scroll with the line running ahead
sound_palette: Music: one solo instrument, one unbroken melodic line, the sound equivalent of the drawing: a bowed or plucked string (cello, violin, viola, harp), a solo woodwind (clarinet, flute, bassoon), a hummed voice, a single guitar. A second colour only as a rare acce
Write the score to the drawing: key notes on marks and corners; fast line = short notes; a stopped line = one long note fading into silence; the highest note on the most important touch.

The pen on paper is the most important sound, synthesised from the pen speed: band-passed noise (brighter when fast, duller when slow), random paper-fibre ticks with density ∝ speed, amplitude ∝ √speed, panned with the nib's screen position; broken up by dry g
Silence is literal: zero the music bus including reverb tails; drop room tone.
pitfalls_limits: Stray connectors ruin a reveal: every extra line reads as a wrinkle, beard or mask. Fix the topology (where each chapter enters and leaves), not the drawing. Plan it like an Euler path: a closed motif is a circuit (you leave where you came in); retrace or reor
Each region of a final picture is drawn exactly once; connectors must fall on natural lines of that picture.
Test the reveal early and often: render the whole path at once at final scale after every change.
Lines drawn too close braid together once width is applied; keep a gap.
A round blot reads as a mole → a sagging teardrop.
Thin lines at wide zoom → clamp the width zoom.
Translucent hand shadows double-darken where they overlap → one layer per hand.
Titles collide with the drawing as the camera moves → check every frame of the title's window.
styles.engine_section: In `demo/`: `geom.js` (samples SVG paths by arc length in the browser, adds tangent-continuous connectors, assigns time by curvature, marks and holds), `ink.js` (the line renderer: pressure, bleed, pooling, tremble, dry brush, accent stretch, blot, minimum screen width), `paper.js` (paper, fibres, tooth, vignette), `cam.js` (composition keys + nib follow + soft clamp), `hands.js` (pen and hand shadows), `subs.js` (written-on subtitles and titles). The drawing itself lives in one file of SVG path strings and a chapter table (`face.js`); replace it with your own path. Debug views (`?all=1`, `?ca

styles.name: Whiteboard Explainer
styles.official_demo_line: How your phone knows where you are: GPS, atomic clocks, and the 38 microseconds relativity adds every day.
styles.principles: - One physical whiteboard. Everything the viewer learns is drawn in dry-erase marker in front of them, in real handwriting order. - The board is a map: each idea lives in its own region; the camera travels between regions, often led by the pen. Distance on the board = distance in the argument. - Real marker, not animated text: ink pools where the nib lands, dry streaks and speckle, strokes overshoot and don't quite close, ghosts of old lessons remain, a glossy sheen drifts slower than the board, and every stroke makes a sound. - No hands. Markers float with a real cast shadow that grows when t
construction: Board: a warm white gradient, a faint scuff and micro-scratch tile, a few dozen ghost marks (old words, circles, arrows) at 5–10 % in grey or pale blue, and a soft diagonal window sheen (white, 10–16 %) moving at ~0.35× the camera: this one detail sells "gloss
Ink: alpha ~0.94, composited with multiply so overlaps darken like real marker. Width 6–11 px for drawing, ~13 % of cap height for lettering.

Stroke character: resampled every ~0.6 × width; low-frequency hand wobble along the normal (a few px, long wavelength) plus a finer tremor; chisel-tip width modulated by direction; a pressure ramp at the start and a small taper at the end; circles start at an
Dry-marker texture: a speckle-and-streak tile subtracted from the ink layer (destination-out), locked to board space, faded out when the camera is wide.
Lettering: a single-line (single-stroke) font written in stroke order, each glyph with small rotation, baseline and scale jitter. Missing symbols (μ ≈ → × − ✓ ² ° ±) are hand-defined.

Props: dry-erase markers (white barrel, colour band and cap in the ink colour, felt nib), a felt eraser, magnets (glossy, with specular highlight and soft cast shadow). Frame, tray and wall appear only if the camera ever goes past the board edge.
colour_logic: Three marker colours at most, each with a meaning held for the whole film: one dark ink for things and structure, one for signals / measurement / process, one accent for the thing that matters (one accent per region).
Monochrome variant: everything in the dark ink, one element in the accent (the "only colour").
Ghost marks and board stay neutral; the accent never appears on props except its own marker cap and the hero magnet.
Example sets: black `#23262c` / blue `#2a5cb3` / orange `#d97757`; black / green `#2e8b57` / red `#c8363a`; navy `#1f2a44` / teal `#1f8a8a` / purple `#7a4fb3`.
motion: Hand speed: every stroke follows a slow-fast-slow curve (`u − sin(2πu)/2π × 0.8`). Strokes are scheduled into a time window and the engine solves the speed, so writing always finishes on time.
Pen hops between strokes lift in proportion to distance (shadow slides and blurs); long gaps send the pen off-frame to park and back shortly before its next stroke.
Magnet: drop with a shrinking shadow; slide with a small lift; lift-off and sink possible.
Eraser: constant speed along a path, a wide band at ~90 % strength (a ghost always remains).
Speed: faster than real hands (a sped-up lesson) but never so fast the stroke order is lost: a label ~0.3–0.8 s, a title ~3 s.
Camera on ones with real motion blur when it moves fast.
camera_grammar: Pull back from a tiny drawing
Ride the line the pen is drawing
Split view of two regions (zoomed out enough for both)
Pull back past the board edge to the wall
sound_palette: Every stroke sounds: band-passed felt-on-gloss noise (a hiss band ~2–7.5 kHz + body ~0.5–1.5 kHz) enveloped by the stroke's own speed curve, a tiny nib tick at the start, stick-slip grains, and on some long strokes the dry-erase squeak (a 1.5–2.6 kHz sine with
Props: magnet on steel = click + metal modes + a low board thump; eraser = felt rub modulated by its zig-zag; cap off/on; marker tray bounce.
Room: low room tone; a single diegetic ticker (a wall clock, a fridge hum, a projector fan) can own a silence.

Music options: a solo piano figure; a small jazz trio with brushes; plucked strings and kalimba; a synth arpeggio for tech topics; clockwork minimalism (marimba, pizzicato, woodblock, glockenspiel). Mickey-mouse details: a rising whistle for growth, pings for
pitfalls_limits: One pen, too many jobs drifts later and later → give each drawing a deadline window and let overlapping jobs go to another pen.
Minimum stroke duration × many dashes makes a dashed line take seconds → dashes need their own floor.
A pooled-ink dot bigger than the stroke start leaves halos on every letter → keep it inside.
Punctuation vanishes (a font period is a 1 px stroke) → render sub-width strokes as dots.
Labels half-cut by a push-in look sloppy.
Motion blur with few sub-frames strobes text.
Eraser paths crossing labels you want to keep.
Voice and phoneme set mismatch (a British voice with US phonemes) mispronounces → match the language code to the voice; ASR-check.
styles.engine_section: `demo/engine/wb.js`: hand-drawn shapes (`line`, `curve`, `poly`, `arc`, `circle`, `rect`, `arrow`, `dashed`, `hatch`), `text()` in writing order from a single-line font (`loadFont`), `Stroke`, floating `Pen`s, `Timeline.draw(pen, shapes, t, {by})` (solves hand speed to a deadline), `Timeline.erase`, `Timeline.cue`, keyed `Camera`, `Board` (ink multiply, dry texture, erasers, sheen, props), prop drawers. API table and a minimal example that draws something new: [DEMO.md](DEMO.md#engine-reference).

styles.name: Chalkboard
styles.official_demo_line: Chalk writes a popular claim about two characters, wipes it, and traces 射 back three thousand years.
styles.principles: - A clean, freshly wiped board. One even deep ink green with its own fine grain and very slow mottling. No history on the slate: no old swirls, no ghost lessons, no floating dust, no bokeh. - Writing that grows like a hand writes. Strokes appear along their centre line in the correct stroke order, with pressure: pressed starts and corners, points that lift, 捺 feet that spread, hooks flicked off. - Three chalks at most. White for structure, one accent chalk for the single part the lesson tracks, one pale chalk for a second hand (a pupil, a visitor). - A real object in a real room. Wooden frame,
construction: Canvas 2D for everything visible; WebGL2 only for the post pass (camera motion blur, a light vignette, grade, dither).

Each stroke is baked once into a board-space coverage sprite (coverage, arc length, lateral position). A partial stroke reveals pixels up to the current arc length with a round leading edge; the board's grain decides which grains take the chalk (deposit with a
Chalk edges are firm; loose powder only at the lift-off of a stroke (two to five grains). Never sugar the board.

Writing strokes carry a width profile per stroke type (start bump, corner bumps, taper for 撇 / 提, foot for 捺, quick lift for hooks) and a pressure profile (heavier at both ends, lighter in the middle). Straight strokes bow slightly; horizontals rise 2–3° to th
Board, panels, frame, tray, clock and wall are baked once in world units; the slate grain is a periodic tile drawn in world space (soft-light) only when the camera is close.
Erasing is a blurred destination-out band along one smooth path on a layer that holds only the strokes being wiped; it leaves a very thin, even haze. One wipe per film is plenty.
colour_logic: Ground: deep ink green slate, wood frame, warm white wall and a coloured dado if the room is seen.
White chalk carries every structure: characters, lines, labels, arrows.
The accent chalk (example: orange) is reserved for the one component the lesson tracks; it never decorates and never draws arrows or underlines that are not that component.
A pale second chalk (example: yellow) marks another person's handwriting.
motion: 30 fps, continuous (render with `--fps 30`: `core/render/video.mjs` defaults to 24).

Chalk speed, measured on our demo: a big character takes about 0.1 s per stroke including the air between strokes (a ten-stroke character about 1 s), labels about 0.04 s per stroke. Writing speeds up rather than making the voice wait, but a big character writt

When reading time and chalk speed pinch in a short film, change the words, not the hand. Ways that work (choose per film): fewer and shorter blocks on the board; big characters only for what the lesson tracks, everything else at label size; start a block while
Camera eases in and out (cubic), never bounces except a whip landing.
Things appear only by being written, wiped, revealed by a sliding panel or by drying. Nothing fades in.
camera_grammar: Slow lateral pan along a line
Pull back to a fixed medium frame
Locked frame while a panel slides
Cut on a line crossing a seam
Wide shot of the whole wall
sound_palette: Voice first: it is the loudest element; music sits 15–18 dB under it and comes up only in the pauses.

Foley: real chalk recordings cut into grains, one grain chain per stroke, level from stroke size; a light knock on landings; the accent chalk slightly softer and duller. A felt pass for the wipe, the low roll of a sliding panel ending on a stop, room tone very
Music: sparse plucked strings (a guqin model or nylon guitar) with marimba and pizzicato bass; a plucked note can be "born" from something drawn. Silence while a question or a verdict is read.
Mix: about −16 LUFS integrated before mastering, true peak ≤ −1.5 dBFS.
native_moves: A line that sews two boards.
pitfalls_limits: Dirty boards (old swirls, ghosts, floating dust) read as "messy", not "real". Keep the slate clean and let the grain carry the realism.
Equal-width polylines look like a plotter and make characters misread. Use stroke-type width and pressure profiles.
Character data that is structurally wrong is caught at once by native readers: check every character against a reference before shooting.
Small writing at 1080p disappears with the same chalk width as large writing; give small text heavier chalk.
Text written while the camera moves away fails reading time; hold the frame or keep the block in view.
Accent colour spread over arrows and decorations stops meaning anything.
A soft halo at the chalk's front reads as glow. The demo's `drawFront` (`props.js`) puts a faint radial gradient under its grains: in your copy, drop the gradient and keep the grains.
A wet streak with a hard edge looks like a cut-out.
styles.engine_section: The demo's code is a working engine; copy it into the project folder and write the film yourself.

styles.name: Sketchnote
styles.official_demo_line: One bee makes 1/12 of a teaspoon of honey in her life; the pen follows one yellow drop from flower to jar until the whole page is a poster.
styles.principles: - The frame is the page. Warm white dot-grid paper fills the screen; there is no desk, no notebook edge, no hand and no pen prop. - Everything is drawn in front of you, at the speed of a pen: outlines first, then the marker, then the words. Nothing fades in, nothing slides in. - Three tools only: one black fineliner, one grey marker (three strengths), one yellow marker. - Hand lettering is the typography: titles on banners, keywords in a bold hand, notes in a thin hand, all written stroke by stroke. - The page is planned as a poster. Every note has its place in the final page; the film is the
construction: Paper: a flat warm white with a faint grain texture anchored to the page, and a dot grid (26 px pitch, 1.3 px dots) drawn in world space so it scales with the camera.

Fineliner: points resampled every 3 px and offset along the normal by three layered sines (a slow wobble, a medium one, a fine tremor); drawn twice, the second pass thinner (≈ 0.6×), lighter (≈ 0.5 alpha) and wobblier; line weight varies in short segments; clo

Marker: clipped to a jittered outline, laid as a row of slightly bowed, semi-transparent broad strokes at one angle, composited with `multiply`, so overlaps darken into streaks; a thin line of pooled ink along the clip edge. Markers are laid stroke by stroke i

Shadow and volume: the shape minus itself shifted (even-odd), filled with grey marker. Drop shadows always fall the same way (down-right, ≈ 9–10 px for boxes); crescent shading on the side away from the light.
Paper fill: a shape that sits on top of others (a banner, a box, a jar label) is first filled with the paper colour, so the lines under it disappear.

Letters written stroke by stroke: each glyph of the real font is thinned to its centre line, ordered like a pen (start at the top-left free end, keep the smoothest direction, lift and jump to the nearest free end), and revealed by a thick mask stroked along th
colour_logic: Ground: warm white paper; dots in a light warm grey. No dark backgrounds, no large black areas.
Ink: one near-black for lines and words; a warm dark grey for secondary notes.
Grey marker: the only way to give volume, shadow and fill; three strengths (light for volume, middle for shadows and banner tails, dark for folds and small dark parts).

One yellow: reserved for the one thread the story follows (say, one raindrop on its way to the sea) and for two structural parts, the numbered banners and the fat arrows. Everything else stays black and grey. A darker yellow only for sparks and the closing loo
motion: 24 fps. The camera is smooth on every frame; only the line wobble boils on twos.

Speed is the pen's speed: outlines in a quarter to half a second per element, words about as fast as a person writes them. Later sections may use several pens at once to build energy, never instant appearance.
Order inside one element: outline → paper fill → marker → shadow → label.
Marker bars in charts grow from the base with an ease-out; liquid fills rise from the bottom.
Nothing moves once drawn: no bouncing icons, no sliding labels. Life comes from the boil and from new strokes.
camera_grammar: Ride the pen (centre trails the pen tip slightly)
Slow push while words are written
Pan along the page between blocks
Shape match cut (one round shape to another of the same screen size)
Pull back to the whole page
sound_palette: Foley from the strokes: fineliner scratch (band-passed noise 2.4–6.5 kHz with paper-tooth grain), lettering (same pen, choppier), marker (softer, 0.7–3.2 kHz, a "fsh" per streak); level follows how many strokes are active on screen, with a soft ceiling; pan fo

Music: small, wooden and plucked: marimba, pizzicato strings, kalimba accents, glockenspiel for sparkle, harp and vibraphone for a closing chord; bowed vibraphone for held, airy moments. No pads that fill the page's silence, no drums.
Silence is pen-only: the first seconds can be just the pen.

Voice: warm and clear, a teacher talking, slow (≈ 2–2.6 words/s), phrases split at commas with short breaths. Compress the voice, keep it ≈ 10 dB over the music by RMS; the music gives way in 300 Hz–4 kHz and ducks while she speaks; pens step back under the vo
pitfalls_limits: Flicker: random numbers drawn per frame make every line jump. Seed every element; let only the wobble phase boil, and only a little.
Text that appears at once: a wipe or a fade reads as a slide. Write along glyph skeletons.
Yellow everywhere: when the accent decorates, it stops meaning. Keep it on one thread plus banners and arrows.
Overcrowded page: if the poster looks like a page of handwriting, the film will too. Leave dot-grid air between blocks.
Heavy black and dirty shadows: big black fills and inconsistent shadow directions break the paper feel. Grey marker for mass, one shadow direction.
Small text in the final frame: plan the poster first; no note below ≈ 26 px at the final zoom.
Empty frames during camera moves: a pan that lands on paper before the pen arrives. Start the words before the move, or keep finished work in frame.
Thick lines when diving: line widths and wobble are in page units; inside a dive, draw micro notes with proportionally thinner lines and smaller wobble.
styles.engine_section: All in `demo/index.html` (Canvas 2D), reusable as is:

styles.name: Tablet Sketch Explainer
styles.official_demo_line: The coffee in your cup turns into a red cherry, then walks back to the cup: ripening, drying, roasting and grinding, one colour change at a time on a single pencil page.
styles.principles: - One canvas. Every frame is a region of one page. The page fills up as the film goes and is seen whole at least once; nothing exists off the page (no device bezel, no app toolbar, no hand). - Line first, colour second. Objects are drawn in graphite (white inside), then coloured as a separate pass. Colour sits *under* the pencil and is visibly shifted off it (offset 5–12 canvas units, down-right), with a ragged edge. - Still drawing. Some evidence that the drawing is in progress always stays: light construction lines left in, a block coloured half way, one object with its line only. - The canv
construction: Paper: cream canvas with a fixed paper grain (fine value noise plus a slow mottle), anchored to the canvas so it pans, zooms and turns with it. A light screen-space corner falloff only.

Pencil: a stamped-dot brush along a Catmull-Rom spline, one stamp every ~0.5 canvas units; pressure = taper in and out × slow noise, driving both width and density; a small low-frequency wobble along the normal. Within one stroke take the max coverage (no self

Grain threshold: at composite, pencil opacity = clamp((coverage · 0.9 − grain · 0.85 + 0.32) · 2.1). Light pressure is eaten by the paper tooth: broken, grainy edges. Lettering goes through the same threshold, so words look pencilled too.

Colour blocks: the object outline, translated off the line and displaced along its normal by noise (ragged edge), filled flat and blended *multiply* under the pencil. Highlights, seams and inner layers are holes cut out of the block (the paper shows through).
Colouring path: a block is revealed along a back-and-forth (boustrophedon) path across its shape, so a half-coloured block ends in visible strokes. A block can stop at any fraction.
Re-registering: to change an object's colour, erase what the new block covers (slightly wider, so no old fringe peeks out) and colour again; the line stays.
colour_logic: Neutral ground: a warm cream paper; graphite (warm dark brown-grey, never pure black) for every line and word.

System colours (every film): a light graphite for construction lines, one coral for the "explaining" marks (arrows, underlines, burst ticks, the one number that matters), one mustard for the highlight block under the key word of a title.

Subject colours (per film): soft, warm, chalky versions of the subject's real colours; each gets a darker variant of the same hue for a second, smaller shadow block (≈40% multiply). Four to eight subject hues in a film.
Colour is information: when a thing changes (ripens, dries, cooks, ages) change its block, not its line. A swatch strip that records each state is the style's way to chart.
motion: Marks appear at the speed of a sped-up drawing: a long line 0.3–1.4 s (slow only when the camera is close), small strokes 0.03–0.1 s, a block 0.05–0.4 s. One stylus: marks are mostly sequential; the stylus lifts and travels in an arc between them, and leaves t
24 fps on ones; no boiling, no paper shake. What moves: the camera, the stylus, the mark being made, and anything the story animates in screen space (particles, a colour flood).
Construction lines come first and fast; outlines next; colour last. A group is drawn white, then coloured as a group.
camera_grammar: Match cut between a small and a magnified copy of a drawing
sound_palette: Foley is the pencil: graphite on paper (band noise 0.7–4.2 kHz with paper-tooth bumps and the slow rhythm of a hand), lighter and higher for construction lines, choppier for lettering, broad and low (0.3–2.6 kHz, 12–14 Hz back-and-forth) for colouring; a tiny
Music: warm, small, acoustic: nylon guitar, double bass, a soft shaker, a soft-mallet vibraphone or kalimba; one soft accent note per new idea. No generic piano and strings.
Silence: a near-silence (pencil and room only) before a reveal; the first sound after it is the reveal.

Mix: voice compressed and set ≈10 dB (RMS) above the music; the music dips 300 Hz–4 kHz while someone speaks; −14 LUFS, true peak ≤ −1 dB. Voice: warm, unhurried, a creator talking over their drawing (≈2.3–2.6 words/s).
native_moves: Colour flood into the next shape.
Match cut to the magnified copy.
pitfalls_limits: Boiling lines turn it into a sketchnote: keep finished marks still.
Colour on top of the line looks like a sticker: composite colour under the pencil, always multiply.
Perfect fills look vector: keep the offset, the ragged edge and an occasional unfinished block.
Grain in screen space crawls during camera moves: generate it in canvas space, at the buffer resolution, and let the camera scale it.
Stylus parked over the subject or a note: park it in empty paper, or take it off frame.

Too many objects on one page: a page for a 50 s film holds about six drawings and a dozen short notes; plan the whole page before drawing the first line, and leave the final title's space empty until the end.
A drawing that is too small to read when the page is whole: size objects for the final pull-back, then push in for detail.
Thin flat transitions (a fade between areas of the same page) break the canvas illusion: move the canvas instead.
styles.engine_section: All in `demo/index.html`:

styles.name: Marker on Paper
styles.official_demo_line: A felt-tip marker works out how far the horizon is from a beach, then shows that climbing a hundred times higher only lets you see ten times farther.
styles.principles: - The frame is the sheet. A warm matte white paper fills the screen; no desk, no pad edge, no props, no hand, no pen. - One bullet-tip marker line. Thick (6–10 px at full frame), near-constant width, a slightly denser touch-down, a slight lift at the end, corners overshot because each side is a separate stroke. - Three inks with fixed meanings. Black builds everything; blue marks the givens; red marks the unknown and, later, the answer. Red is always the last stroke on a sheet. - One question per sheet, written top-left in hand lettering as it is asked, the page number circled top-right. - Ink
construction: Canvas 2D. Each stroke is a filled ribbon (bullet nib, width ≈ constant, ±3 % noise, a 0.86→1 ramp over the first 3 widths, a 10 % lift over the last 2) built from a resampled, Chaikin-smoothed polyline with a slow arm wobble and a little finger tremor along t

Drawn up to a length: a stroke in progress is cut at its head with a round cap; a letter in progress is revealed by a fat mask along its glyph's centre line (stroke order from a thinned skeleton), so letters keep the real font's outlines.

Ink density, not alpha: every stroke or letter adds one unit to its colour's density layer (`lighter`). Compose per pixel by transmittance: one unit = the palette colour at its opacity; n units = that transmittance to the power 1 + 0.6 (n − 1). Touch-down and
Paper: warm white, sub-2-level grain, faint cloudy formation, a few hundred 1-px fibres, one lamp's falloff of about 3 levels from top-left. Baked once per sheet, drawn through the camera.

The camera moves over the paper by drawing strokes and letters *through* the camera transform: pushed in, lines get thicker and stay crisp, like a lens closer to the sheet. Never scale a rendered bitmap.
No vignette, no film grain, no scan dirt, no glow, no drop shadows. The only shadow in the style is the peel's (≤ 0.16 opacity, narrow).
colour_logic: Ground: warm white paper. Ink: black for structure (≈ 90 % of the ink on any sheet).

Blue = given, red = wanted. The meaning is fixed for the whole film: the same quantity keeps its colour in the drawing and in the algebra. Where the topic has a hot/cold axis, red/blue may also carry it, in the same direction.
Each sheet: blue and red each ≤ 10 % of the ink; one red focus per sheet (it may be a group: arrow + label + circle).
Red never decorates and never draws structure. Grey, yellow and fills do not exist; a red bar is a thick red stroke.
motion: Drawings change on twos: 12 drawings a second at 24 fps. The camera moves smoothly at 24 fps.

Three boil drawings per sheet, built with the same seeds and differing only by a boil term (≤ 1 px along the normal), cycled on twos. Letters do not boil; random numbers are consumed independently of progress, so a half-written sheet and a finished one agree.
Speeds: a long arc is one sweep of 0.4–0.6 s; a hatch is a run of ~10 ms flicks; dashes are drawn one by one; an arrow is a shaft then two head strokes.
Black, then blue, then red. Structure first, the givens, then the unknown/answer. The red stroke lands on a beat and is held ≥ 1.5 s.
A finished sheet holds still except for the boil.
sound_palette: Foley follows every pen-down: a felt tip on matte paper — band-limited noise lower and softer than a fineliner, brightening with nib speed, with the paper's tooth in it; a faint squeak on long fast strokes; a soft "tok" at touch-down (a low body through the pa
Paper: the peel is a corner crackle then a slide; a push-through carries a little air.

Music: small acoustic ensemble that thinks — pizzicato double bass walking, staccato clarinet and bassoon, shaker and claves; harp and glockenspiel only where red lands. A question can hang on an unresolved chord; an answer resolves. Avoid generic piano-and-st

Silence: at least two near-silences (a peel; a scale reveal). Voice: a calm, unhurried narrator (≈ 2.3–2.6 English words/s), compressed, ≈ 10 dB over the music by RMS; music gives way 300 Hz–4 kHz. Master −14 LUFS, true peak ≤ −1 dB.
native_moves: Bars to scale, even when one is a dot.
pitfalls_limits: Flicker in letters. Never re-randomise letters per frame; lay them out once, fixed seeds, no boil.
Dirty paper. Shadows under text, vignettes and scan grime read as "unclean". Only the peel casts a shadow.
Red everywhere. Two red foci on one sheet kill the semantics; demote one to black.
Text cut by the frame edge when leaning in: pick the zoom from the text boxes (wholly in or wholly out).
Corners that pop. Detect corner ink on the un-wobbled path; otherwise the boil switches pools on and off.
Zooming a bitmap. Strokes must be redrawn through the camera, or a push-in looks blurred.
Algebra on a slide. Centred, typeset, faded-in equations break the hand; write them left to right in the drawing's colours.
A page of everything. One question per sheet; a new step is a new sheet.
styles.engine_section: - `demo/pen.js`: `Stroke` (resample, smooth, wobble, boil, corners), shapes (`line`, `poly`, `curve`, `arc`, `circle`, `rect`, `arrow`, `arrow2`, `wavy`, `dashed`, `hatch`), `Ink` (`stroke(s, upTo)`, `layout()` / `write(T, upTo)` for skeleton handwriting, `setCamera(M)`), `makePaper`, `paperCanvas`, `composeOn` (density → transmittance). - `demo/film.js`: the sheet/element timeline (`E(t0, t1, kind, items)`), camera keys and `matrix()`, the push-through match cut, the peel compositor, the subtitle slip, `window.EV` for foley and `window.TEXTS` for the reading check. - `demo/tools/skeleton.py`:

styles.name: Shadow Puppetry
styles.official_demo_line: Ten suns scorch the earth until the archer Hou Yi draws his bow, told with leather puppets on a lit screen.
styles.principles: A white cloth screen; behind it, flat puppets cut from translucent dyed hide, lit by an oil lamp. Colour arrives *by transmitted light*: dyes glow like stained glass, carved holes shine brightest, overlaps go darker. Puppets are jointed with visible thread rivets and moved by thin rods (neck and hands) that show as soft grey lines just off the screen. It is live theatre, not stop-motion: the screen flickers with the lamp, puppets tremble in the hand, loose parts swing on their rivets.
construction: `hideTransmission`: a 2D canvas that starts white; every piece is drawn with `multiply`. Holes stay white, overlaps darken by themselves.
`lampLight`: per lamp a broad lobe plus a tight hotspot (~6 : 1), each flickering independently (a few % of ~7 Hz value noise plus a faster sine). Warm light, never white.
`tonemap = 1 − exp(−hdr)`, exposure ∝ `1/√(lamps lit)`: more lamps bleach the frame but keep it readable. Lamp count is a dial the story can turn.

Cloth: procedural weave (sin × sin, noise-warped), fibre speckle, low-frequency density blotches, darker edges at the frame. Post: warm-tinted bloom, a warm vignette (toward brown, never grey), slight saturation, soft S-curve, light grain; heat haze only when
colour_logic: All colour is transmitted: a dye filters warm lamplight, so nothing is brighter than the lamp and every hue leans warm.
3–5 saturated dyes + raw hide (the neutral) + ink (outlines, hair, boots). Holes are the brightest value.
Overlap is darkness: plan which pieces cross.
Brightness comes from the number of lamps, not grading. Night is fewer lamps, never added blue.
motion: 24 fps continuous for puppets and camera; only swapped effect pieces (fire, water) step at 12 fps.
Hand tremor on every puppet (a few px, ~0.02 rad, low-frequency), stronger under tension.
Body glides with the main rod; legs, plumes, tassels are simulated (damped pendulums / spring chains driven by body acceleration, pre-simulated at a fixed rate for determinism).
Operatic phrasing: shuffling run → hop → crouch → freeze pose on a percussion accent (~1 s, only loose parts quiver) → head turn.
Faces never change; attitude = head angle + body tilt (up = resolve, down = sorrow).
Press on / lift off: arrivals come large and blurred onto the cloth and snap sharp (~0.5 s); exits grow, blur and fade (~1 s).
camera_grammar: Push through the frame onto the cloth
Lateral pan across a wide cloth
**Crash zoom** of a few frames on a percussion hit
Whip pan along a moving piece
Medium-close, empty cloth between two pieces
Tilt from ground strip to top of cloth
Truck round to the back (mirror view)
Pull back from cloth into the dark room
sound_palette: Percussion first, not piano and strings (gong-and-drum pattern thinking, 锣鼓经): low barrel drum, hard high clapper drum (woodblock), cymbals, small gong with rising pitch ("tai"), big gong with falling pitch ("kuang"); also a bamboo clapper board, pellet drum,

Bowed and reed voices: a bright nasal fiddle (erhu-like: pitched up, nasal formant, pitch-curve resampling for slides and vibrato), plain pentatonic (huan-yin) or sorrowful microtonal (ku-yin: raised 4th, lowered 7th); a shrill suona-like reed (oboe + 1.2–3 kH

Techniques, as options: a single tap inside a silence; one big gong per decisive hit; a heartbeat drum under dread; accelerating rolls into an entrance; one hit per visual step; a gong scrape to change space; a hard stop (≤ 30 ms, tails included).
Silence: hard-cut the whole bed; at most one sound inside (a breath, a tap, a sizzle).
native_moves: Off the screen = big and blurry.
pitfalls_limits: Flat clip-art look → hide texture, denser openwork, deeper dyes, carved outlines everywhere.
Figures unreadable in profile → bigger head, fuller lower body, collar piece, contrasting sleeves.
Radiating shapes read as saw blades or petals → flame tongues with a fat base, belly and hooked tip, alternating curl.
Grey corners when overexposed → warm vignette.
Thin pale pieces vanish → make them dark.
Mirror view flips pieces when rotation uses the x scale for both axes → x scale for x, y scale for y.
Smoke with `lighter` is invisible on bright cloth → dark wisps, warm additive only near a lamp.
Push-in centred on an edge lamp shoves figures out → push on frame centre.
styles.engine_section: In `demo/`: `carve.js` (piece sprites, `cut` / `cutLine` / `cutTaper`, pattern library, hide texture, rivets), `gl.js` (WebGL2 compositor: lamp field × transmission × cloth, mirror, bloom, haze, warm fade), `stage.js` (frame, audience, pillar wipe, cut-letter plaques), `backstage.js` (rim-lit silhouettes, flame, smoke), `hud.js` (placard), `scenery.js` (landscape pieces, ground strip, fire), plus the jointed rig with IK and pendulum parts; `?test=model|frame|hands` draws sheets from the real engine. A first test unlike the demo: carve a lantern-seller with a lattice basket, press it onto one l

styles.name: Red Paper-cut
styles.official_demo_line: On New Year's Eve the beast Nian comes to town, and one girl's giant paper-cut lights up the village to scare it off.
styles.principles: Every visible thing is a piece of paper that was cut with scissors and laid flat on another sheet. There is no painting, no gradient shading, no outline stroke: detail, volume and expression come only from what was cut away. Red paper is the hero material; grounds are paper too (a light paper by day, a deep dyed paper by night). Characters are jointed cut-outs (head, torso, upper and lower limbs pinned at rivets) animated in hard 12 fps steps.
construction: Paper grain: a neutral-grey texture in `soft-light` inside each piece (dye mottling, fibres, specks), then the piece's alpha restored with `destination-in`, so holes stay holes.

Cut edge: every silhouette is a polyline with a slight low-frequency wobble (hand-cut), a 1 px light rim upper-left and a dark rim lower-right (the cut face). Architecture and machines use straight segments + wobble, never smoothing.
Paper thickness: each piece casts a tight soft shadow on the layer below; stacked folded paper shows 2–6 offset darker edges.

Figures: red block + yin lines. Every figure piece gets an inset contour (a thin slit a few units inside the outline): the classic double outline, which also separates red-on-red overlaps (an arm over a coat).
Folk cutting vocabulary (`demo/motifs.js`): sawtooth rows (fur, grass, tiles, fringe), serrated edges, crescents (scales, quilting), swirls (joints), clouds, rosettes, plum, coin, tapered slits.
No floating islands. A closed ring cut would drop its centre out of real paper. Eyes are two crescents (upper and lower lid) that leave bridges, plus a pupil *hole*.
colour_logic: China red (around `#d2201f`, range `#c8102e`–`#d7261e`) is the hero material. Depth and role are shown by paper tones one step apart, not by shading: near pieces one step brighter, far pieces one step darker, an antagonist or a heavy object one step deeper.

Ground and hero must be different paper families. If background and hero are both red, the silhouettes stop popping. At night, all background layers are one dark dyed family and only the pieces that matter to the story are red; by day, a light paper ground wit
Gold foil is an accent kept for one late moment (a sun, a title, a coin); never a second main colour.

Examples of ground families: indigo night papers (far layers lighter blue, near darker); a warm rice-paper day with pale-red far hills; a jade-green or black paper for a story that isn't festive. Choose from the topic.
motion: Characters step at 12 fps (pose sampled at `floor(t·12)/12`); camera, light, weather, flames and flying pieces move on ones at 24 fps.
Rigs pin pieces at rivets (neck, shoulders, elbows, hips, knees, jaws, tails). Hard poses, tiny eases, 1-frame overshoots ("pop" = 1.15× for one step). Weight comes from size and camera shake.
In profile, a raised near arm crosses the face: keep hands forward of the face or let a prop cover them.

Folding: the flap is split into ~16 strips; each is compressed by cosθ and enlarged along the fold by `1 + 0.28·height` (fake perspective), darkened as it stands up, in a lighter back colour past 90°, with a growing shadow and a crease after. About half a seco

Cutting: the pattern is revealed through a mask of circles along the scissor path; the offcut drops once the outer edge is passed; blades open and close on a subdivision of the beat; scraps flutter out and land.
Unfolding: successive unfolds a fraction of a second apart, each flap swinging from folded to flat with ease-out (the "pa!" snap), then a scale bump and warm flash on the accent.
camera_grammar: Extreme close-up tracking the scissor tip
Low wide, a shape standing up from the ground layer
Push toward a lit piece, pull back to many
Pull back to an object in a room
sound_palette: Foley follows the material: scissors = metallic shear sweep (2.5–9 kHz) + a short ring + a fibre crack; folds = swish + crease tap; unfold = sharp snap; heavy steps = *cardboard* thud, not flesh; paper peel; pasting = a palm pat; match strike, puff; firecracke

Instruments: a bright Chinese chamber ensemble, not piano and strings and not the opera percussion of shadow puppetry: pipa (tremolo on long notes), zheng (`dan_tranh`: broken chords, glissandi, tremolo), erhu (glides), dizi (flute), sheng or yangqin colours,
Options: one snip = one beat subdivision; a rising zheng run, one note per thing that appears; a frame-drum heartbeat for weight; one big gong saved for one accent; total silence for a held breath.
Voice: warm storyteller, few lines. Duck music ≈ 9 dB and foley ≈ 3 dB under the voice; keep impacts out of voice windows. Folk names may need an `asr` alias in `lines.json`.
pitfalls_limits: Red on red reads as one blob → different ground family, near/far paper tones, inset contours for overlaps.
Darkening a layer through the light map also darkens what covers it → tint the layer itself (multiply + restore alpha).
A flat cos-squashed flap reads as a sliding card, not a fold → strips with fake perspective, darken as it stands up, show the back colour.
Cut reveal shows the uncut stack through the holes → stack thickness inside the "uncut" mask only; the cut part gets its own offset copies.
Scissors pointing backwards → the blade axis follows the direction of travel, the rivet a little behind the cutting point.
Blank frames between shots → overlap outgoing and incoming paper actions.
Engine traps (`put()` transforms, piece boxes, test pages) are in DEMO.md build notes.
styles.engine_section: In `demo/`: `paper.js` (paper textures, piece builder: fill, cut, inset, edge, grain, shadows, transmission), `motifs.js` (folk pattern library), `rig.js` (2D affine rig helpers), `tuanhua.js` (8-fold rosette from one wedge × D4), `light.js` (night lightmap, backlit pieces, bloom, rays, masked projected light), `fold.js` (fold – cut – unfold sequence), `hud.js` (subtitle banner, cut-letter text); `?test=` pages draw model sheets from the real engine. A first test not in the demo: a bicycle from `paper.js` pieces (`sawRow` spokes), wheels riveted in `rig.js`, rolling on 12 fps steps.

styles.name: Stained Glass
styles.official_demo: The Dragon of the East Window
styles.official_demo_line: Sunlight crosses a cathedral window from dawn to dusk, waking each pane of a knight-and-dragon tale.
styles.principles: - Cut pieces of coloured glass in dark lead cames, faces and folds painted in brown grisaille. - Glass has no light of its own: it glows only when the sun is behind it and throws a soft coloured copy onto the stone floor; unlit, it is dark and milky. - Figures move piece by piece, rigid and stepped. - The room is always there: stone, a splayed embrasure, iron saddle bars, a floor that catches light. - Secular: no crosses, saints, halos or other religious imagery; borrow the craft, not the subjects.
construction: Hue-preserving tone mapping: per-channel `1-exp(-x)` turns cobalt pastel; blend to per-channel only at the very top so a sun disc burns white while blue stays jewel blue.
Unlit panes: weak sky light + room-lit weathering haze, figures ghostly but readable. Lit panes: backlight ~2–3×, a soft, slightly skewed moving band edge.

Pieces: smooth Catmull-Rom cuts (no deep concave corners). Every piece is textured (`multiply` in its clip): streaks at a per-piece angle, hue drift (±10 %), darker aged edges by the lead, ±9 % thickness variation. The shader adds seed bubbles, scratches and t
Lead: near-black, one planar network, thinner on small pieces, round joins, faint grey flange, solder blobs; only where colours meet (one colour = one piece).

Grisaille: tapered trace lines in translucent dark brown; matting (stippled wash, graded shade, soft band inside the lead); scraped highlights (a thin stroke beside each fold in the piece's own colour: the only highlight transmitted light allows). Patterns (ma
Faces: almond eyes, heavy upper lid, big pupils, brow flowing into the nose. Expression lives in brows and mouth; change it by swapping the face piece, never morphing.
colour_logic: Two hues carry the picture (one deep, one hot); three or four more only as small touches. Example (Chartres logic): cobalt ground, ruby, touches of gold, green, murrey.
Greenish white glass sparingly (faces, fillets, sky). Flesh darker than you think, or backlit faces burn white.
A story light (candle, lamp, screen) may take a colour no glass uses, so it reads as a source.

The sun's colour is the clock: blue-white dawn, near-white brightest noon, gold afternoon, deep orange dusk (raise intensity rather than redness), weak blue moonlight. Patch length follows sun height.
motion: Figures step at 8 fps; light, camera, shafts and dust move on ones (24 fps): stepped light reads as flicker.
Rigid pieces on 2D FK (`setTransform(base · T(part))`, free draw order); long bodies are spine chains of banded pieces.
Freeze rule: a pane's figures use `min(t, t_lightLeft)`. Actions land on the beat.
Crack: jagged lines race from the impact in ~¼ s, bright with light, a short white flash and a 2-frame shake.
Re-leading: piece groups slide one beat each with a small outward bump along the lead, each ending in a weld spark; cracks become mending leads.
Glass never bends or morphs; things appear by being lit, not faded in.
camera_grammar: Truck sideways with the band of light
Pull back to the whole window
Tilt down the shafts to the floor, then top-down
Hold through a crack, no cut
Slow push toward a small light
Tilt up to a rose or tracery
Rack between two panes, one lit, one dark
Low angle along the embrasure, glass raking
Return to an earlier framing under new light
sound_palette: Instruments: organ (pedal drone, soft stops, full), harp, hand chimes, tubular bells, recorder or a chant-like voice, water-glass notes, timpani; also hurdy-gurdy drone, psaltery, portative organ. No generic piano or strings.
Mode families: church modes (Dorian, Mixolydian, Aeolian, Lydian), open fifths, drones, parallel organum.
Options: free unmetred chant for darkness; one note meaning "the light" each time a pane wakes; an organ pedal that holds and then cuts out; a rising scale, one step per lit piece.

Foley, material first (synthesizable): struck glass = inharmonic partials ~1 : 2.32 : 4.25 : 6.63 : 9.38; crack = snap + pane thump + rain of tinkles; lead = stick-slip creak; glass sliding in a came = gritty band noise + faint squeal; solder = hiss + tick; ai
native_moves: Light is time, and the camera.
A window holds its own light.
pitfalls_limits: Hidden leads show through front pieces → erase the surface under each piece before stroking its lead.
Pastel glass → hue-preserving tone mapping; darker flesh. Red dusk × blue glass = mud → keep blue alive, raise intensity.
Voronoi reads as a filter; flat fills read as clip-art → hand-cut lozenges, texture on every piece, heavy grisaille.
A sharp floor patch looks like a decal → blur, desaturate, stone-modulate, halo. Shafts at full strength at the window wash out the pane.
Top-down projection is flipped → put the wall at the frame bottom so figures stand upright (mirrored, correct).
Patch-map canvas size mismatched with the code draws into a corner of the texture → one constant size.
Carved text in a dark wide is unreadable → push in, park a light on it.
styles.engine_section: In `demo/`: `glass.js` (pieces, textures, lead, grisaille, lozenges), `comp.js` (WebGL2 compositor), `window.js` (lancets, rose, borders, wall, carving), `scene.js` (camera, floor projection, shafts, dust), `subs.js` (banderole), `test.js` / `frames.js` (model sheets and style frames from the real engine), `music/score.py`, `mix.py` (glass/lead foley). `knight.js` / `dragon.js` show the rigid-piece FK rig pattern; build your own subjects with it.

styles.name: Gilded Illumination
styles.official_demo_line: In a painted world where only gold shines, the sun goes out; a girl carries the last lamp up the mountain and gives it its light back.
styles.principles: - Flat pigment, firm line. Every shape is one flat colour, a darker band just inside the outline, a firm ink outline (never hairline: at least ~2.5 px on screen in a wide shot, thicker in close-ups) and white-lead strokes on the edges that face the light. No gradients that model form, no soft shading. - Gold is a material, not a colour. Gold leaf is laid in squares: you can see the leaf blocks, their seams and overlaps, a little red bole where the leaf broke, punched dots. It lies dark and warm until a light crosses it; then the squares flash one by one (each one tilted a little differently) w
construction: Pigment shapes: `fill` + `rimShade` (the same path stroked inside its own clip in a darker tone) + ink `stroke` + white-lead `hiLine` + white-lead dots. This recipe is the whole look; keep line widths tied to the camera so they never thin out to a hairline in

Gold leaf: a tileable texture laid in leaf squares (each square its own tone, a thin dark seam with a bright overlap ridge, a few cracks, specks of red bole), filled through a pattern into any path, then a burnish, a speck layer, an inner rim and an ink outlin

Light only on gold: every gold path is also written into a screen-space mask; light from the picture's own sources is added only inside that mask, per leaf square (each square has its own tilt, so the light moves across the squares unevenly), with star-shaped

Lit gold stays gold: light pulls the leaf toward a warm gold with a cap on each colour channel (ours stops at 82% of the way), so the brightest leaf still shows its squares and seams and never burns to white or flat yellow. A soft bloom, if any, belongs only t
Ground pigment (ultramarine and friends): a granular pattern (coarse grains, not noise) mapped between a dark and a light tone of the hue.
*Reference:* vellum (procedural sheet with grain and stains) is kept for the parts that are written on: speech scrolls and the end plaque.
colour_logic: The ground is ultramarine (sky) or gold (gold-ground panels and frames). Everything else is a short list of medieval pigments: lapis/ultramarine blue, vermilion, verdigris green, rose, azure, lilac-grey, white lead, iron-gall brown ink, gold, rarely silver. Oc
Each pigment comes in three values only: body, darker rim, white-lead highlight.
Blue and gold are the pair the eye goes to; keep the biggest blue field and the brightest gold for the moment that matters. Vermilion is for the hero, frames and marks of importance.

*Reference palette:* ultramarine `#22379a`, vermilion `#c8321f`, verdigris `#3f8f7a`, rose `#d97a8a`, ink `#2a1a10`, gold leaf (texture, mid tone `#c99a3e`); vellum `#efe2c4` only for scrolls and the plaque.
motion: 30 fps, smooth (on ones). Things appear the way they are made: shapes pop up with a small spring, strokes are laid along their path, writing is wiped on, gold is laid then shines, a figure is painted in layers (gold, colour, ink and white lead).
Easing is calm (ease-in-out, ease-out); springs only on small things appearing.
What never moves: the painted picture and the gold already laid. Only the light, the hero and the camera move across them.
Paint and gold build up; they never fade in as a whole.
camera_grammar: exponential pull out of the leaf
push through a quatrefoil / foliate frame
follow along the path of a continuous narration
foreground spire or cloud wiping across
a band of light sweeping the whole picture
a ring of gold light spreading from a touch
hard cuts on circles, centre to centre
the big pull back to the whole painting
sound_palette: *Reference band:* bowed fiddle (a solo violin played plainly stands in), harp, portative organ (a soft organ register), frame drum, recorder; bells (tubular, glockenspiel, hand chimes) for gold.
Modes: dorian, mixolydian, aeolian; a Picardy third for arrival. No piano, no modern string section, no synth pads.
*Reference foley:* the painted world's own sounds: wind, running water, footsteps on stone, a door, a far bell. Workshop sounds (quill, brush, mortar) are optional, for a film about making.
Silence is a tool: drop the band to one held note when the picture asks a question.
pitfalls_limits: Shading creeps in. Soft gradients make objects look plastic; model with the rim band and white-lead strokes only.
Flat-illustration drift. Thin lines, no white dots, gold as plain yellow discs: the picture turns into a modern vector illustration. Keep the ink firm, add white-lead dots, show the leaf squares.
Gold everywhere, lit all the time. If gold shines all the time, the light has nothing to reveal. Keep gold dark until its moment.

The white-out climax. Pushing the lit leaf's brightness up (or adding a big glow) turns the brightest moment into a yellow-white blur and erases the leaf squares. Light the climax with more gold, not with more white: rings, squares lighting in turn, a capped g

Day by brightening. Raising the whole frame's brightness or saturation, or turning the night sky light blue, to show that the light came back looks like a colour-correction slip and kills the deep ultramarine. The sky stays deep; the gold does the work.
Wandering subtitles. A scroll that jumps between left, centre and right, or changes width with each line, reads as an error. Fix its place and size; move the camera or the hero instead.

Picket-fence mountains. A row of spires of the same height reads as a fence. Group spires in clusters (one tall, smaller ones leaning off it), vary the gaps, and stack two or three ranges, paler and smaller behind.
Stacked-box mountains. Rectangular ledges read as buildings; spires must lean and taper, with small stair-steps on both flanks.
styles.engine_section: - `lib.js`: math and easing, `monotone`/`track`, the pigment palette, the leaf-square gold texture (`makeGold`, `leafAt`), `gold()` / `goldStroke()` with the glint mask (`MK`), `shape`, `rimShade`, `hiLine`, `dots`/`pearls` (white lead), `tubePath`, `spirePts`, `camMatrix`, `reg()` for `window.TEXTS`. - `world.js`: the demo's one painted world (its subjects are the demo's; your film paints its own): `leaf()` with its dark (`dim`) state, layered rock clusters (`makeRange`, `drawSpire`), the sun (`drawSun`, dark or lit, rays lighting in turn), trees with gold fruit, the chapel with a gold-ground

styles.name: Risograph Print
styles.official_demo_line: A Sunday-morning bike ride through the city — bakery, park, riverside — each stop adding an ink until three misregistered plates overprint.
styles.principles: A risograph prints one colour at a time: each colour is its own stencil ("plate") with its own drum of translucent ink. That one fact makes the look:
construction: per plate: offset in px + tiny rotation → misregistration;
halftone: cosine spot function on a rotated grid, period ~6–8 px at 1080p, anti-aliased threshold; densities ≥ ~0.9 print solid; screen angles ≥ 15° apart;
grain on the dot threshold, pinholes in solids, density varying with a feed-direction streak and a slow blot noise;
composite `paper × Π mix(1, ink_i, coverage_i)`, with faint paper fibre;
dots anchored to the paper (screen), not to objects: a pan slides the image under a fixed screen, as if each frame were printed anew;
a per-plate gate and a roller sweep (moving edge, slightly heavier ink band) let a plate arrive mid-shot.
colour_logic: 2–3 spot inks, never more, plus paper; every other colour is an overprint or a tint. No gradients except stepped halftone.
Pick inks whose pairs mix into useful colours; at least one must carry a silhouette alone.
Paper is warm off-white (around `#F4EEE2`), never pure white; paper white is a colour too (knockouts, highlights, subtitles).
Light neutral surfaces (skin): a light tint of the palest ink. Dots of a saturated ink on skin look like a rash.
motion: Characters act on twos (12 fps); camera moves on ones (24 fps): a stepped camera reads as judder.

Registration is not jittered every frame. One fixed set of offsets per shot (±1–3 px). A kick (≈ 8–14 px, decaying in ~0.25 s with slight ringing) on an accent; a drift up to ~25 px through a held moment, snapping back on the downbeat.
Grain boils partly (about a third re-rolls per print); sheet streaks and blots change only at cuts.
Simple cycles on few drawings; secondary motion (scarf, flag, tail) as a travelling sine wave.
camera_grammar: Wide lateral tracking, small figure, empty sky
Static wide, the subject crosses the frame
Ground-level low angle, big foreground shapes
Medium two-shot held for a look
Push into a halftone field until dots are shapes
Pull back to reveal the paper
Match cut on a flat shape
sound_palette: Instruments, as options: warm, dry, handmade, slightly lo-fi: upright or electric bass, vibraphone or marimba, nylon guitar, whistled or hummed melody, Rhodes, toy piano, brushed kit, shaker and rim clave, a small drum machine through tape saturation.
Layering like plates (an option): each new plate brings one instrument, and they can leave one by one.

The machine is the signature foley: feed "shhk", drum "ka-chunk" at a plate arrival, motor hum, a sheet landing on a stack, a guillotine cut. Other foley dry, close and papery, following the story's materials.
Silence: a held bar with reverb tails cut, at most ambience or one distant sound; it pairs with a registration drift, and the snap brings everything back.
native_moves: Two inks, a third where they meet.
It is a sheet of paper.
pitfalls_limits: Three halftoned plates in one area = mud → two plates, one tint.
`fract(p*vec2(233.34,851.73))` draws vertical stripes across solids at 1080p → a well-mixed hash (`fract(vec3(p.xyx)*.1031)` family).
Per-frame registration jitter and sheet streaks flicker and blow up file size → fixed offsets per shot, kicks on accents, sheet noise at cuts, partial boil.
JPEG screenshots (4:2:0) smear saturated dots → PNG frames into a lossless yuv444 intermediate, encoded once with `-tune grain`; check at 100 % and 50 % for moiré.
The halo layer must copy the canvas transform, or zoomed shots draw the subject at the wrong scale.
Additive `over()` inside a transparent layer loses its meaning → overprint on the plate canvas.
A main colour without the first plate floats loose in one-ink frames → build palette recipes up from the one-ink silhouette.
`evenodd` fills of arches fill solid → trace the inner edge in the opposite direction.
styles.engine_section: In `demo/`: `riso.js` (print shader: plates, halftone, grain, registration, kicks and drift, gates, roller sweeps, reflection wobble), `draw.js` (`ink(b,y,p)` densities, `over()` overprint, `layer()` paper halo, 2-bone IK, limbs), `sheet.js` (model sheet with a "plates = story" row via `S.mask`), `tools/video_png.mjs` (PNG frames → lossless intermediate), `tools/mux.sh`. Minimal new frame: two plates (R = teal, G = orange); a solid teal hill, an orange disc drawn with `lighter` so it darkens where it crosses the hill, a 40 % teal sky band, a figure knocked out with `layer()`.

styles.name: Halftone Dossier
styles.official_demo_line: A chubby orange cat stands trial for testing gravity and 4 a.m. parkour, and walks free.
styles.principles: - The whole film is paper. A warm cream sheet with low-frequency mottling, fine grain, a vignette and a fold; dark scenes are printed on it too, never glowing. - Shading is never a gradient: it is halftone dots whose size follows a density field. Two or three dot layers at different screen angles overprint (multiply); that is the "printed" feel. - Bureaucratic apparatus: case numbers, file chips, numbered exhibits, height charts, name plates, stamps. Their seriousness is the frame; the subject can be grave or trivial. - Loud but readable: one idea per 2–4 s card, one big headline, one visual g
construction: Paper layer (canvas, multiply over everything, built once): an upscaled random tile for mottling, per-pixel noise with a slight warm bias, a radial vignette, a faint centre fold.
Grain layer (per frame): a few hundred paper-coloured specks and fewer ink specks, reseeded every 2 frames: dust on the print, not film grain.

Halftone: a rotated grid of circles drawn as one path; step 20–26 px; screen angle different per layer; radius = density × step × k with k 0.6–0.72 (around 0.7 dots merge into solid ink). Density fields: radial (halos, blooms, corner glows), edge (dots crowdin
Halftone-filled numerals and shapes: a flat fill overprinted with a darker halftone clipped to the glyph; giant numerals may bleed off the frame.

Line boil: turbulence displacement (small, ~5 px) reseeded ~10×/s plus a fine ink-grain mask that eats a little of every fill. Characters and hand-drawn props only; never on text, halftone, HUD or captions.

Characters: chunky shapes with a heavy ink outline (~7 px), flat fills, a lighter belly or face area, glossy eyes (ink ellipse + two highlights) that can squint, blink or close into a happy arc. One head rig shared by all body poses.
colour_logic: A paper ground, one dark ink, and four or five flat spot inks. The dark ink (navy, black-brown or deep green) carries every outline, body text and the caption bar, and is the fade-out colour.
One ink is the overprint shadow colour (misregistration offsets, caption shadows); one is the highlight for keywords and numerals; one warm red is reserved for stamps and alarms.
Flat inks only. No gradients, no transparency ramps; tone comes from dot size and overprint.
Night or "secret" scenes switch to a dark ink ground with a lighter dot layer of the same family, still multiplied by the paper.
motion: 30 fps transforms; line boil at ~10 fps on characters, so the drawing breathes while positions stay smooth.
Everything enters with overshoot (back ease, 0.3–0.45 s): rising from below the frame or scaling from 0. Nothing fades in.
Per-character pop for headlines: each glyph drops 30–100 px and squashes in, stagger 0.05–0.08 s (0.02 s for small text).
Stamp slam: ~0.09 s from ~2.6× to 1× (ease-in), then a small damped bounce; camera shake, flash and stamp sound on the same frame.
Squash landings preserve volume (`scale(1/sq, sq)` with a damped cosine).
Idle life: breathing, tail or hair sway, blinks at scripted times, twinkles, a blinking REC dot or clock colon.
camera_grammar: Locked frontal with a small beat pulse (~0.6 %)
Flash frames (white overlay ≤ 0.95 → 0, capped at 0.5 for big hits)
Snap zoom into a halftone detail until dots are huge
Pull back to reveal the whole desk
sound_palette: Synth pop-print toolkit: synth kick, snare, clap, hat; a square-ish 8th-note bass; triangle pad; a marimba-like pluck (fundamental + ~4× partial) for melody; pizzicato and finger snaps for sneaking; music-box bell for tenderness.

Foley follows the print and the gag: stamp = pitch-dropping boom + click (a crackle for big ones), camera shutter, paper slides and folder flaps, typewriter or keyboard clicks, whooshes into wipes, pops on every glyph, boings and plops for characters, glass or

Silence before the stamp: empty the music just before a verdict so the stamp lands alone. Other options: a snare roll + rising sweep into a reveal; stripping to bass and snaps for a secret scene; a bell arpeggio as a tag; a single sustained pad under a sad exh
Voice is optional; cards carry the film. If narrated: a dry, deadpan report voice, never breathless.
pitfalls_limits: Fonts not loaded before layout → per-character positions computed with a fallback font, glyphs overlap. Preload every family against the whole page source and the built text; runtime strings must use only characters that appear in the file. Use `font-display:
Boil on text or dots turns them to mush → filter only characters and props.
Clip-path ids are global → every clipped numeral needs a unique id.
Time-windowed scenes → an element invisible before its cue needs explicit opacity 0 for `t < t0`.
A dot wipe short of full coverage at the cut shows the hard switch; make the max radius cover the grid cell's diagonal.
A 100 % white flash reads as a dropped frame → cap at ~0.5.
Dots too small (< ~14 px step at 1080p) alias into moiré after encoding.
Too many inks lose the print feel → at most five plus paper.
styles.engine_section: Everything lives in `demo/index.html`: helpers (`el`, `txt`, `tf`, `seg`, easings, `measure`), per-character text (`chars` + `charsPop`), halftone (`halftone()` with `radial`/`edge` density fields), `caption()` bar, stamp (`stampEl` + `stampAnim`), a mascot rig with a `setFace` interface, `scene(t0, t1, build)`, HUD chips, dot wipe (`WIPES`), paper + grain (`buildPaper`, `drawFx`), `render(t)`. `demo/render.mjs` renders stills and video; `demo/music.py` synthesizes score and SFX. Line ranges and a minimal scene: [DEMO.md](DEMO.md#engine-reference).

styles.name: Woodcut Print
styles.official_demo_line: A village spends a whole winter casting one bell; the first time it rings, the snow stops.
styles.principles: Each shot is one printed plate: black ink on laid paper, framed by a paper margin. It follows three rules of real relief printing:
construction: Print frame: the printed image area sits inside a paper margin; the wider bottom margin holds captions. The image edge is the block edge: ragged ink, never a clean rectangle.
Knife classes (widths in 1080p pixels at 1× camera):

Hatching (Doré grammar in wood): line direction follows form (a round object is wrapped in arcs, slopes follow the fall line, fire and light radiate, cloth follows its folds). Width follows tone: bright = wide cuts almost merging into white, mid-tone = thin cu
Figures: black silhouette + white knife halo + grazing-light hatching on the lit edge only (light z ≈ 0.2, so flat areas stay black). Skin carved white, features left black (the wordless-novel rule).
Close-ups (hands, objects): sculpt a small height field (capsules, blobs, planks, creases), light it and run it through `woodcutFilter` (§10), so cuts follow the isophotes like an engraver's.

Printing: the mask (white = cut) goes through a WebGL2 compositor: knife burr on edges, ±6 % ink unevenness, wood-grain streaks, specks where ink didn't take, a mottled colour plate with a small fixed misregistration. Block mode: glossy inked wood with grain s
colour_logic: Two values carry everything: near-black ink and warm laid-paper white. The raw wood colour appears only in shots that show the block itself.
At most one colour plate, printed only where white has been carved, so it glows out of the cuts and never sits on the black. A colour plate over ink is nearly invisible, so plan it on carved white.
The colour is reserved for the one thing that matters (a flame, molten metal, a heart, a signal lamp). It can spread at a peak and shrink to a single highlight afterwards; it is never decoration.
Examples of a plate: a burnt copper-orange for heat; a cold Prussian blue for water or night; a deep oxblood for a wound or a seal. Choose it from the topic.
motion: Characters on twos (12 fps); camera, particles, fire and light on ones (24 fps). Hatching lives in each body part's local space, so cuts move with the limb and don't boil; only fire and liquids re-cut every 2 frames, as deliberate boil.
Anticipation / action / follow-through on every key action: a few frames back → a 2-frame strike → settle + a short shake.
Carve reveal: each stroke has its own start time and speed (0.08–0.35 s). Reveal keys: `light` (bright areas first, coarse to fine), `radial` (from a point: rays, a pour), `down`, or any function.
Hard cut = a new impression: two frames of misregistration (a few pixels, then back).

Paper transition (the one transition grammar): brayer rolls ink (a wet highlight sweeps) → paper lays down → baren spirals, the image soaks through → the sheet peels on a cylinder toward camera, heavy then fast, its back showing the mirrored show-through.
What never moves: the paper margin.
camera_grammar: Slow macro push on a sculpted close-up
Frame in a frame (door, window, arch)
Hard cuts on the beat, each a new impression
Crane up from a detail to the whole
Rack between two plates via the peel
sound_palette: Instruments: low strings (contrabass, cellos; spiccato, pizzicato), wood and skin (log drum, woodblock, frame drum), gran cassa, timpani, one tam-tam, synthesised struck metal (modal: 3–5 inharmonic partials + hammer transient); a bowed saw or hurdy-gurdy dron
Options: withhold the timbre of the story's object until it appears; a metric modulation instead of a tempo jump; a modal shift inside a long decay; one drone under a locked plate.

Foley follows the material, all synthesisable: knife into wood (transient + band-passed fibre tearing tied to knife speed), chips, brayer tack, paper air, baren rasp, the wet peel; metals by size (large = low, small = high and pure); resonant objects as modal
Silence is a tool: near-silence with one faint ambience, or true digital silence before the loudest moment; the first sound after it is chosen.
native_moves: The one colour plate spreads and withdraws.
Filter a sculpt or a frame
pitfalls_limits: White marks on white areas are invisible → stab cuts need dark masses behind them.
Hatching every surface looks like fur or rain → grazing light; 3–6 cuts on the lit edge only.
Black faces with white cuts don't read small → skin white, features black, a black keep-line around white parts.
Hand-drawn close-up props look like mittens and blobs → height field + `woodcutFilter`.
Short hatch segments with a tonal wobble turn into zig-zag chevrons → long cuts (14–50 × spacing), one broad highlight band, a thin rim light, a stronger halo.
Steam or smoke on top of the subject reads as flames → draw it behind, so only wisps escape.
Lazily cached strokes shared between shots make frames depend on the render worker → every cache builds itself on first use.
Fine hatching + ink noise + grain inflate the file → a higher CRF with `-tune grain`; check a 1:1 crop. `woodcutFilter` NaN in flat areas → clamp before `sqrt`.
styles.engine_section: `demo/engine/index.js` (imports only `/core/lib.js`) carves and prints any path or shape, on two canvases: a mask (black = uncut, white = cut) and an optional colour plate. Main functions: `shape` (carved solid with halo and form-following hatching), `cutAlong` (a path as hand-cut strokes), `hatch` (streamline hatching of a region), `flecks` (stab cuts), `rays` (carved light), `drawStrokes`, `plate`, `woodcutFilter` (image or frame → cuts), `makePrinter(W,H).render` (print / block compositor). Reusable demo pieces: `demo/trans.js` (paper peel), `demo/hands.js` (height-field sculpts). Option ta

styles.name: Copperplate Engraving
styles.official_demo_line: A natural-history plate engraves itself: the burin cuts the copper, the bee builds up line by line, and a watercolour wash brings it to life.
styles.principles: An intaglio print: the line is ink held in a groove a burin cut into copper. Three rules:
construction: The sheet is the world: 1920×1080 world units of laid paper (cream, ~`#f1e8d2`) with world-space texture (fibres, laid lines, sparse foxing) that zooms with the camera; a pressed, bevelled plate mark and a ruled border (rule + hairline) frame it.

Ink is one warm near-black (~`#1c1510`). Width ratios: outlines heaviest (swelling ×0.45–1.35), first hatching from a hair (~0.18 px) to ~2 px, crossing ~0.8×, third family ~0.6×, hair and stipple finest. Spacing is relative to the figure (~1/180 of its height
Swell law for every hatch line: width × (0.2 + 0.8·sin(πu)^0.7), tapered over its first and last ~22 %. Families switch on by tone thresholds (~0.14, ~0.5, ~0.75 on a 0–1 tone).
