API table and a minimal example (a shape the demo never uses): [DEMO.md](DEMO.md) "Engine reference".

styles.name: Exploded Teardown
styles.official_demo_line: Half an open-source keyboard comes apart in one orbit, down to the chip, then closes with its real dimensions.
styles.principles: A frame reads as this style when:
construction: Real-time PBR (three.js `MeshPhysicalMaterial`) at 2× and downsampled, ambient occlusion, a depth of field with one aperture for wide and macro (blur follows 1/focus − 1/z, so it grows as the camera comes close), a high-threshold bloom for emitters only, a vig

Each material keeps its character: plastics with soft sheen (roughness 0.55–0.7), boards with a thin clearcoat and traces as a raised, lighter relief under the mask, metallic pads, tight highlights on machined metal, matte rubber.

Boards are painted from their layout files: copper pours, every trace, via, pad and drill, silkscreen, on both sides, at 14–20 px per millimetre, with roughness, metalness and bump maps from the same drawing. Components stand at their footprint positions with

Light: a warm key from above front, a cool rectangular rim behind that follows the camera so edges separate from the ground, a soft top light, a low HDRI for reflections; a practical fill only where the camera goes inside.
Background: a dark graphite seamless sweep (screen-space radial gradient), floor visible only as soft shadow.
Effects anchored to the world (leaders, dimension lines, glows) are projected from 3D points every frame; only subtitles and title cards live in screen space.
colour_logic: The product brings its own colours; the frame around it is neutral and dark, so the product is always the brightest, most saturated thing.

Interface ink is one warm white at two strengths (names at full, specs at about 60 %), plus one accent reserved for measured things: dimension lines, label indices and one matching detail on the product itself.
Values are ordered: ground darkest, product mid to light, labels lightest. Never put text on a busy, bright part without a dark backing.
Example (our demo): ground #34363a → #0d0e10, ink #f1efe9, accent #ff6b3d.
motion: 24 fps on ones; everything is smooth and deterministic.
Separation: smooth start, fast middle, long settle (ease-in-out cubed); layers leave top first, 0.15–0.2 s apart; repeated parts (keys, screws) fan out in a wave ordered by distance from a corner.
Closing: bottom first, quicker (about 1 s per layer), the last layer lands with a real mechanical response (a key travels its stroke and returns; nothing bounces like rubber unless it is rubber).
While held apart, layers may float a millimetre or two with offset phases; during macro shots they hold perfectly still.
Labels draw in (anchor dot, leader growing, text sliding 10 px) and fade out before the parts move again.
Never moves: the floor, the light rig's relation to the camera, the label column's x position.
camera_grammar: Slow push on one still part
sound_palette: Instruments: tuned mallets (marimba, vibraphone, glockenspiel, glass), a round bass, a short synthetic kick and small dry percussion. Precise and dry outside the object; sustained and airy inside it.

Foley is the material: hollow plastic clacks for keycaps or housings, a switch click with a low thock, dry taps for boards, inharmonic rings for small machined metal, a soft thud for the enclosure, airy swooshes for layers lifting and for camera dives, a fine
Every separation and every landing has its sound, panned to where the part is.
Silence: at least two near-silences (room tone only) before the big separations or the turn back; the first sound after each is the most important hit around it.
native_moves: The leader that lands on the part.
pitfalls_limits: Invented numbers. A size that no file gives. Fix: measure it from the CAD and say "measured" in the facts file, or leave it out.
Mixed-up revisions. Plates, cases and boards from different versions of a project. Fix: check hole positions and stack heights across the files (they must coincide), and pin the commit.
Panelised boards. Layout files may hold a panel with breakaway tabs. Fix: take the outline from a plate or case of the same revision, or flood-fill from an interior point.
Zero-length edges. Duplicate outline points give zero normals → NaN → black squares after bloom. Fix: clean outlines, repair zero normals, scan frames for one-frame black tiles.
Overshooting camera splines. Catmull-Rom over unevenly spaced keys flies past a macro stop. Fix: monotone interpolation per component.
Labels too short. Macro stops last about three seconds. Fix: one fact per label, opened before the camera settles; check with `readcheck`.
Over-bright light sweeps. Area lights blow plastics to white. Fix: sweeps at a fraction of the key, bloom threshold above the brightest diffuse surface.
Brand marks on parts. Chip tops and connector shells carry trademarks. Fix: plain package tops; drop logo footprints unless the product is the user's own.
styles.engine_section: All in `demo/src/` (three.js r170, the library's `core/three/post.js` and `core/lib.js`):

styles.name: Line-Art Cutaway
styles.official_demo_line: A phone loses signal when held by the corner; taken apart, its metal frame turns out to be the antenna, cut into pieces your hand can bridge.
styles.principles: A frame reads as this style when:
construction: Live line drawing from 3D. Each frame renders the scene twice into float targets: a grey value pass and a normal + linear depth pass. A full-screen shader traces edges, at 2× resolution, downsampled:

Stable lines in motion. 8 rotated-grid sub-pixel jitters per frame, accumulated, inside a very short shutter (about 0.12 frame). This removes crawling and flicker on hundreds of small parts without visible motion blur; a long shutter would draw ghost copies of
Values: surfaces are light greys (#FBFBF9 to #DCDCD8), dense parts (battery, chips) a dark grey, all lit by one soft directional term only to separate planes.

Sections: a clipping plane cuts the model; back faces show 45° screen-space hatching. A part made of a different material (plastic between metal) carries its own lighter hatch, so a cross-section reads as "metal | plastic | metal".

Diagrammatic people: a hand or tool that is not the subject is drawn one tier lighter: nearly paper-white flat fill, thinner grey outline, few inner lines, knuckles as fine segment lines, and it fades out of frame at the wrist (alpha falls off along the screen
World-anchored 2D: leaders, dimension lines, signal arcs and magnifier connectors are drawn in 2D but projected from 3D anchors every frame. Only subtitles and the end card sit in screen space.
colour_logic: Ground: warm white paper with a 40 px grid at about 4 % ink and small crosses every 200 px.
Ink: one near-black for outlines and titles, one graphite for secondary text and inner lines.

One accent only, reserved for the explained path: the traces, cable and clip that carry it, the part it ends in, the leaders and badges that point at it, the waves it sends out, and one key word in a title. If the film has two paths, they are the same path at
Never colour the background, panels or decoration. Large flat dark areas are avoided except where a real part is dark (a battery, a chip).
motion: 24 fps on ones, everything deterministic. The camera and parts move smoothly; nothing boils.

Explosion: layers lift one by one on the beat, fast start and a long settle with a tiny overshoot (about 2.5 %); assembly guides (dashed grey lines) grow while they lift. Closing reverses it, bottom first, each layer landing with a small click.
The accent travels along the path at a steady speed, with a slightly lighter head, then floods the end part outward from its feed point; turning it off drains it back the same way.
Labels and dimension lines draw in over 0.3–0.6 s; dimension lines grow from their middle, then arrowheads land, then the number.
Never moves: the paper grid, the subtitle plate, a label column's x position.
Frame rate and grain: no film grain (mux grain 0).
camera_grammar: Tip-over plus crane up while layers lift
Dive into a gap until a material fills the frame
Locked top-down with a magnifier inset
Pull back with a slow orbit
sound_palette: Score: tuned mallets and plucks — vibraphone (hard mallets for pulses, bowed for pads), glockenspiel, harp sweeps, pizzicato or jazz bass — plus a very quiet sixteenth-note "plotter tick". Clean, precise, never orchestral swells or drums.

Foley is generated from picture events and sounds like drafting and small mechanics: a narrow noise band sweeping with the section plane, light ticks when text writes, a ratchet when a ruler extends, soft whooshes when layers lift, a metallic click plus a low
Two near-silences per film (only a bowed pad or room tone) before the turn and before the solution; the first sound after each is one of the most important in the film.

Mix: narration compressed, then about 10 dB above music + foley by RMS; music yields 300 Hz–4 kHz; foley that would sit in the speech band (high hiss, sweeps) stays under the voice and swells only between sentences. Master at −14 LUFS, true peak ≤ −1 dB.
pitfalls_limits: Uniform line width makes the drawing look like a mesh preview. Keep the three tiers, and the lighter fourth tier for hands and tools.
Crawling and flickering small parts. Without sub-pixel accumulation, passives and holes shimmer. Use the jitter accumulation; with a long shutter it turns into ghost lines.
Coplanar touching parts draw no line (a plastic insert flush with metal). Recess one by a fraction of a millimetre or give it its own hatch.
A 2D anchor on a hidden part. A dot drawn on an occluded component floats on top of the part in front. Place the anchor on a visible face, or move the part.
Render targets cached at one size. An inset that grows (a magnifier opening) must use targets keyed by size, or it is upscaled from its first, tiny size and comes out blurred.
Accent creep. A second use of the accent (a title bar, a button) makes the path unreadable. Check every frame for accent outside the path.
Label pile-up. Labels that outlive their part's moment crowd the frame. A label leaves before the camera does.
Hands that read as dolls. Round capsules and a cylinder wrist look like toys. Taper the phalanges, mark the knuckles with fine lines, add nails, fade the wrist out.

styles.name: Color-Coded Mechanism
styles.official_demo_line: A watch with no battery is cut open: its three systems are dyed one by one, the train races when the escapement is pulled out, and one slowed tick lets it all out again.
styles.principles: - Colour is the structure. Every part takes the colour of the system it belongs to (energy source, transmission, control), everything else is one light neutral. A viewer reads the machine's organisation from the colours before reading a word. - Soft cel, own-colour outlines. Two-tone flat shading with no reflections; every part is ringed in a darker shade of its own colour, never in black. - The machine is true. Wheels turn by their tooth ratios, the oscillator swings at its real rate, numbers on screen are computed from the model. Slow motion is stated on screen. - Cut, explode, follow. The c
construction: Geometry is engineered, not sculpted: involute gears with real module and tooth counts, extruded profiles (wheels, bridges, levers), cylinders for arbors. No bevels (a bevel doubles the outline). Choose module and camera so one tooth pitch is ≥ 12 px at 1080p.

Soft cel shading (`cel()` in `demo/film.js`): lit faces are the flat colour, shade faces × 0.80 and slightly cool, a third tone for faces turned away. No environment map, no cast shadows between parts.

Outlines (`demo/film-outline.js`): a second pass of view normals and depth; an edge on the near side of a depth step or on a crease is drawn in the part's own colour × 0.52 mixed with 28 % ink. 2× supersampling; lines 1–1.3 px.

Section cuts: clipping planes through an axis; the back faces seen through the cut are shaded as the cut face, with 45° hatching computed where the view ray meets the cut plane, in world units (it never swims when the camera moves). Cut only the housing, never
Dye: colour arrives as a spherical front spreading from the point where energy enters a part (a mesh point, an arbor, an impulse pin), with a thin pale wet edge. Never a global crossfade.
One soft contact shadow under the base plate (a blurred silhouette, 20 % opacity), drawn in the colour pass only.
colour_logic: A warm off-white ground, flat, no gradient or vignette.
One light neutral for the frame, plates, bridges, housings and every part not being discussed.

Three system hues, mid-value and slightly greyed, always in the same roles: warm yellow = energy source, grey-green = transmission, grey-violet = control or measurement. In a different machine the roles carry over (battery / gearbox / governor; lens / shutter
One accent (a saturated red-orange), only for the protagonist part at its moment, and for the control that drives it. Never two accents.
motion: 24 fps on ones, smooth camera; no stepping.
Motion is driven by one master clock: a smooth speed curve (real time, a fraction of it, deep slow motion, stopped) whose integral moves everything. Speed changes never jump.
Ratios are exact: every wheel's angle comes from the driver through tooth counts; meshing stays meshed (a free-run must end on a whole number of teeth).
Stepped motion (an escapement, a ratchet, an indexing table): the stepped part advances inside a short impulse window; the oscillator is a sine through its centre at each beat.
Things appear by dye, cut, lift or draw-on; never by a fade-in of a whole object.
What never moves: the ground, the palette roles, the light direction.
camera_grammar: fast pull-back from a detail to the whole object
low tracking shot skimming over the parts
side view of an exploded stack
push-in to a contact point at slow speed
big pull-out to the whole object, cut still open
sound_palette: Foley from the mechanism: metal ticks built from three micro-clicks (unlock, impulse, drop) panned to the part; a thin metallic swish for a section cut; brass clacks for parts landing; a tooth-rate gear buzz that follows the speed curve; air for lifts.

Instruments: plucked and struck pitched percussion over a light bass (harp, marimba, glockenspiel, vibraphone, cello pizzicato); tremolo strings only for tension. A part taking its colour may sound one note, panned to it.
Grid: the mechanism's real beat sits on the music grid (e.g. a press at 120 strokes a minute = quarter notes at 120 bpm); slowed time keeps the tick on the grid.
Silence before the key mechanical event; the first sound after it is that event.
native_moves: Explode by system, remove one layer.
True slow motion of one contact.
pitfalls_limits: Outline flicker on fine teeth → keep tooth pitch ≥ 12 px, render at 2×, no bevels, do not spin fine teeth fast (≤ 45° per frame for a part with 4-fold symmetry; slow the time instead).
Wagon-wheel aliasing of fast oscillators → show them slowed and say so.
Rainbow parts → colour by system, never by part.
Plastic or metal look → no reflections, no transparency, no specular.
Labels everywhere at equal weight → one primary; the rest secondary or gone.
Labels on parts or under subtitles → pin to clear space with a leader; keep the subtitle corner empty.
A housing that moves through the parts (a case lifting through the movement) → move each piece the way it would come apart (dial up, case down).
Meshing that drifts after a free run → make the extra rotation a whole number of teeth.

styles.name: Instruction Manual Art
styles.official_demo_line: Two first-timers build a crib from a flat-pack manual, ten steps on one 45° page; step ten was never in the manual.
styles.principles: Rules (they define the style):
construction: Projection: world units in centimetres, y up; `makeView({cx, cy, s, az: 45, el: 35.264})` maps world → screen. A sphere always projects to a circle, so limbs, hands and cylinders are hulls of circles and stay right at any heading.

Painter's order by view depth. Long parts (rails, posts) are sorted by their nearest point; an assembly that interlocks is drawn in groups from back to front (far end and back rail → the board and what lies on it → front rail, near end, bolt heads), so large f
Fill, then outline, per part: overlapping parts are separated by a line, a part has no lines inside itself.
Paper: off-white stock with faint fibres that travel with the page on a pan and keep their size on a zoom (printed stock, not a photo of it).
Line weight is set in screen pixels (2.6 px at 1080p) and follows the zoom only partly (about z^0.55, clamped), so the whole page stays crisp when pulled back and lines don't go clumsy close up.
Appearing (reference): a drawing first shows its complete line art with paper-coloured fills, then its colours come in over it. A part is never drawn half-built or floating.
motion: Parts fly along dotted guide lines in straight paths, ease in, and stop with a small settle; a beat of stillness after each one lands.
Arrow first, motion second: the arrow is drawn, then the part follows it once and holds.
The new part's yellow fades to white once it is fitted.
People move between a few key poses with eased interpolation; walking is short shuffled steps when carrying.
Never moves: the angle, the page, the step numbers' positions.
Frame rate and grain: 30 fps (parts glide along their guides without stepping); mux grain 1, since the paper fibres carry the texture.
camera_grammar: Push into a parts box / object
Pan or whip along the page to the next step
Tilt to the next row, the step number entering first
Locked frame on a do/don't box
Push through a shape (the ✓ cell, a magnifier circle)
Shape-matched cut (a bolt head → a round knob)
Pull back to the whole page
sound_palette: A small tidy ensemble that counts steps: pizzicato strings, marimba, glockenspiel, felt piano; one bright note per part landing, rising through the chord.
Paper and flat-pack foley: a carton set down, a lid, wood knocking, a pencil, paper sliding, bolts, a ratchet, the click, a rubber stamp for ✗ and ✓.
A mistake stops the music dead before the ✗; the ending is near silence, then a single chime.
Voice (optional): a calm, dry narrator, as if the manual itself were speaking; few words, never reading out the numbers on the page.
pitfalls_limits: The assembly must be one model with a state table. Every picture of the object (every step, the parts list, the final page) is drawn from the same function with a state; write the table first (step → what is added → what the object has when the step ends → par

Footprints and guide lines come from the same geometry. A dotted footprint must be the finished object's real corners; a guide line runs from where the part lies to where it lands. Parts in a box lie flat, stacked at real sizes, and the box is empty only after
Knees bend with the body, not the world. Set the knee hint from the body's heading, or a pose that is right facing one way breaks when the figure turns.

Kneeling hip height comes from leg length: knee on the floor + one thigh length. A half-kneel: the kneeling knee under the hip, thigh vertical, shin and instep flat behind; the other foot flat, knee about 90°, shin vertical.
The far leg is one shade darker than the near leg, so crossed or overlapping legs never merge into one shape.
Sitting on the floor: cross-legged with the knees open and low and the shins crossed in front reads as sitting; a pelvis on the floor with legs straight forward reads as falling over.
Standing: weight on one leg, the other relaxed and turned out, hips and shoulders tilted against each other. Feet together and arms hanging make figurines.

Placement: never put a person between the viewer and what the step is about, and keep their feet outside the object's footprint. Behind slatted furniture their legs show between the bars and they read as standing inside it: put them at a front corner, or at on

styles.name: Pen Plotter
styles.official_demo_line: At night under a desk lamp, a pen plotter draws Mount Qomolangma from real elevation data with four pens, and writes its height last.
styles.principles: - Every mark is a stroke. Nothing appears that a pen could not have drawn: no fills, no gradients, no type set as a font. Tone is hatching; weight is a wider nib or the same stroke traced twice; letters are single-line strokes or traced outlines. - The machine is in the shot. Gantry, carriage, pen holder and pen rack are physical objects with weight; the pen is where the line ends. - Machine time is honest. Pens move at plotter speed with acceleration and braking, drop and lift, and go to the rack to change. Time is saved by editing and by the camera, never by a pen that flies. - Information d
construction: Strokes are data. Every mark is a polyline in sheet millimetres, in plotting order, tagged with its pen. A program turns the list into machine time: pen-up travel, drop, ink, lift, pen changes. One function gives the pen's position and how much ink is down at

Kinematics: trapezoidal velocity per move. Reference values: pen-down ≈ 60–125 mm/s, pen-up ≈ 200–300 mm/s, acceleration ≈ 1000–2500 mm/s²; drop and lift ≈ 0.07–0.1 s; a pen change ≈ 2–4 s (travel to the rack, lower, release, move one stall, lower, grip, raise

Paper: a canvas texture of the whole sheet (≈ 10 px/mm) plus high-resolution patches (20–40 px/mm) only where the camera is close; ink drawn with multiply blending, round caps; a slightly wetter dot where a pen lands; paper grain and a few fibres as a bump map
Ink: semi-opaque, never pure black; light inks (grey) at 0.6–0.75 opacity; strokes traced twice read darker, as on paper.

Machine: rails, a moving beam, carriage, Z holder with a gripper, drag chain, a rack of capped stalls; metals with roughness 0.15–0.35, matte plastics, clearcoat pen barrels colour-coded to their ink. Cast shadows from one lamp are part of the look.

Lettering: a single-line font (one stroke per subpath) for Latin and figures; CJK as the outline of a hairline-weight font drawn with a pen wider than the stroke, so it reads as single-line; display titles as outlines filled with fine hatching.
colour_logic: Neutral ground: cream paper (≈ #F1ECDF) under a warm lamp; the room falls to near-black with one cool counter-light (a window).

One ink per job, three to four inks at most: a dark ink for the frame and text, a terrain or data ink, a light ink for tone and grids, and one accent reserved for the finding (the path, the answer, the circle around the result).
The accent appears late and on purpose; it never fills an area except by hatching.
Pen barrels carry their ink colour, so a pen change reads at a glance.
motion: 30 fps, no stepping; the pen eases into and out of every move; the carriage never teleports inside a shot.

Jump-cut time-lapse: inside a stretch the pen moves at real speed; between stretches machine time jumps forward, on the beat. The camera keeps moving through the jumps; only the machine jumps. Space the jumps closer as the work grows.
Lines appear only under the nib; labels appear stroke by stroke; nothing fades in.
What never moves: the sheet (taped down), the rack, the room.
camera_grammar: Macro on the nib, paper fibre in focus
Locked three-quarter on a panel, slight creep
Pull-back from the sheet to the desk and room
sound_palette: The machine is the rhythm: stepper whine whose pitch follows pen speed, pen-on-paper scratch while the pen is down, the tick of a drop, a servo buzz on lifts, the solenoid clack of the gripper at the rack, a drag chain's rattle.

One instrument per pen (an option worth keeping): tuned percussion for the first ink (marimba), bowed and struck metal for tone (vibraphone, strings), bells and harp for the accent (glockenspiel), plucked strings for the text pen.
Jumps can carry a soft woodblock on the beat.
Room: mains hum, the night outside, almost nothing else. Silence before a verdict: music out, the room and an off-screen pen change stay.
native_moves: The path in the accent ink.
The hero number in single line
pitfalls_limits: Flying pens. Speeding the plot to fit the film reads as animation. Keep real speed and jump between stretches; a full sheet can take an hour of machine time.
The carriage hides the work. It sits above the line being drawn; frame from the open side, hold until it leaves, or show the result from a different shot.
Beam shadows. One lamp casts the beam's shadow as a hard bar; place the lamp on the camera's side of the beam for reading shots.
Thin lines vanish in wide shots (mipmapping). Use darker inks, retrace key lines, keep wide shots for shapes, close shots for text.
Fat lines in 3D. World-unit line widths grow huge near the lens; use screen-space widths for lifted strokes.
Fonts that are fills. Outline fonts drawn as outlines look like stencils; use single-line fonts, or hairline weights narrower than the pen.
Made-up data on a "real" map. If a sheet looks like a survey, its data must be real (DEM, published figures) and its sources in FACTS/SOURCES; mark approximations on the sheet.
Partial redraw cost. Big canvases must be drawn incrementally and reset only when time runs backward.

styles.name: Assembly-Line Diagram
styles.official_demo_line: A body cut open as a factory that runs backwards: a 12:30 sandwich is taken apart station by station, and six hours later it runs for the bus.
styles.principles: - One line, one direction. The subject is a process that turns one thing into another in steps. The film is a single continuous production line the cargo travels; every shot is a station on it, in order. - Metaphor per station, said straight. Each step is one machine everyone can read (a press, a sieve, a weighing scale, a crane, a loading dock, a paint booth). The plaque gives both names: the machine's in English, the real thing's in Chinese (`SIEVE | 沉砂池`). The humour comes from the metaphor being literal, never from cartoon faces. - Colour is the legend. Each kind of output gets one spot co
construction: All vector, drawn in code: SVG built per frame from shapes and paths. Clean ink outlines with round caps and joins, flat fills, no gradients.

Print, lightly. Every colour plate is shifted by its own 1–1.6 px misregistration, the same direction across the frame (ink, paper and walls stay put), and a faint paper grain and fibre sit on top (multiply). Nothing more: no aging, no torn edges, no yellow st
Flat shadows. A Holmes shadow is the same shape offset down-right in one pale flat colour (plaques 5–6 px, large shapes 14–18 px). No soft shadows, no blur except motion blur on whip moves.

The cut-away. The silhouette is a dark ground with a thick body wall (a band about 56 px thick with ink on both sides); where goods enter (an intake, a hatch, a door) the wall breaks and both ends get an ink cap. Rooms have a coloured frame, a pale wall and a

Pipes: ink edge (width + 6 px), colour, then a highlight stripe (0.2 × width, offset up-left, masked inside the pipe); rounded elbows; flanges every so often. Width encodes importance (main duct, arteries, branches).

One printed sheet at every distance. Line weight follows the camera (thinner when pulling back, roughly `z^-0.6`; only slightly heavier when pushing in), and below a set scale small workers, plaques and small text are not drawn while the big machines stay. The
colour_logic: Paper + ink + one ground + four spot colours. Paper outside the silhouette; one dark ground inside the cut; pale walls for rooms; a body colour for walls and slabs; then three or four spot colours that are the legend. No other hues.

Spot colours have one meaning each for the whole film (in a recycling plant, say: ochre = paper, vermilion = plastic, teal = glass). Room frames may rotate through the spot colours by station; the cargo's own colours stay fixed.

Ground dark enough to frame, never black: a deep indigo or wine reads as "inside" and lets the spot colours sit on it. Check that every spot colour separates from the ground (cobalt on indigo does not).
Numbered station circles are one colour (ochre fill, ink edge); a circle is an outline until its station is reached, then fills.
motion: The belt never stops moving; cargo travels at constant speed and eases into stations.

A station starts on arrival. Its machine starts on the beat the cargo lands (rollers turn, sprays fall, a press stamps), its worker does a two-frame action, its number circle fills and pops (scale 0.9 → 1 with overshoot).
Signs drop on chains and bounce once; a second-language sign swings in half a beat later.
Repetition is the joke. A gatekeeper raises STOP, lets one portion through, raises STOP again; machines repeat their cycle on the music's grid.
Time compresses on clocks and dials: hands spin, lamps dim, workers doze; never a title card saying "later".

Big figures move by procedure, grounded: a running figure plants its support foot on the ground line and moves with the ground, knees solved from two bones and always bending forward; nothing slides, floats or crosses scissor-wise on a held frame.
camera_grammar: Tilt down a chute, slabs wiping past
Pull back from a part to the whole floor
sound_palette: Score as a production line: a march on a fixed figure (around 120 BPM) that the stations add to; each line or machine brings in its own voice (bassoon, clarinet, flute…); woodblock and bass drum on presses and stamps; glockenspiel or celesta when a station lig
The stop is a sound: when a gate closes or an alarm goes, the whole band stops dead and restarts on the next release.

Foley from machines on every visible action: hoppers, chains, sign bounce, roller shutters, presses, sprays, drums, whistles, ladles, clocks, alarm bells, ignition, doors. Procedural, short, on the frame.

Voice (optional): a calm explainer, one idea per line, saying what the picture cannot (the reversal, what a part becomes, why it waits); leave arrivals, the big lighting-up and the end card without words. Compress it and set it about 9–10 dB over the music, ca
pitfalls_limits: Process diagram, not a story. A station-by-station walk is a flowchart. Give it a hook (a reversal, a deadline, a question) and a payoff picture; let each station say one thing.
Text creep. Plaques, tags, leaders and subtitles add up fast; keep to about seven pieces per frame and let colours carry meaning.
Hairlines and blobs at distance. Without camera-dependent line weight and level of detail, the pull-back turns into a grey mesh of strokes and unreadable labels.
The silhouette disappears when rooms fill the cut edge to edge: keep at least 30 px of dark ground between rooms and the outer wall.
Spot colours that vanish on the ground. Test each against the dark ground and against the walls before committing.

Bodies that look like barrels. When a figure has to hold a lot of rooms, its torso grows and its head shrinks; cross-fade to a schematic figure with human proportions for the full-body shot rather than inflating the cut-away.
Feet. Procedural legs that swing on sine curves float, sink and slide; solve them against the ground line, and hold the final frame on a readable phase (one leg reaching, not crossed).

Metaphors that lie. Every simplification the metaphor makes (one input → one output, a valve where there is really a gradient) goes into FACTS.md; the voice should not claim what the drawing only implies.

styles.name: Comic History Cartoon
styles.official_demo_line: Alsace-Lorraine changed hands four times between 1871 and 1945: each time someone tore off the paper and pasted a new piece, and the woman living on it never moved.
styles.principles: - Every change of territory is a paper action. Land changes hands by being cut, slapped down, torn off, pressed flat, peeled at a corner, or covered with another layer. A country is never simply recoloured. - The map is printed matter. An old engraved map on paper (coast ripples, graticule, ink borders, flat printed fills, small-caps names), not a map standing in a room and not a vector infographic. - Countries are people made of paper. Puppets cut from card, joined with brass split pins, with oversized round heads and swapped expression heads. They personify a country or a side, never a real
construction: Printed map (rule): equirectangular projection with longitude compressed by cos(centre latitude); about six engraved ripple lines outside each coast; dashed graticule; thin ink borders; flat fills with a lighter rim about 20 % wide inside each shape, as if the

Borders: Natural Earth for modern lines, except where China is in frame (DIRECTOR.md §13); historical borders are pieced from modern ones and hand-traced where the difference shows in frame. Name the error margin in the credits.

Puppets (rule): green-screen part sheets keyed and cut into parts; each part gets a cream card edge (dilated a few px) so it reads as cut paper. Parts rotate about their pins (2D forward kinematics); arms reach targets with two-bone IK. Small part-on-part shad

Paper patches: opaque card with a dashed line printed inside the edge and a thin cream rim; torn edges are jagged with white fibres; a peeled corner is a fold transform with the back of the paper showing.
Height is shadow (rule): a patch held in the air throws a large soft shadow offset 30–45 px; once down it keeps only a 3–4 px paper-edge shadow.

The page: panels drawn into their own canvases at 1:1 so a panel pushed to full screen stays sharp; ink panel frames, cream gutters, a warm grey textured table that only shows when the camera pulls back.
colour_logic: Two protagonists, two colours, kept for the whole film (for example a printed blue and a printed grey). Neighbours are low-saturation print colours (sand, sage, brick, ochre) and never compete.
A new patch is one step away from the printed colour of its owner (lighter or deeper), so it reads as another piece of paper laid on the print.
Ink is one warm near-black for all type and lines; paper is a warm cream. One accent red is reserved for scissors handles and the Chinese line in speech bubbles.
A serious panel drops saturation and value (darker, colder) instead of adding new colours.
motion: Puppets on twos (12 poses a second); camera and shadows move every frame.

Keyframes with spring overshoot: hop (legs swing, squat on landing), wind-up (lean back, tremble), strike (lunge, every joint rebounds), settle (arms crossed with overshoot). A head swap pops the head 1.07–1.10× for a frame or two.
One in-between drawing carries a big strike: the pose at the top holds and trembles, then a single frame with ink motion arcs lands it.
Impact spreads: the camera shakes, paper scraps fly, ink lines burst, the other puppet's hat jumps off and lands back.
Emotions are paper: jagged-edged card bubbles for shouts, two paper clouds of steam for anger.
camera_grammar: Pull back to the whole page
Lateral slide into the next panel
Whip across a gutter with speed lines
Tilt down and push in until the map becomes a tabletop
sound_palette: Accents per side: each country gets one instrument family (e.g. tuba and trombone oom-pah, accordion), so the audience hears who is winning. Xylophone steps for hops and snips, a music-box glockenspiel for a civilian moment, low strings and slow timpani for th

Paper foley: slaps (a high crack, the paper body, a low thump), scissors (two metal clicks and a short ring), rubbing paper flat, tearing, crumpling, tape, a slide whistle for a flying hat, small clicks of the pins.
A near-silence (a thin tremolo) before the biggest slap; the music can stop dead on a stamp.

Voice: a dry, slightly amused narrator. Compress it and set it about 10 dB over the music; while it speaks, the music and foley dip about 3 dB and the music's 300 Hz–4 kHz band another 6–7 dB. Master at −14 LUFS, true peak ≤ −1 dB.
pitfalls_limits: Recolouring a country without a paper action: the style disappears.
A new patch in exactly the printed colour of its owner: once it moves it reads as a white outline only.
Outlines, glows or drop shadows on type; old-style figures in years; system fonts.
Two speech bubbles on screen at once, bubbles over place names, tails pointing at hats instead of mouths.
Characters' feet, names or the scale bar in the caption band.
Smooth on-ones puppet motion or ease curves with no overshoot: it reads as software, not paper.
Comic sound effects or slapstick on war deaths, massacres or persecution; those panels go darker and quieter.
Real flags with political symbols, Nazi symbols, real people's likenesses. Uniforms personify a country; say in the narration who the actual party was when the costume simplifies it.
styles.engine_section: - The part sheets come from an image generator, one set per film, and the user provides it: their Codex CLI through `core/image/gen_image.py` (`--check` first), or another image API or app, where they make the sheets from your prompts and save them under your file names. With neither, a film in this style cannot start: say so in the brief (core/README.md, "Image generation"); never draw stand-in puppets in code. Before generating, ask the user whether they have their own character designs; if not, tell them how many sheets and for whom (one per puppet), then generate them for the user's own si

styles.name: Microgame Frenzy
styles.official_demo_line: A clumsy cadet survives a five-second boot camp, faster and faster, until the boss: landing home.
styles.principles: - A microgame = a shouted command word + 2.5–4 s + one action + one result (success, or a funny failure). - Each microgame uses a different visual medium (crayon, ink wash, terminal, risograph, pixel, blueprint, Swiss type, clay, cut paper, woodcut…). The jolt of each switch is both the joke and the beat. - One fixed home look holds the film together: a show stage with a host, a lives counter and a stage number, which the film returns to between games. - It keeps accelerating: every few games tempo, game length, dwell, command hold and animation frame rate step up together. - The hero survives
construction: Home stage: flat toon, thick near-black outline (~7 px), flat fills, one hard-edged shadow (fill in the shade colour, clip to the shape, refill shifted up-left). Fixed furniture: a frame-within-the-frame where games play (a TV, an arcade cabinet, a phone, a wi
Each medium is a simplified re-drawing, 100–200 lines of code, built around one channel trick that makes it read at a glance:
drawn media store pressure or wetness in a channel (crayon: alpha = pressure against paper tooth; ink: wet and dry ink channels);
print media store plate densities (riso: a channel per plate, additive overprint, halftone, misregistration);
screen media are low-res buffers scaled up (pixel: indexed buffer, auto outline, dither; terminal: hand-authored glyph art, phosphor shader);
technical media are line systems (blueprint: line weights and dimensions; Swiss: a strict grid, one sans, one signal colour).
colour_logic: The home stage owns a saturated party palette: a deep ground behind a rotating sunburst, two or three loud accents, plus a fixed success colour and a fixed fail colour used by stamps and the lives board only.

Each medium brings its own palette from its tradition (wax colours, one-ink-plus-vermilion, amber phosphor, three riso plates, a limited pixel palette, white-on-blue, black-white-red). Never tint a medium with the home palette.

One accent follows the hero across media where the medium allows (a single vermilion dot in ink, an inverse glyph in a terminal, a signal-red circle in Swiss type): it is how the eye finds the hero after a switch.
Example home palettes: violet `#2a0f5c` with magenta `#ff2e88`, gold `#ffc928`, cyan `#1fd1d1`; teal ground with coral and lemon; black stage with hot orange and electric blue.
motion: The frame rate is part of the ladder: characters step on twos or at 8 fps early, faster later, on ones at the climax. Camera moves, transitions and the timer spark always run on ones.
Five things accelerate together at each speed-up: tempo, game length, stage dwell, command hold, character frame rate.
The timer is visible and on the beat: e.g. a fuse with one knot per beat, the spark passing each knot exactly on it. It freezes in a replay.
Unified transition through the frame-within-the-frame: push into the screen to start a game (~0.25 s), shrink the game back into it to return (~0.33 s) with a ✓ / ✗ stamp. No fades, no blank frames.
Failure is performed: the action overshoots, splats, bonks or rolls off; the medium's own physics makes the joke.
Instant replay for a failure that must be understood: freeze, half speed, push-in, letterbox, a caption in the medium's type.
camera_grammar: Start inside a game, command already slamming
Pull back out of the game screen
Slot reels (the stage splits into spinning strips of earlier frames, stopping one per beat)
Extreme insert on the trigger prop
Lights cut to one top spot, frame unchanged
Tile flip (last frames of past games flip into pieces of a new frame)
Snap back to wide on one beat
Split screen, two media side by side
sound_palette: Music first: a tempo grid and a cue table before any animation; every picture hit lands on a listed cue.

A constant groove + one colour instrument per medium. The groove (kit with ghost notes, slap or synth bass, brass stabs, keys) runs throughout; each medium adds its own timbre: toy piano for crayon, shakuhachi or guqin for ink, square beeps for terminals, vibe

Foley follows the medium: wax squeaks, wet splats, teletype relays, paper crunch, bit-crushed noise, ratchets and stamps, hollow bonks. Home stage: a spring trigger click, glass crack for a lost life, card flips, a reel whirr, sparse claps.

Acceleration options (use what fits): a rising brass run into each speed-up; the key rising a step per round; halving note values instead of changing tempo; dropping the groove to a heartbeat on the last life.
pitfalls_limits: A luminance-ramp ASCII figure is mush → hand-authored glyph art with structural glyphs, an inverse glyph for the accent.
Ink shapes read as smoke unless their silhouette is designed (a short round blot phase, then a clear structure with seams and light edges).
A failure at high tempo goes unread → make the action overshoot and hit something, or give it an instant replay.
Alpha-coverage media show the background through gaps → a full-pressure base where it must be solid.
Drawing helpers with a global context draw on the wrong canvas when scenes render into offscreen buffers (game screen, reels, tiles) → set and restore the context.
Command tags pile up → secondary commands fly out.
A 100 % white flash reads as a blank frame → cap at ~60 %.

TTS single-word commands gain a vowel tail ("Pump!" → "Pompey") → generate a two-word phrase and cut after the first word using ASR timestamps; verify each clip, since ASR mishears 0.2 s words in a dense mix.
styles.engine_section: `demo/timeline.js` (tempo grid and segments, the single source of truth), `demo/toon.js` + `demo/stage.js` + `demo/hud.js` (home look, stage, timer, command word, stamps, lives, subtitle cards; call `setCtx` when drawing offscreen), `demo/chars.js` (host and hero rigs), `demo/glpass.js` (WebGL2 material shaders: riso, crayon, CRT, ink, blueprint paper), one `demo/g_<medium>.js` per medium (`sceneX(g, lt)` + the hero translation), `demo/film.js` (transitions through the TV, slot reels, tiles, events). Module map and build: [DEMO.md](DEMO.md#build-notes).

styles.name: Rhythm Game Show
styles.official_demo_line: The history of AI as a rhythm game: models take the stage on the beat, and a report card closes the show.
styles.principles: - Everything is on the grid. One fixed, fast tempo. Every pop, drop, stamp, typed character and camera punch sits at a (bar, beat) and is also a sound event; the score is generated from the picture's own timeline, so they can't drift. - One drawing kit, many sets. Flat fills, one heavy ink outline, round caps, hard offset shadows; each round gets a new saturated background colour and pattern. - Characters are toys. One body construction for the whole cast, told apart by colour, a belly patch, one head accessory and a name tag. They hop on the beat, squash on hits, throw arms up on a shout. - A
construction: Vector only, SVG or canvas paths at 1920×1080: flat fills, one outline colour (near-black), 8 px outlines on characters and props, 5–7 px on small parts, round joins and caps.

No gradients, no blur, no texture, no soft shadow. Depth is a hard offset shadow: the same shape in outline colour shifted ~10 px (stickers, banners) to ~14 px (cards), then the coloured shape on top.

Sets = one saturated background + a same-hue pattern one step lighter: diagonal stripes (often scrolling slowly), offset polka dots (~20 % white), or a rotating sunburst. A darker floor band with an ink line on top grounds the characters.

Characters: a rounded bean body, stubby arms with mitten hands, oval eyes with a catch-light, a mouth that swaps to an open one. Humans share the construction; older machines or eras read through a boxier silhouette.
UI kit: round card, corner sticker banner, judgement word, burst (star + ring + speed lines), scoreboards.
`render(t)` is a pure function of `t`: every element's state is recomputed from `t`, never carried over from the previous frame.
colour_logic: Ink + paper + candy. Near-black ink, white, and a warm cream for cards and paper props; around eight saturated candy hues (yellow, orange, red, pink, green, lime, sky, blue) plus two or three deep hues with darker partners for night or finale sets.
One set = one hue. The background, its pattern and the round card share a hue; the card changes colour to match the set it introduces. Neighbouring rounds never share a hue.
Characters own colours. A contestant's body colour is its identity and never changes; keep it distinct from the set it stands on (a character is never the same hue as the background).
Big words are white or yellow with a thick ink stroke; judgement words may be pink or yellow.
motion: Idle = hop on the beat: a parabola per beat (8–30 px); neighbours hop on the off-beat so a crowd ripples.
Hit = squash: a damped wobble (~30 rad/s, ~0.35 s) after each hit; a small squash on every downbeat.
Entrances drop from the sky with ease-in and land exactly on their beat, so the sound lands with them. Crowds drop in one per beat or half-beat.
Pops use back-ease for anything appearing (cards, stickers, stamps, words); ease-in for exits. Nothing fades in slowly: things are either on or popping.
Shout pose: arms up + open mouth for about half a beat.
Typewriter reveals on fractions of a beat, with a click every few characters.
camera_grammar: Beat punch (zoom 0.8–5 % around centre, decays in ~0.16 s)
Hard cut on the bar line + flash
Shrink to thumbnail (a finished bit scales down into a slot)
Vertical scroll of the set (floor to sky)
Snap zoom onto one prop (hard cut to a 2× framing, back on the next bar)
sound_palette: All synthesized from the picture's events: a sine kick with soft saturation, band-passed noise snare and clap, hats, slap bass, detuned-saw brass stabs with a closing filter, square lead with vibrato, marimba-like pluck, music-box bell, triangle pad, square ar
A bright major pop harmony on a short chord loop, one chord per bar; each round gets its own flavour (funk, quiz, electro, dream, heavy…), not a new song.
Event foley is toy-like and pitched: pops, plop + boing landings, stamps, typewriter clicks, buzzers, dings, servo whirs, splats; pitched pips can spell a melody as a crowd drops in.

Shouts, not sentences: one- to three-word calls ("Hey!", a number, a verdict), placed 20–30 ms before the beat so the consonant lands on it. A crowd shout = several different voices stacked a few ms apart and panned across the stereo field.
pitfalls_limits: Stateful updates break parallel renders: a worker starting cold shows the initial state. Recompute every pose from `t`; compare single stills with a sequential render.
Cue lists drift when cut flashes, jingles and arrangement are separate hand lists: derive them from one table.
Fixed-length audio buffers cut the tail: size them from the duration.
Text measured before fonts load overflows plates: load fonts, then build.
TTS misreads digits and symbols in shouts: spell them out.
Real products as characters: names on tags, original mascots, no logos or UI; real people only as generic stand-ins.
styles.engine_section: `demo/frame_head.html` (SVG helpers: `el`, `txt`, `tf`, `op`, easing `E`, per-glyph `chars`/`charsPop`, `measure`), `demo/main_v1.js` (tempo grid `at(bar, beat)`, `ev()` sound events, `punch()`, `hopY`/`hitSq`, `gtext` telops, `stripes`/`dots`/`raysEl` sets, `burst`, `judge`, `banner`), `demo/main_b.js` (`bean()` characters + `pose()`, `human()`, `scene(t0, t1, build)`, `card()`, `dropY`, `heyAt`), `demo/music.py` + `demo/synth_lib.py` (event-driven score and SFX). The contract: `scene()` builds nodes once and returns `update(t)`, which only sets attributes. Module table and a minimal new roun

styles.name: CRT ASCII Terminal
styles.official_demo_line: A moon-base AI wakes after forty years to a signal from Earth, and replies by drawing “home” in characters.
styles.principles: A single monochrome terminal screen: P3 amber (or P1 green) phosphor glowing on dark glass, curved at the edges, with scanlines. Every image, including title, landscape, face, room and subtitles, is made of real glyphs placed on a character grid and chosen by ink density. The film has one camera, the screen itself. It moves only by changing the font size of the grid: bigger characters push in, smaller characters pull out.
construction: Font: one monospace bitmap-style font (VT323, OFL); cell 0.4 em × 0.8 em (1:2). A large prerendered glyph atlas with a stroke for beam spread, scaled with `drawImage`, keeps zooms continuous and sharp.
Grids: column count per shot (title ~20, terminal 80, picture 200+); a push-in can go until one cell holds a sub-grid of its own.

Density ramp: each glyph's measured ink coverage × dim / normal / bold → about 20 levels, near-duplicates dropped; a small ordered-plus-hash dither per cell; cells below a threshold stay blank. Negative space makes ASCII art readable.

Picture pipeline: paint grayscale into an offscreen "negative" aligned exactly to the grid (several samples per cell; channels for phosphor, second colour, a flag), average per cell, pick a glyph. Interiors get local contrast (`m + 0.9·(m − mean)`) to keep out

Recognisable subjects: silhouettes, not noise (real coastline polygons, a face from a few planes); dark = sparse dim glyphs, bright = dense bold, shadow sides sparse `.` only; an angle with a clear silhouette.
Depth on a grid: far = darker and sparser, near = brighter and denser; a thin bright rim separates planes.
colour_logic: One phosphor carries everything: amber, green or white, in its own brightness ramp. No second hue for decoration.
At most one soft second colour, used for one thing only (the emotional object), switched on at a single moment, on a downbeat, and never taken back casually.
Examples: amber screen with an ice blue-white for something far away; green screen with a warm pink for a living thing; white P4 screen with a pale gold for a memory.
Brightness is the only other tool: dim / normal / bold and inverse video.
motion: Characters never move off-grid, except in a declared transformation moment. Typing, scrolling and counters jump from cell to cell. A roller flips digits discretely, fast then slowing.
Only three things move continuously: grid scale (the camera), CRT physics, and particles in a transformation.
Typing speed is performance: machine output is even and fast (~10–40 ms/char); dramatic lines slow to note values of the score; human typing is hand-timed, uneven, with pauses and bursts.
Particles spawn from random points inside source glyphs, start small, fade in, ease to their cell, and flash briefly on landing, so they never stack into bright bars.

Push to a character: hold where the whole glyph reads, then push until its inner text reads; inner text full brightness, outside text a few percent, neighbours dimmed, so the shape reads before the text.
camera_grammar: Text becomes image (grid shrinks as glyphs fall)
Pull back off the glass into a drawn room
sound_palette: Music: an original analog-synth score, rendered in code (numpy / numba): PolyBLEP saw and square oscillators, a resonant 4-pole ladder filter with moving cutoff, filter envelopes, square-wave sequencers, slow tape wow (± a few cents), long reverb on pads, gate

Technique options: grow a single arpeggio as an image forms; hold the only major chord for one moment; drop everything, reverb tails included, to digital zero on a shock; open a chord on the colour change.
Silence is the main instrument: room tone alone under typing and blinking cursors; a short near-silence before a transformation.

Foley (all synthesised): relay click and degauss hum (mains hum plus harmonics with a thump); buckling-spring keys (plastic click, spring ping, key-cap thock; duller space bar, heavier Enter); teletype ticks for remote text; modem and phone-line tones (answer
native_moves: The picture is made of words.
pitfalls_limits: Inverse video: `destination-out` only changes alpha, which the upload ignores → opaque black canvas, cut letters with a *black* atlas.
Negative not aligned to the grid drifts across hundreds of columns → map with cell width / samples exactly.
Wrong cell centre: cells are 2·cw tall, so the centre is `(j + .5)·2cw`, not `(j + 1)·cw`.
Every dark pixel becomes a character (`-+-+` walls) → threshold, gamma ≈ 1.25, local contrast.
Noise-textured subjects read as textured blobs → silhouettes, a dark sparse background, a dot-only shadow side.
Particles from letter centres stack into bars → random points inside the glyph, small, faded in.
Stroked atlas glyphs close their counters (`M`, `B`) → sample a thin fill-only glyph bitmap for masks.
Lazily built data never reaches the exporter → build particle schedules and their sound events before `window.EV` is exported.
styles.engine_section: In `demo/`: `term.js` (glyph atlas, grid drawing, density ramps, image → cells), `art.js` (procedural grayscale scenes for the negative), `crt.js` (monochrome phosphor CRT post, WebGL2), `main.js` (timeline, events `EV`, subtitles `SUBS`), `voice_fx.py` (machine-voice processing), `mix.py` (synthesised foley + ducking), `music/score.py` (analog-synth score), `tools/subs.mjs` (export `window.SUBS`). File map and commands: [DEMO.md](DEMO.md#build-notes).

styles.name: 1920s Silent Film
styles.official_demo_line: A baker's boy chases a runaway loaf downhill, then breaks it in half for a hungry girl.
styles.principles: A one-reel film as it would look *projected*: - A 4:3 print in a gate between theatre curtains; the sides of the 16:9 frame are the picture house. - An ink drawing with washed greys and hatching, printed on silver stock that flickers, weaves, scratches and burns at the edges. - Nobody speaks. Beats are told by action in wide shots and by intertitle cards. - The only sound is a cinema instrument (piano, organ) and the projector in the booth.
construction: Tonal painting + Redraw. Scenes are painted in grey values only (print densities roughly: ink 0.07, dark cloth 0.15–0.3, mid wood 0.45–0.6, skin 0.8, white linen 0.9–0.95), with soft light gradients and a thin separation line. A Redraw pass (WebGL2) inks the w

Print pass: silver tone with a sepia amount between ~0.1 and ~0.36, print black ~0.055 and white ~0.93, S-curve, halation on highlights, uneven density, flicker, gate weave with occasional perforation jumps, broken vertical scratches (white = scraped emulsion,
Frame: 1440×1080 in the centre of 1920×1080, a rounded aperture with a soft dark rim; velvet drapes at the sides lit by the screen's spill and by footlights. Curtains can part and close.

Figures: realistic proportions (7.5-head adults, ~5-head children) on a 2.5D rig (joints solved in 3D, projected with a yaw), silent-era make-up (pale skin, dark lids and lips); identity by silhouette marks (a hat, a garment, a tool).
colour_logic: Monochrome silver, tinted only by the print: colder and harsher (more damage, less sepia) when things go wrong, warmer and cleaner when the film turns tender. Tint and damage are mood controls, set per section.
Values carry everything: dark clothes against pale walls, pale faces against dark interiors; check every shot as a thumbnail.

One colour, at most: an element drawn into a separate colour mask keeps its hue through the print (still getting grain, flicker, vignette). Use it for the single thing the film is about, or not at all.
Period tinting of whole scenes (amber for day interiors, blue for night, rose for romance) is a valid alternative to sepia; one tint per section.
motion: Hand-cranked sampling: character and camera motion sampled at 16 fps (18 or more to undercrank a fast scene); flicker, weave, grain and scratches change every output frame (24 fps). That mix makes it look projected rather than merely low-frame-rate.
Speed is an emotion: undercrank chases and panic (faster motion, faster flicker); return to 16 fps and a calmer print for tender scenes.

Deadpan performance: the face barely changes; the body acts (crouch before effort, held poses, the two-frame snap of a double take, hands on knees). Objects act too (a wobble before a fall, a ritardando to rest).
Keyframed, eased poses; only deliberate gags snap.
sound_palette: The instrument is the sound design, as in a picture house: an upright piano (optionally a reed organ, theatre organ, violin or small ensemble) plays every event. Mickey-mousing vocabulary (options): chromatic creep in the bass (sneaking), grace note (a wink),
Photoplay idiom: stride left hand, music by mood section in the manner of cue sheets (Hurry, Misterioso, Agitato, Tenderly, Maestoso), a theme that returns changed. Original music only.
No foley, no voice. The projector is the ambience: lamp click, motor spin-up, claw-and-motor purr, film flapping on the take-up reel.
Silence: the music stops and the projector alone remains; it frames a held moment.
pitfalls_limits: Too much content kills a silent film: a many-step chain at small figure scale is noise in a thumbnail. One legible chain with a pause in the middle beats three busy ones.

Puppet arms: apply abduction before flexion, let the shoulder rise and swing forward as the arm goes up, slim the torso's shoulder corner on the raised side, hide the arm's contour where it lies over the torso. Raise arms sideways (or turn the figure) so they
Pose pops: drive every figure by eased keyframe lists, never by `if` branches.
Floating props: hold a prop between the palms at the depth between the arms; tie a rolling object's rotation to distance (angle = distance / radius).
Brow angles flip with facing direction: check expressions in a crop at final size.
An iris must track its target in film coordinates after any camera zoom.
A grab must put the hand exactly where the object is at the beat, or it doesn't read.
Closed curtains lit only by a dark screen go pure black: add footlights.
styles.engine_section: In `demo/engine/`: `ink.js` (tonal forms, ink line, wash, hatch; `drawShape()` draws any path in this style), `redraw.js` (`Redraw`: tonal painting or real footage → ink drawing, WebGL2), `film.js` (`FilmPost` print pass + `damage()`, stackable on any 2D canvas, with an optional colour mask), `cards.js` (intertitles, deco borders, iris, theatre), `figure.js` + `heads.js` (2.5D rig). `demo/timeline.js` is a cue sheet that drives both picture and score. API table and a minimal example (a one-colour shape through the whole pipeline): [DEMO.md](DEMO.md) "Engine reference".

styles.name: Scratch Film
styles.official_demo_line: A finger-long lanternfish climbs half a kilometre in the dark, hides its shadow with its own lights, and turns out to be one of countless animals rising every night.
styles.principles: These define the style; keep all of them.
construction: Layers. One 2D canvas per frame: a mottled emulsion plate (warm and cool blotches, a rotating set of four), the scene's marks in painter's order, then the light pass: two blurred additive copies for halation (about 9 px and 28 px at 1080p), dust specks and sho

The needle line (`scratch`): a Catmull-Rom path resampled in screen space, 2–3 passes offset by the tremble, width varying along the stroke, about 1 % skips, small triangular chips on heavy lines, a thin overshoot tail. Width follows the picture's scale; the t
Dye (`dye`): 4–8 thin translucent bristles along a path, tapered at both ends: reflections, rays, wakes.

Fills (`hatch`): back-and-forth zigzag hatching that overshoots the outline, two passes at different angles. Large light (a sky, a glow from above) is several sparse hatch layers stacked into a gradient, or drawn on its own layer and faded with a gradient mask
Text as cuts. Words are rendered once as images with thin skips through them and cut in left to right behind the hot point; they tremble by less than a pixel and are never re-lettered per drawing.

Depth. Depth of field is a blurred copy masked by a disc around the subject; background creatures can be drawn on their own layer and blurred. Keep blur ≤ 5 px on bright hatching or it melts into a flat fill.
colour_logic: Ground: warm black `#050403` with brown and blue mottles; never grey.
Light: one cream `#FFF4DC` for every cut. Strong light (a sun, a glow from above, the hot point) is the same cream, denser.

Dye: a few transparent colours laid by hand, alpha 0.5–0.9, always with cream lines on top. One dye, one kind of thing, for the whole film. Our demo: teal `#1FB39A` the hero, blue `#2F86FF` living light, red `#FF3220` danger, yellow `#FFC81C` sun and moon, gre
Values: black dominates (≥ 50 % of most frames); the brightest point is a fresh cut or a light source.
motion: Everything steps on twos: 15 drawings a second at 30 fps. Each drawing reseeds the tremble.
Camera moves and characters move on the same steps; a stepped camera is part of the look, but keep it smooth in time (eased), not jerky in position.
Cuts appear progressively behind the hot point; dye sweeps in behind a brush edge; lights switch on with a short bloom.
Characters: anticipation, a flick, follow-through (2–4 drawing anticipation, big poses held 4–6 drawings).
At a cut between shots, nothing jumps: the same subject keeps its place, size and angle across the cut, new elements come in after it.
camera_grammar: a mark cut live, the camera still
one continuous log-scale pull from one mark to a whole place
a descent or climb past a scratched ruler
tracking alongside, specks streaming in parallax
from below into hatched light, the subject a black silhouette
split screen, two views on one beat
sound_palette: Hand-made instruments: struck and bowed vibraphone, glockenspiel for each new light, pizzicato double bass, log drum for a threat, brushes. Avoid generic piano and strings.
The cut is heard: a gritty high scrape with a thin wandering squeal, a dry tick per small mark.
Drawn tones: a sine read at 24 drawings a second flutters like a hand-drawn sound stripe; good under each light that switches on.
Silence: cutting all music before a key moment is the strongest accent; the first sound after it should be a mark being made.
native_moves: One mark to a whole place.
pitfalls_limits: Flat bright areas look digital: always hatch; stack sparse layers for gradients.
Large light drawn as segments or bands reads as film frames: fade it with a mask instead.
Tremble scaled with zoom shakes macros and blurs wide shots: tremble in screen pixels, width from the picture.
Boiling text becomes unreadable: tremble ≤ 1 px on text, never re-letter a word per drawing.
Too many full characters overlapping on screen turn into noise: fewer, smaller, placed by hand around the hero.
Particles positioned by speed × absolute time jump whenever the speed changes: offset them by the camera's displacement instead.
A crowd of glowing points generated in boxes shows the box edges: use soft (Gaussian) distributions per level of detail.
styles.engine_section: - `demo/js/base.js`: maths, `scratch`, `dye`, `hatch`, `glow`, emulsion / dust / grain plates. - `demo/js/creatures.js`: characters drawn in their own units and mapped anywhere (`MAPF`); a scratch-in order for the hero; a silhouette that is filled segment by segment. - `demo/js/main.js`: `render(t)` stepping on twos, depth of field, halation, dust, flicker, weave, subtitles, `TEXTS`, `EV`. - Minimal example, not in the demo: a horizon cut left to right on black, with a hatched sun.

styles.name: Double Exposure
styles.official_demo_line: From the mountains to the sea as night falls: a stag, a wolf, an eagle, a salmon and a whale, each carrying its own place inside its silhouette, until the whale's harbour lands on the real shore.
styles.principles: - Animal silhouette × landscape. The subject is a clean, recognisable animal profile (a horse, a fox, an owl in flight, a hare, a turtle); its fill is a real landscape or townscape photograph that belongs to it (its meadow, its marsh, the farm it grew up on, the island it returns to). The pairing is the meaning; the outline is never filled with a flat colour or a texture. - Two speeds. Whenever the camera or the animal moves, the photograph inside the silhouette moves more slowly than the outline (or follows the body, never the frame). That parallax is what makes the medium move on screen. - T
construction: Silhouette masks come from public-domain or CC0 vector silhouettes (PhyloPic is a good source for animals, but many of its images are CC BY or non-commercial: keep only those marked CC0 or Public Domain Mark), rasterised once in the page into a mask texture wi

Fills are photographs sampled in a layer that moves with the camera at a lower depth factor than the outline (e.g. 0.6–0.85 of the outline's motion), so the inside drifts more slowly. Place the most legible band of the photograph (a ridge, a skyline, a row of

The first exposure (outside) is built in code from simple things: a high-key dusk sky, mist, cloud layers, the sea from below with light shafts and silt, a moonlit sea. Keep it simpler and lighter than the fill, or the two images mush.

Bodies deform along their own axis. An animal's mask is sampled through a displacement field defined along its body axis (head to tail, spine line), and the photograph inside is sampled through the same field, so the place bends with the body. Cross-sections s

Swimming follows real locomotion. When the subject swims, a fish is carangiform: the head barely moves, a wave travels from head to tail with an amplitude growing roughly with the square of the distance along the body, the tail fin lags in phase; seen from the

Between two silhouettes, superimpose; never interpolate the shape. When one animal becomes another, the second whole silhouette fades in at the same place and size while the first fades out, both drawn complete, the overlap and the two photographs blended with
colour_logic: Neutral ground: black-and-white photographs and code-drawn greys, from near-black forest to paper-white sky. Sky and water are the lightest areas outside; the fill sits darker than the outside so the silhouette holds.
One warm hue, reserved for light inside a window: lamps, lit windows, a city at night, its reflection on the water. No orange skies, no golden-hour grading, no coloured animals.
The warm light can grow over a film (one lamp, then a forest of them, then a whole city) to carry the arc.
Titles may take a pale warm white; nothing else is tinted.
motion: On ones, smooth, everything a pure function of time.

Animals: breathing, weight shifts between legs, a head lift, wing beats with small tip flex between beats, swimming as in §2. Leaps have a wind-up, a fast exit and a slower landing with splash or settle; nothing rises in a straight line.
Inner photographs move slowly and continuously and never cut on their own.
Lamps light in a direction that follows the body (head to tail, one cabin after another), each with a small swell.
Alignments ease out: the last pixels take the longest. Moves start and stop with ease; no jump at the start of a move.
camera_grammar: Tracking with the animal, the fill slower than the outline
Push into the silhouette until its edge leaves the frame
Pull back from inside to reveal the outline
Push and return during a gesture (a wing beat, a turn)
Crossing a surface (waterline, cloud layer) in one move
Locked frame, only the inner layer and the light moving
sound_palette: The shutter is the medium's sound: a click when an image develops into a shape, another when two images become one.

Strings for the bed (cello, double bass, violas, violins), one harmonic colour per subject; harp, glockenspiel or bowed vibraphone for each lamp; horn, clarinet, cello pizzicato for character; bass drum or timpani sparingly for a whip, a dive, a breach.
Foley of each place inside the windows: wind, water (muffled under it), the animal's own call, wing beats or hoofbeats, a town's bells, rain. Procedural is fine.
Silence is a tool: thin the music before an alignment and let the light carry it.
pitfalls_limits: Mush. Two busy photographs overlaid read as grey noise. Fix: one side simple (sky, water, mist), the other detailed; outside lighter than inside; rim darkening and halo.
Sticker silhouettes. A hard-edged shape sliding at constant speed reads as a cut-out on a background. Fix: rim and halo, a slower fill, and a body that deforms with its locomotion.

Shear instead of swimming. Offsetting the mask's sampling with a sine makes the whole body shear left and right while the photograph stays fixed. Fix: a displacement field along the body axis, sections perpendicular to the spine, the fill sampled through the s
The averaged loaf. Interpolating two outlines gives an in-between shape that is neither animal. Fix: superimpose the two whole silhouettes (§2).

Features in the wrong place. A bright window in the photograph landing on an eye, a gill or a fin reads as a light bulb or as something poking through the outline. Fix: move the photograph so the lit band crosses the middle of the body, darken thin parts (fins
Unreadable fills. The photograph's sky becomes a flat grey band inside the body. Fix: place the strongest band across the body; lift the sky.

Misaligned "same place". Two different photographs never register. Fix: one photograph used twice, inside and outside, with two grades or keyed differently (lit buildings for the shore, a broken reflection for the water).
Mirrored tiling seams when a photograph fills a long shape. Fix: scale the photograph to the shape, keep any seam outside the frame.
styles.engine_section: The demo's code is all in `demo/index.html` (WebGL2; each scene is one full-screen fragment shader into a float target, then a composite pass). The names below are the demo's subjects (its stag, fish and whale); your film draws its own:

styles.name: Dark Tech Keynote
styles.official_demo_line: Launch film for Tidy, a fictional app: one buried cursor snaps hundreds of windows back into place.
styles.principles: A keynote-grade product film for software. There is no physical product and no glass render: the protagonist is the interface (a cursor, windows, notifications, tiles, a number). It lives on a dark stage lit by soft, cool light, with one brand accent reserved for the single most important element.
construction: Stage: a near-black base with a radial lift at the upper centre, one large cool glow at single-digit opacity off-centre, a 50–55 % corner vignette. A hairline grid (white at ~3 %, every 4th line ~6 %) on a 48 px module. No grain.

UI kit, all original and drawn in code: rounded windows (title bar with only a small glyph and title; never traffic-light buttons, menu bars or docks), notification cards, file icons with mono filenames, procedural thumbnails, list rows, tabs, badges, bars, un
Surfaces: three steps of raised dark surface, 1 px border (~8 % white), 1 px inner top highlight, soft shadows.
Depth: a 2.5D camera (`s = 1/(1/zoom − z)`); cards near the lens blur with magnification. Rotations use strip-rendered perspective (rotY ≤ ~24°).
Light is the reveal tool: only pixels the light has passed turn on; unlit areas sit at a few percent.
colour_logic: A cool neutral ladder only: near-black stage, three surface steps, text in three greys (primary, secondary, label). Neutrals are slightly blue, never warm brown.

One accent, saturated and luminous, with its own glow. It is reserved for what the product *is* or *does*: the protagonist element, the call to action, confirmations, the key number. If two things are accent-coloured, one is wrong.
A problem colour (typically a red for badges and warnings) may exist only while the problem exists; after the turn it never returns. Problem colour = noise, accent = the product.
Secondary hues only as category codes in motion (a trail per data type), desaturated, and never on static UI.
motion: 24 fps on ones, no stepping, no boil: this is precision, not craft.
Everything lands on the grid and on the beat. Moves start a beat early and land on it. Easing is fast-out with one small overshoot (`back`, s ≈ 1.3) and an immediate settle. No floaty sine drift.
Spawns are short and typed (drop + bounce, fling, slide-in, pop; 0.2–0.3 s), one motion per element type. Tension can be a tremble of a few px.
Flights follow curved paths with overshoot along the final tangent; same-type elements bend the same way and never cross.
A living element can act: squash, stretch, anticipation (≥ 8 frames of wind-up), a 2-frame contact, spring follow-through. The blink of a cursor makes a natural metronome.
Disappearing is designed (retract one part per beat, CRT-off squash into a point); nothing just fades.
camera_grammar: Locked extreme close-up on a tiny UI element
Continuous pull-back, keyed per bar in log space
Dive into a small UI element (log-zoom) + match cut
Half-second inserts expanding from their source
Near-locked frame while an object turns and light sweeps
Slow lateral track across a UI plane
sound_palette: Tuned percussion and pads: marimba, vibraphone (mallet or bowed), glockenspiel, celesta, a synth pad or drone, a low sine pulse, a shaker, plucked synth, felt piano. Clean, dry, minimal; samples e.g. VCSL (CC0).

Music as a visible process: options include phasing (two voices on one pattern, one drifting), additive build (one note per bar), subtractive process (notes removed until one is left), dividing the beat to accelerate instead of changing tempo, or one chord tha

Two sound families = story: disorder sounds *scattered* (detuned by tens of cents, random pans, a different timbre per source); the product's sounds are *one family* (felt ticks, glass taps, all in one mode, centred), so many landings form one in-key shimmer.

Foley materials: cursor tick, low-profile keys, notification glass, file plop, window whoosh, glitch accents, stacking thumps, felt mallet + sine drop for a press, light-sweep shimmer, digit grains, CRT-off.
pitfalls_limits: Strip perspective of a semi-transparent canvas shows vertical seams (overlapping slices double alpha) → project the *opaque* surface, then light it in screen space.
A hard white glint reads as a sticker reflection → soft front, glint ≤ 20 %.
Nearest-slot snapping looks like a flicker, not a collapse → typed destinations, curved paths, trails.
Too few elements leave holes in a grid that read as a mistake → generate by rule, then trim or pad to exactly the slot count per group.
A flat tinted rectangle for "closing" looks like a placeholder → squash the real surface.
styles.engine_section: `demo/engine.js` (Canvas 2D ES module): `setAccent`, `bg`, `grid`, `panel`, `litShape` (any shape in this style), `trail`, `caret`, the UI kit, `flyPose`, `lightReveal`, `perspective`, `scramble`, `toast`, `camera` (2.5D). Function table and a minimal example: [DEMO.md](DEMO.md#engine-reference); `?scene=engineDemo` renders it.

styles.name: Mascot Screencast
styles.official_demo_line: Clawd hops out of the terminal into the Claude app and acts out plan mode and self-checks in one take.
styles.principles: The film looks like a screen recording of the real product, but it is not a recording. Every window, menu, diff line and button is redrawn in 2D (HTML/CSS/SVG), so the camera can go anywhere, every pixel is controllable and text stays sharp at any zoom.
construction: Real UI, redrawn: every label, mode name and shortcut matches the real product; no screenshots, no lorem ipsum. Demo content (code, data, test output) is coherent, and the app under test really changes.

Pixel grid is sacred: the mascot, its props (pencil, "!", sparkles, heart, dust) and trails share one square-pixel grid with crisp edges. It scales with the camera; its position snaps to half-pixels, so its motion feels stepped.

Gravity = top edges of UI: the mascot only stands on the top edge of a real element (input box, menu, list row, code line, button, status bar, the letters of a heading). Its position comes from measuring the live DOM every frame, never hand-placed coordinates.
Window on wallpaper: the app floats on a desktop with a soft shadow; zoom never shows beyond the monitor.
Depth only where it serves attention: rack focus (blur the pane that doesn't matter), a vignette spotlight. Never blur text the viewer must read.
Motion blur is derived from camera speed and applied as an anisotropic blur on an untransformed wrapper, only on whips. Slow moves stay sharp.
colour_logic: The product's own interface colours rule: follow its real light and dark themes exactly.
The mascot keeps the product's or brand's mascot colour, or one saturated hue that no UI element uses, so it finds the eye in any frame.
Overlays (chapter pill, key HUD, captions) are neutral frosted glass; one accent at most, taken from the product.
A theme switch can be a story event: the whole film may change state with it.
motion: 30 fps; UI on ones; mascot position stepped to its pixel grid.

Mascot acting: jumps with anticipation crouch, stretch on take-off, tucked legs, landing squash with a damped bounce and dust. Idle breathes (a tiny squash) on the score's beat and blinks irregularly. Walks by leg alternation, flipping the sprite for direction
Eyes carry the acting (neutral / left / right / up / down / wide / happy / shut / blink): they look at what matters. Arms: down / up (cheer) / wave.
Cursor: smoothed, spring-eased paths, small push on click, never teleports.
Cause and effect: every mascot action triggers a real UI state change; every user action is a cursor move, click or keystroke shown on the HUD.
UI animates like the real product (its own menus, popovers, diff reveals); don't invent flourishes the product doesn't have.
camera_grammar: Push-in to the cursor or caret
Pull back to the full window
Follow the mascot along a list
sound_palette: Two resolutions in the music: a hi-fi layer (piano, upright or electric bass, brushed or tight kit, glockenspiel, real samples) is the world; a chiptune square or pulse voice is the mascot. They can trade, duet or merge.

Options: a low-passed "night" version of the band for a dark theme; a tom fill and crash at chapter seams; dropping the drums to build tension; the mascot's notes on words it lands on; a stereo split for split screens; a single held pad under a freeze.

Foley: keyboard (a thock plus a click, human timing jitter), trackpad clicks, pane swishes, popup pops, notification chimes, CI ticks, a shutter for screenshots. Mascot steps, jumps and landings are 8-bit.
