Silence: a short drop to room tone before the key promise makes it land.
pitfalls_limits: Invented features or renamed modes → check every button, mode and shortcut against the product's documentation; if it isn't in the docs, it isn't in the film.
The mascot floats or drifts off its element → measure the DOM every frame, stand only on top edges.
The mascot covers text or sits under a caption → reserve a text-free lane for it.
Blur-filter "fake depth" on text you want read, or zooming out past the screen → rack focus only on panes not being read; zoom ≥ 1.
A hand, arm or finger on screen → the cursor is the user.
Motion blur applied to a transformed layer smears the pixel sprite wrong → blur an untransformed wrapper, and only on whips.
A keypress or pop landing on a product name masks it → shift foley off word onsets; re-check with whisper on the final mix.
TTS mispronounces the product name → try voices and spellings, verify with whisper.
styles.engine_section: In `demo/`: `film.js` (timeline: VO at fixed times, every visual beat hung on a spoken word with `W(id, word)`, camera moves, `Actor` mascot segments, `Cursor`, sound events), `ui.js` (state → HTML for each interface), `clawd.js` (sprite grid, poses, pixel props: replace the sprite with your own mascot), `main.js` (light/dark layers, DOM anchor measurement, motion blur, HUD: captions, keys, pixel wipes, spotlight), `sound.py` (score, foley and VO from `events.json`, with ducking). Build notes: [DEMO.md](DEMO.md#build-notes).

styles.name: Sci-fi Hologram HUD
styles.official_demo_line: An e-bike is scanned into a hologram; target boxes lock onto the battery, motor and brakes.
styles.principles: The subject is always a line wireframe made of light above a round projector pad on a near-black stage, never a rendered object. Everything reads as *scanned data*: a scan plane grows the model, parts pull apart along their assembly axes, numbers are *computed* on screen.
construction: Stage: near-black tinted by the hue, a radial lift behind the subject, a fading dot grid, a strong vignette.
Projector pad in true perspective: concentric rings (one bright, one dashed), ticks, faint rays; it rotates slowly and spins with any turntable move.
Wireframe: additive ~1.3 px strokes in a few alpha levels set by depth fog (near bright, far ~25 %), plus two low-res glow passes.
Hot edges (near-white of the hue) only for what matters now: the scan front, inner pieces flagged `hot` when opened, a light wave, a part being pinged.
Real CAD topology: tubes are rings plus longitudinal lines. Every part is physically connected: a floating piece is noticed first.

Solid hologram: faces filled with a screen-space Fresnel × a scrolling interlace; lines thicken as it ignites; a light wave climbs the model. A beam (one path, nonzero winding) with faint rays and dust.
colour_logic: One cold hue plus one warm accent, both parameters (e.g. mint/orange, violet/lime, ice-blue/red; choose from the subject).
The hue carries lines, HUD and fills. The accent is spent on locked values only: a number turns accent-coloured at the frame it becomes true. Nothing else ever uses it.
White is heat: near-white edges and one-frame flashes mark what is active. Everything at rest sits in the hue's alpha levels.
One object may keep its own colour (the single-colour exception, `keep`), for a brand mark, never for decoration.
motion: Everything on ones at 24 fps. Only glyph scrambling steps, every frame.
Target lock: oversized, rotated 45°, faint; snaps to fit in ~0.2 s (cubic ease-out), flashes white 3 frames on the downbeat.
Explode along each piece's assembly axis: the shell slides *along its own axis*, the contents stay in place and glow. Open over a beat or two, close fast.
Leader: anchor ring → diagonal → horizontal to the card in ~0.5 s. Rolling value: characters lock right-to-left and turn accent on the downbeat with a one-frame flash.
Chip dock: a finished value slides into a side rail and stays until the end.
The camera follows the box: cubic ease, starting *before* the next lock, real motion blur only inside the whip (sub-frames, 180° shutter); HUD stays sharp.
camera_grammar: Orbit around a part's own axis
Lateral dolly along a long part
Crane to eye level or back up
sound_palette: Music first, on a grid (a bar = one information beat); locks land on downbeats, checked against the score.
Synth palette: saw/square arpeggio with ping-pong delay (scooped 1–4 kHz for the voice), square pulse, 8th bass, synth hats and claps, detuned saw pads.

Density follows information. Tools to pick from, in any order (most films need two or three): half-time for reading time; one beat of true digital silence (nothing, not even UI blips); a drop (808-style glide + wide saw chord) for the biggest change; a layer a

Foley follows the material: light = sines and FM blips in the key; machines = servo slides, pneumatic puffs, hydraulic hiss, metal tinks (J-cuts); a lock = thump + clack + two-tone beep; rolls tick at frame rate. Ambience: projector hum (40/80/120 Hz) and room
native_moves: Local explode = "why the number is true."
Solid hologram + beam = "the whole is ready."
pitfalls_limits: Target boxes balloon → rest pose, skip `internal` pieces, long attachments `box:false`.
Long diagonal leaders point at the wrong part → ring on the part body, flash the part.
Two parallel boxes moving don't read as an explode → shell slides on its axis, contents stay and glow.
A part built from generic boxes doesn't read as that part → give it its characteristic silhouette.
Voice masked by foley, not music → duck foley too, hold the duck through word gaps.
UI blips inside a silence break it → check cues against silence windows.
A whip written inside the next segment plays as a hard cut → start it in the previous one.
styles.engine_section: `demo/engine/holo.js` (wireframe engine: projection, scan, explode, Fresnel faces, glow, pad, scan plane, `normalizeModel`, `modelFromPath` to extrude any 2D path), `demo/engine/hud.js` (theme, plate, target box, leader, rolling text, spec card, chip, marker, beam, subtitle, chrome, glitch), `demo/models/mkmodel.mjs` (primitives: tube, ring, disc, box, wheel, cells…). Models are normalised on load, so cameras work for any object. API, model format and an example: [DEMO.md](DEMO.md#engine-reference).

styles.name: Tabletop App Flythrough
styles.official_demo_line: A cat photo hops across app cards on a sunlit desk, from one phone to a friend's.
styles.principles: - The desk is the world. A matte paper mat with a regular dot grid lies on a light wooden desk, lit by one low warm sun through a window. Everything sits on it and casts a long, soft shadow. A few everyday desk things (a pen, sticky notes, a mug, earbuds) sit around the edges as foreground and background layers. - Interfaces are paper cards. Phones, tools and dashboards are rounded slabs a few millimetres thick with the interface printed on top. They are places: characters stand and hop on them, and parts of the interface rise out of them as small 3D objects. - The cast are pixel sprites made
construction: three.js, physically based, neutral tone mapping. Scale: a card is 0.3–0.7 units wide (1000 canvas px per unit); dots 0.03 apart. A character must be big enough to show its eyes: in the demo about 1/5–1/3 of the card it stands on (0.006–0.0075 units per pixel,

Light: one directional sun low from the back-left (about 20° up, so a toy's shadow is two or three times its height), a 4096 soft shadow map that follows the camera target and resizes with distance; a cool-sky / warm-ground hemisphere fill, so shadows read blu

Desk: a dotted paper mat (a thin rounded slab whose size is a multiple of two dot spacings, so the printed dots line up with any 3D dots) on a procedural light-oak plane (planks, long soft grain). Soft window-light patches (blurred four-pane shapes, warm, addi

Cards and screens: a rounded slab plus a canvas texture on top with a faint deterministic grain. Print is flat: one ink, mono labels in spaced caps, bold numerals, thin rules; a card head carries two lines (English mono caps over the other language in bold). A

Voxel cast: instanced bevelled cubes per pixel; depth grows with distance from the silhouette; pure-black pixels are eyes, which protrude and blink (they take the colour of the pixel above). Rig: root (feet, yaw) → hinge (lying flat ↔ standing) → squash (scale

Props: the same voxel recipe (crosses, ticks, bells) or plain rounded primitives (bricks, presses, drawers, towers, tent cards, stamps). Data that rises out of a card is extruded from its printed shape, so it still reads from above.
colour_logic: One light ground (the mat) with a slightly darker dot, cool-tinted so the warm sun leaves it fresh; a warm wooden desk around it; cards in a near-white of the same temperature; one dark ink for print; one accent reserved for what matters now: the route, the cu

Two or three support hues for the cast and props, mid-saturated, never neon; one warm cast colour against the cool ground. Red only for failure or trouble (an error, a weak signal), green only for success; data in motion may take one bright support hue so it r
Judge the rendered frame: avoid grey on grey; keep the vignette light and the shadows tinted by the sky fill.
Brand use: the brand colour becomes the accent; the brand's interface colours print on the cards; the ground stays light.
motion: 30 fps. One steady tempo (110–130 BPM); every action on the 16th grid, big moments on downbeats.

Hops: an arc with squash and stretch (stretch about 14 % in the air, squash about 30 % for 0.2 s on landing, a small anticipation squash before take-off). Groups move follow-the-leader, each a 16th behind the one ahead, so they never close up.
Characters act: they blink every couple of seconds, bounce on the beat while they wait, squint when they are squashed, lean towards what they look at.

Pop: sticker → toy in 0.25–0.5 s (hinge up with overshoot, cells extrude from the centre, a small jump, squash on landing). Reverse pop: toy → sticker or print when it is stored, delivered or taped down.
Slam: drops from above with ease-in, lands on a downbeat, squashes, jolts the card, sends out a ring.
UI comes alive in sequence: digits, bars, ticks, typed characters appear on 16ths with an overshooting ease.
camera_grammar: Macro glide with a slow orbit (close, 20–45° down)
Whip from card to card (0.3–0.5 s, banking into the turn)
Ride along, low behind the subject
sound_palette: Score: bright and warm, acoustic in feel: marimba (with vibraphone under long notes), plucked bass, a soft synthetic kick (a short sine sweep), claps, shaker, a quiet string pad. One key, diatonic chords, about one chord per bar. Under a voice the score is a l

Foley: every action has a sound. Pop: a marimba note from the current chord plus an upward sweep. Hop: a soft tick. Landing: a felt thump. Press or stamp: a low thump with a crumble. Typing: dry key clicks. Ding: two bell notes from the chord. Camera whip: a w

Mix: the voice leads (about −16 LUFS before delivery, −14 after); music 15–18 dB under the voice and lifted in the gaps; foley under the voice; the mix peaks under −1.5 dBFS and `mux.sh` masters it to −14 LUFS, true peak ≤ −1 dBTP. The final chord holds to the
pitfalls_limits: Softness: depth of field and motion blur easily turn a subject or its words to mush. Blur only what lies behind a focus plane set a little beyond the subject, lightly (≤ 5 px), never anything in front; let the shutter shrink with camera speed so a streak never
Flat print read at a low angle: text on a card seen from 20° is unreadable. Rise to 55–70° to read a card; put text the low camera must read on a standing object.
A standing toy hides the row behind it: place characters beside or behind the text being read, or off the card, and check every reading frame for overlap.

Text under the subtitle bar or cut at the frame edge: keep the fixed vertical offset; show name plates and labels only in the shots that frame them whole; take camera-facing pills away before the camera moves on.
Screens that read as blank: a phone card without a whole interface reads as an empty white slab in close-up.

Shadows of floating labels: with the sun at 20°, a pill a few centimetres up throws a long shadow across the card and greys out its print. Labels and pills cast no shadow (`pill()` turns it on: set `castShadow = false`); a real floating object (a bell) may, bu

Characters lost in the wide: on screen a character is about `width × 1080 / (2 · dist · tan(fov / 2))` px wide. In the closing wide view keep every character at least about 35 px wide (the demo's smallest is about 37 px); otherwise frame closer, bring it forwa

Voxels seen edge-on: a standing sprite seen from far to the side reads as stripes and its eyes vanish; turn it towards the camera (`yaw`) for its key moments, and give a large picture-like sprite a thinner `depthK` (0.6–0.9).
styles.engine_section: In `demo/` (three.js r170 + Canvas 2D). Copy the folder into the project; the engine files work as they are, the film is yours to write.

styles.name: Spreadsheet Film
styles.official_demo_line: The total says treatment B; unhide the stone-size columns and A wins every group. Simpson's paradox told in one sheet, 1 cell = 1 patient.
styles.principles: What makes a frame read as this style in one glance:
construction: Canvas 2D, one world → screen function. The sheet is a grid in world units (column widths × row height); the camera is a centre and a zoom. Everything that belongs to the sheet (fills, values, merged cells, reference boxes, the selection) goes through that fun

Variable column widths are part of the model: a hidden column has width 0 and every x position is a prefix sum of widths, so opening or closing columns reflows the whole sheet and the camera rides along.
Grid lines: white cells get light grey lines (≈ `#dad9d3`); painted cells get thin dark lines (≈ rgba(6,4,18,0.42)), as if "all borders" were applied.
Cell values at 11 px × zoom; below about 6.5 px they are not drawn, so the far view becomes pure colour instead of grey noise.
A painted cell flashes white for ~0.12 s when its rule fires. That flash is the style's only "light".
Merged cells are the layout: labels, results, titles and the end card are merged ranges with a cell border, never floating text.
colour_logic: The sheet is white; colour means a rule fired. Every fill on a cell is a conditional format with a meaning the viewer can learn in one look (success / failure, a category, a scale step).

At most five working hues plus the shell's warm greys: two for the main binary or categories, one for a second variable, one for the hero (the selected cell, a winning result), and ink. Office-style conditional-format colours (lime, red, indigo, amber, sky) re

A colour scale is a payoff, not wallpaper. A banded scale (6–8 steps radiating from one cell, neighbouring bands alternating light and dark) can paint the empty background once the argument is made; until then the background stays white.
Reference boxes take their colour from the formula: each referenced name in the formula bar and the box around its range share one hue.
motion: 24 fps; the camera (zoom, scroll) is smooth every frame. Cells themselves move on the grid: positions snap to whole cells, so a moving cell hops.
Paint happens in rings or sweeps from one cell, a few tens of milliseconds per cell, with the status bar counting cells.

Typing is even within a line, about 14–30 characters per second: the longer the formula, the faster, so that one formula is typed in about 0.8–1.4 s; the caret blinks at 4 Hz. Enter is a hard cut of state: the edit box closes, the value pops.
Column-width changes ease in and out (~0.5 s per column) and ripple across neighbouring columns.
The shell never moves; only its state changes (pressed buttons, the name box, the zoom slider, status messages).
Frame rate and grain: no film grain (mux grain 0).
camera_grammar: Push into a cell or range
Track along a row or column
sound_palette: The sheet's foley: key clicks for every typed character, a clack + low thump on Enter, a short tick per hop of the selected cell, one tiny sine blip per painted cell (pitch rising with progress), a ratchet click per opened column, a soft blip per landing cell

Music: office-pop instruments (kit, electric bass, piano stabs, marimba, xylophone, glockenspiel). Accelerate by thickening the pattern (half-time → four on the floor, sixteenth mallets), not by changing tempo.
Silence is a real cut of the music (foley may stay) right before a clue or a turn; the first sound after it should be a key moment.
Mix: voice compressed and about 10 dB over the music by RMS, music carved 300 Hz–4 kHz under speech, −14 LUFS, true peak ≤ −1 dB. Voice: a calm explainer.
native_moves: Pull out from a formula cell.
pitfalls_limits: Grey mush when zoomed out: values drawn at 3–5 px turn the picture to noise. Stop drawing values below ~6.5 px.
Text unreadable at the zoom it is shown: size merged-cell text for the zoom of its shot; a number the voice uses must be ≥ 26 px on screen.
Wide-and-short compositions: a sheet that is wider than tall forces a low zoom; add a meaningful row of cells (a count, a total) below, or crop to the part being discussed.
Selection box drawn over the value: a thick border on a small cell hides its content; select merged ranges for results, single cells only when zoomed in.
Brand look-alike: a green ribbon, a familiar grid font, a product name; keep the shell generic and drawn by hand.
Moving cells smearing: interpolated sub-cell positions read as sliding stickers; snap to whole cells.
Too many formulas: one formula per beat; a formula bar that changes every second is noise.
styles.engine_section: All in `demo/index.html` (Canvas 2D, no dependencies):

styles.name: 1-bit Dither
styles.official_demo_line: February 1966: the first close-up of the Moon arrives at an English radio telescope as a newspaper fax, printed one line at a time in two inks, a day early and stretched too tall.
styles.principles: - Two inks, no grey. Every pixel is ink or paper. Tone is density of dots; there is no anti-aliasing, no grey text, no soft gradient on screen. - The dots belong to the surface. The dither threshold is attached to each object (object-space, octave chosen from the screen footprint), so when the camera dollies or an object turns, the pattern rides with it like a printed texture. - Drawn edges. Depth and normal breaks become one-pixel lines: ink where the surface is light, paper where it is dark. A black object against a black sky still has a white rim. - Each medium has its own dot. The world is
construction: Three passes. (1) Shading: the scene with ordinary lights and shadows into a half-float target at 960×540. (2) G-buffer: an override material writes octahedral normal, the surface-anchored Bayer threshold and view depth (negative depth marks layers that get no

Anchoring the threshold. Project the object-space position (times the object's scale) on its dominant object-space axis; pick the Bayer octave per axis so a cell is 1–2 screen pixels along each surface direction, blend to the next octave. This is what keeps gr

Printed paper. Paper textures hold ink 0 / paper 1 at a fixed pitch (a print's dots, a page's letters). When a texel covers more than ~2 screen pixels, the bilinear value is thresholded, so magnified print reads as crisp dots and letters; when minified, the mi

Halftone screen. A shader cell grid at 45°, dot radius from the tone at the cell centre; large cells are hard dots, cells under ~3 px fall back to tone. The same mechanism lets a camera fall from a single dot to a whole town without moiré.

Light is the only drama. Hard key light with real shadow maps (a low sun, a desk lamp, headlights), little or no ambient fill. Shadows are solid ink; lit faces are sparse dots. Emissive things (a phosphor trace, frost sparkles, lamps) are white and get no outl

Screen space only for cuts and transitions, and every transition stays two-ink on every frame: a block dissolve (whole 16–32 px cells swap at once), a fax-scan wipe (the next picture replaces the frame row by row under a two-row inverted scan head), a full-fra
colour_logic: Exactly two colours on screen, chosen once per film: a near-black ink and a paper white with a slight tint (warm, cool or green-grey). No third colour, not even for text or the end card.
Value is the only variable. Order the frame by value: the subject either the lightest or the darkest mass, the background in the middle density.
Large pure-ink areas (night sky, shadow, a CRT face) are the strongest graphic element; keep one in most frames.
Inversion (ink and paper swapped for one or two frames) is the medium's accent: use it for an impact, never as decoration.
motion: 30 fps, on ones. Because every pixel flips between two states, motion is visible as pattern change: keep camera moves smooth (spline keys, ease in and out) and avoid fast lateral pans across fine repeating structure.

No velocity cliffs. A sudden stop, a start at full speed or a 0.1 s hold mid-move reads as a stutter, because the whole pattern freezes or jumps at once. Join camera segments with continuous velocity (Hermite or Bézier, overlap and blend two segments), start a

Big scale changes in log distance. A pull-back from one dot to a town is keyed on log(distance), starts from rest and peaks around 15 % per frame; a linear pull that is fastest on its first frame smears the whole picture.
Fine regular structure (lattice, mesh, grilles, rigging) must be built as few thick members or kept in silhouette; one-pixel lines that move produce crawling stairs.
Things appear by being printed, lit or uncovered, not by fading: a line of print, a lamp switching on, a stamp landing with a two-frame scale pop.
Time-lapse is natural to the medium: dither density changing steadily over a window or a sky reads as hours passing.
sound_palette: The medium has a mechanical, printed character: clocks, relays, scanning tones, stylus scratch, paper, rubber stamps on cork, switches, motors.

Score: small, slightly cold ensemble that can sit under mechanical sound — clarinet or bass clarinet, glockenspiel, pizzicato and bowed low strings, a slightly detuned upright piano, brushed percussion. A machine rhythm in the picture can become the pulse (a s
Silence is a tool: drop all music for vacuum, night or verdict holds, keep one far, filtered element so the silence is not dead.
Mix: effects on the cut, music under them, −16 LUFS integrated before mastering, true peak ≤ −3 dBTP, little energy below 45 Hz.
pitfalls_limits: Swimming pattern when the threshold is screen-locked: anchor it to objects and choose octaves per axis.

Octave rings on large grazing planes (fields, floors, roofs seen far off): the octave switch draws concentric bands. Put those planes on a screen-locked threshold layer; they carry no texture, so nothing swims.
Stencil bridges on CJK: cutting bridges through hanzi changes the character (图 reads as 圖). Stencil Latin only, or not at all.
Moiré on thin repeating structure: thicken, reduce the count, or keep it in silhouette; check adjacent frames, not single stills.
Grey text: thin strokes average to paper when minified and vanish; draw text bold or stroked, bias the threshold towards ink, check at 1080p.
Emissive or specular lift on ink: any emissive term or specular highlight on printed paper turns black letters into grey dots; use diffuse-only paper materials with no emission.

Grey from the encoder: every lossy generation (a JPEG frame grab, then an H.264 encode, then another at the mux) smears dot edges into grey, worst on fast moves. Capture lossless frames (PNG into a lossless master) and encode once, with a low CRF and `-tune an
Coarse cells that are not nested: a resolve whose cell size steps 26, 25, 24… re-lays the whole grid every frame and flickers. Use powers of two so each step splits every cell into four.
styles.engine_section: - `pipe.js` — `Pipe(renderer, w, h).render(scene, camera, target, opts)`: shading, anchored G-buffer, 1-bit pass. `opts`: `exp, lo, hi, gam, cell` (coarse resolve), `edge, edgeK, lineLum, farEdge`, `focus, ap, maxCoc` (depth of field), `screenT`. `Present.draw(a, b, mix, invert, mode, block)`: mode 0 ordered dissolve, 1 block dissolve, 2 fax-scan wipe; inversion. Layers: `L_EDGE` gets outlines, `L_FLAT` does not, `L_SCREEN` gets outlines and a screen-locked threshold (large plain planes). - `kit.js` — `printMat(tex, {bias, text})` printed paper; `halftoneMat(tex, cells)` newspaper screen; `pap

styles.name: Circuit Board
styles.official_demo_line: Rivers become copper traces as current runs 2,080 km from a dam to a phone charger.
styles.principles: - A top-down board in every frame: copper pour with clearances cut around everything, traces with 0/45/90° runs and mitred corners, gold pads and vias, white monoline silkscreen. Nothing is drawn in perspective. - Information moves as light on copper. The way the light moves *is* the explanation: a pulse, a stream, a rocking dash, a pad that flashes. - Two scales on one board: whole regions (a map, a supply chain, a city) are drawn in the same language as single components, and the camera passes between them without changing medium. - Only real things are drawn. Every trace, pad and label stan
colour_logic: Ground: green solder mask in three values (dark laminate, mid pour, light rim/trace). The film is green; never recolour the mask per scene.
Metal: gold for pads and vias, one bare-copper accent at most.
Ink: one off-white for all silkscreen.

Light carries meaning and is the only saturated colour: amber for energy/current (with a near-white core), silver-cyan for a second kind of flow (water, data, goods) when the story has two. A third flow gets a third light colour only if it must be told apart;
motion: 30 fps, everything on ones. `render(t)` depends on t only; motion blur from measured screen motion (180° shutter, sub-frames from 1 to ~20), never across a cut.
Kinds of current, told apart only by how the light moves:
AC / alternating: short dashes rocking back and forth along the trace (a slowed mains frequency) over a faint energised line.
DC / one-way: a continuous lit stream behind a travelling head, with slow streaks inside and an afterglow that dims slowly behind the head.
Step-down: the trace gets thinner and the dashes smaller.
Water / second flow: several parallel streamlines of moving dashes at different speeds, faster in the middle, with short glints.
camera_grammar: Ride the pulse (camera locked to a moving head, head on a third)
Rise while following (zoom out during the ride until both ends are in frame)
Matched cut on a centred symbol (same symbol, same screen size, the world around it changes scale)
Plunge through a hole / via, reverse out of another hole
pitfalls_limits: Flat pour. A board that is all mid-green reads as an empty slide. Fill with real board texture: stitching vias that stay visible at map scale, fences along every clearance, mottling, micro silk, other unlit routes that exist in the subject.
Decorative routing. Traces that mean nothing make viewers ask what they are. Draw only real routes; texture comes from vias and mask, not invented traces.
Lines crossing on one layer. Two traces can't cross on the same copper: use a via to the bottom layer, or route around. A trace may cross a bare channel (a river, a street).
Overexposed light. Wide traces with additive bloom turn into white bars. Cap glow widths and flash radii in pixels, keep the amber body and a thin core.
Text in the blur or under the frame edge. Depth of field and the vignette eat the top and bottom bands: keep labels out of them, or turn the blur down in reading shots.
Too-fast holes. A plunge into a hole under 0.6 s reads only as "darkness". Hold on the hole first, then plunge; come out of another hole the opposite way.
Precision. Zooming a single coordinate system over many orders of magnitude breaks the canvas transform. Nest boards (each with moderate units) and convert cameras between levels in double precision.

Hanzi in a stroke font. Automatic skeletons of fonts lose dots and strokes; route each character by hand and proof traditional/simplified forms (鹤 not 鶴, 换 not 換). A glyph that only works at small size (one component missing, two strokes merged) reads as anoth
styles.engine_section: Reference code in `demo/src/`. Copy what you use into the project's `src/` (never import from `styles/`); edit your copies freely. The build order (subtitle font, voice and check, events, score, render at 30 fps, mux, `.srt`, readcheck, stills) is in `demo/build.sh`.

styles.name: Firefly Pointillism
styles.official_demo_line: A firefly's blink is a question: a girl gets her answer as a deer, loses every light in a storm, and asks the whole dark with the last one.
styles.principles: - Black is more than half the frame. All light comes from the points themselves: no ambient light, no gradient sky, no solid surfaces. - Everything is the same kind of point. Characters, grass, moon, stars, rain and titles come out of one renderer and differ only in colour, density and focus. - Depth is size and blur. In-focus points are small and sharp, out-of-focus points become large, faint discs. Particles pulling from blur to sharp *is* focusing, and focusing is how a form appears. - Forms are outlines. A character is a dotted silhouette (dense outline points, sparse fill), read through p
construction: Splatting into five blur levels: σ ≈ 1.0 / 2.1 / 4.8 / 10.5 / 23 px, rendered at 1 / 1 / ½ / ¼ / ⅛ resolution; each particle carries a fractional blur level and is split between the two neighbouring levels, so focus can be pulled continuously. Energy gain per
Halo: each point puts ~16 % of its energy two levels up, so bright points glow.
Exposure and tone: linear light × exposure, `1 − exp(−x)`, gamma 2.2. Point cores burn towards white and the edges keep their hue.

Motion blur: a 180° shutter; each point is drawn as samples between its positions at the two ends of the shutter, so fast flight turns into light streaks by itself. Points that wrap around the frame (rain, flows) must not draw a streak across the screen.
Grain: very light, darker areas slightly more, plus 1–2 LSB dither against banding. Heavy grain multiplies the file size.

Characters: a 2D bone rig (tapered capsules and polygons). Points are bound to normalised local coordinates on each part, so poses, scale and mirroring never resample. Outline points that fall inside another part on the same or a nearer layer are dimmed to a f
colour_logic: One warm yellow-green family. Each character owns one colour and keeps it through every transformation: after a scatter and re-gathering, the audience recognises who is who by colour alone. Colours are never swapped.
Cold colour only for stars and rain, under 5 % of the frame. No pure white, no saturated red or blue.
motion: 60 fps, every frame (no stepping). Particle paths are always curves: straight flight gets a rotation or scatter added.

Breathing: character points pulse slowly (± 22 %), and a few points are much brighter than the rest (pointillist sparkle). Fireflies are mostly dark: a narrow pulse, so only about a quarter are lit at any moment.
Drift instead of physics: a sum of slow sines (0.3–1.4 rad/s) for floating points; easing replaces damping (ease-out to land, smootherstep elsewhere).

Performance: big silhouette actions only (look up, reach, lower the head, jump, run, fall, kneel, stand, raise an arm). Blinks and fingers cannot be drawn. A large figure keeps its full silhouette while it acts: when it bows or leaps, move the head, neck and l
Three speeds: fast (transitions, climaxes, points streaking), medium (performance, one pose change per beat), still (reading, emotional pauses: positions frozen ≥ 1.5 s, brightness breathing only).
sound_palette: Real sampled instruments (`core/audio/sampler.py`): harp (glissandi for flows, arpeggios for gathering, chords for landing), glockenspiel, hand chimes, glass harp and vibraphone for single lights, touches and flashes, string pads and tremolo, flute melody, tim

Particle action ↔ sound: gathering = rising arpeggio or glissando plus cymbal swell, landing exactly on the chord; scattering = wind and a falling glockenspiel run; a landing = a harp pluck or a hand chime; a synchronous flash = a fast harp sweep.
Procedural ambience: crickets (short 4–5 kHz pulse trains), wind, rain; footsteps of animals from the gait phase.
A light can carry a motif: a two-note rising figure for a "question", a falling figure to the tonic for an "answer".
pitfalls_limits: Green fog: background bokeh, out-of-focus grass and fireflies add up to a haze and the black is lost. Keep fireflies mostly dark, background bokeh at 0.1–0.38, near blurred grass around 0.2.
Walls of light: distant points on one horizontal line read as a lit wall; give them height above ground and random depth, and soften ripple fronts.
Hard distribution edges: a uniform random band draws a visible line; use power-law vertical distributions.

Unreadable characters: fill points alone are a cloud; outlines need about 0.7 points per pixel and occlusion culling. A standing animal seen from the side hides its far legs behind the near ones: stagger the feet so all four read.
Shapes dissolving at the peak: a per-particle scatter on a big character turns it into a column of dots; for a hero action, move the rig and keep the shape.
Unreadable text: random sampling or moving after landing; sample on a jittered grid and freeze.
Low-resolution levels: energy splatted at ⅛ resolution must be divided by res², or the frame turns white.
Variable counts: optional flashes must be fixed slots with zero brightness, or the two shutter evaluations differ in length.
styles.engine_section: A numpy/scipy renderer, no browser: `engine.py` (rig, occlusion, text sampling, pyramid splatting) and a film module with one state function per group per scene, a `blend()` for transitions, a camera function and `render(t)`. Frames stream into ffmpeg from a multiprocessing pool (about 0.3–1 s per frame per core at 1080p with ~19,000 particles).

styles.name: Flow-field Wind Lines
styles.official_demo_line: Thousands of ink wind lines, computed from the best track, draw Super Typhoon Yagi: the eye opening over the South China Sea, the landfall on Hainan, the spiral coming apart in Vietnam, and a whole week folded into one last line.
styles.principles: - Every line is a streamline of a real field. Thousands of long, thin, continuous lines that never cross; their pattern *is* the information (a vortex, a jet, a sink, a wake). - Two layers of ink: a fine engraved base line, and short tapered strokes that run along it, faster where the field is stronger. Motion comes from the strokes and the field changing, not from the lines jittering. - Warm paper, blue-black ink, one warm ramp for magnitude. The paper is the screen; the world under the lines is printed (a chart, a landscape, a sky), not photographed. - The field meets things: coasts, relief,
construction: Field first. Write the field as a function `field(x, y, t)` from data or a published model (wind from a best track and a parametric vortex, currents from a grid, flow round an obstacle from a potential). Never place vortices by eye. Land, relief and objects ac

Streamline engine (time-varying fields): seeds are fixed points of a jittered grid *in world units*, one grid per level of detail (spacing halves each level); every line is integrated for a fixed number of RK2 steps of fixed length in both directions, with the

Level of detail: a level's weight is 1 − |log₂(on-screen seed spacing / target)|; two neighbouring levels always sum to one, so density stays constant through any zoom. Seed spacing ≈ 36 px at 1080p and a half-length of 4 spacings give lines ~6 px apart on ave
Static fields may instead use evenly spaced streamlines (Jobard–Lefer) computed once and frozen; moving obstacles then deform the frozen lines continuously (r → √(r² + k²) in the obstacle's frame).

Strokes: a phase along each line's time of flight (∫ ds / f(|v|), f compressive, e.g. v^0.6) compared with one global flow clock Φ(t); a comet profile, bright head, fading tail. Lines fade at both ends (sin^0.8 taper) and inside calm cores (an eye clears by fa
Batching: quantise alpha (1/40) and width (1/6 px) into buckets per colour; draw runs as polylines, round joins. Thousands of lines and tens of thousands of strokes render in well under a second.
colour_logic: Neutral ground: warm paper (around #ECE0C4 to #E9D3A6), land a slightly darker umber wash, water a faint cool grey.
Ink: blue-black (around #262C38) for calm, for coastlines and for text.

One magnitude ramp, ink → slate → umber → ochre → orange → vermilion, stepped at thresholds that mean something (wind grades, speed limits, safety levels). The same ramp prints the legend, so the lines are their own key.
Vermilion is reserved for the extreme band and for the single verdict or event on screen.
motion: 30 fps on ones. Lines never pop, flicker or reorder: every change is continuous in time (field, level weights, fades, the camera).
Strokes run at 60–300 px/s; compress the speed so the fastest stroke moves less than its own length per frame.
Time in the story may run at any rate but never backwards, and is mapped through a monotone curve (no kinks).
Readings roll through real records and land with a sound; legends print row by row; tracks draw on with beads.
During holds the camera keeps a slow creep and the strokes keep running: the world never freezes.
Never moves: the printed world under its labels, the paper fibre.
camera_grammar: High oblique push over a calm field
Orbit round a centre while descending
Pull-up to the whole map, north up
Dive to a grazing pass over the surface
Top-down follow of the moving feature
sound_palette: The field is the lead instrument: filtered noise in three bands (body 90–420 Hz, mid 0.4–1.6 kHz, air 1.8–6.5 kHz) whose levels follow the mean magnitude on screen, and a narrow-band whistle whose pitch follows the strongest value (≈ 400 Hz + 24 Hz per m/s); s

Score underneath: low sustained strings, a single long harmonic, sparse plucks or mallets. One soft pitched tone per data record (pitch rising with the category); a harp or pizzicato for each printed row.
Silence: music cut for a beat before a verdict; the field keeps blowing; the verdict lands on a low piano and timpani.
Events: contact with land is a low, muffled boom, never a crash; camera moves get soft whooshes.
pitfalls_limits: Flicker comes from anything discrete that changes with t: collision-terminated streamlines recomputed per frame, seeds in screen space, a level switched on or off, a step count that changes, a seed culled when it crosses the near plane. Fix: world-fixed seeds,
Piling at sinks: convergent fields bunch lines into black knots. Shrink the step with the speed, fade lines in calm cores, keep line length moderate.
Shimmer: 1-px lines under a fast rotating camera alias. Keep rotations slow (under ~20°/s), widths ≥ 1 px, and strokes shorter than they move.
Fake fields: vortices placed by hand read as decoration. Derive the field; document the model, its parameters and what is approximated (terrain, friction) next to the film.
Perspective text: plane-printed text at grazing angles is unreadable; print it for top-down shots and pin labels on low ones.
Rainbow ramps and glow turn the engraving into a weather app. One warm ramp, flat ink.
Horizon: a low camera shows the end of the world; haze it into paper and cap the footprint there.
Text over the strongest lines gets lost; place it beside the feature with a leader, or give it a paper halo.
styles.engine_section: - `demo/field.js`: Mercator kilometres (`toXY`, `toLL`), `makeStorm(track)` (spline track, monotone intensity, Holland B, Rmax, translation), `wind(X, Y, S)` (vortex, inflow, background, land and terrain), `buildTerrainGrid` for fast slope and land lookups. - `demo/wind.js`: `drawWind(g, cam, S, o)`, the streamline engine (levels, fixed-step RK2, time-of-flight strokes, buckets); `GRADES` (thresholds and ramp). - `demo/camera.js`: `makeCam({tx, ty, dist, tilt, head, fov, lift})` with `project`, `ray`, `footprint`, `rowAt`. - `demo/chartgl.js`: the printed ground in WebGL2 (height grids, land w

styles.name: Oscilloscope Math
styles.official_demo_line: How do you roll a square out of circles? Spinning circles stack into a square wave, until a dive into one corner finds the 9% spike that never goes away.
styles.principles: - The maths is real. Circles, curves, readouts, cursors and the formula come from one set of numbers: an epicycle chain is the actual Fourier series, a readout is the value at the drawn point, a measured distance is computed. Freeze any frame and it checks out. - Light, not ink. Everything is emitted light: a sharp core, a soft bloom, a white-hot centre where the beam is fast or new. Nothing is filled with flat colour. - The screen is glass in front of a world. HUD (formula, readouts, subtitles, credits) is fixed to the glass; the world (curves, circles, axis, graticule) moves behind it. - Tex
construction: Vector beam on a phosphor screen. Draw with constant-width lines in screen pixels (1.2–3.2 px), so a line stays a beam at any zoom. No scanlines (an analogue scope is a vector display).

Light channels. Draw three layers of light (beam trace, graticule and text, white-hot cores) plus an optional second channel for measurements; a post pass gives each its phosphor colour and glow. Beam layers bloom strongly; text blooms faintly so it stays cris
Bloom: several Gaussian blurs at 1/2 to 1/16 size added back; where light piles up it turns towards white, through a soft shoulder rather than clipping.

Afterglow is drawn, not accumulated. Earlier instants of moving objects (8–10 ghosts a few milliseconds apart, fading by a power curve) and a short trail behind a moving point. Frame-to-frame decay strobes at 24 fps; do not use it for anything that moves fast.
A fast beam leaves less light. Steep segments of a trace are drawn dimmer (about 55–60 % on a vertical edge); older parts of a scrolling trace fade with age.
Graticule: dotted minor lines, a solid centre axis with 0.2-division ticks, refined in levels of 5 as the camera zooms (the finer level fades in).
colour_logic: One phosphor family; colour means role, not decoration.
Beam green for anything the signal draws; paler green for graticule and text; white-hot for the beam's newest point, joints and arms, and the flash of anything just created.
Amber = the second channel: measurement cursors, measured values, markers of a finding. Never used for decoration, never for the signal itself.
No other hues. Grey cards only for unfinished placeholders.
motion: Rotation is uniform and real (the frequencies are the maths). Growth eases in: a new element grows from nothing at the point it attaches to in about 0.45 s, flashing white (in our demo, a new circle at its parent's tip).
Additions accelerate rather than repeat: one, then a few, then too many to count.
Live values update every frame; when a value is the point, it is shown at the precision that stays constant.
STOP freezes the signal; the camera may keep moving through the frozen world.
camera_grammar: Push onto a rotation, then ride a moving point
Match cut between two curves of the same shape
Pull back over a whole curve
Dive into a detail (×10 and more), graticule refining, TIME/DIV shrinking
sound_palette: The signal is audible: a quiet tone computed from the same numbers as the trace on screen (in our demo, the same partial sum as the picture: each new circle adds its harmonic).

Lead: plucked synth tones whose timbre follows the signal on screen (in our demo, a pure sine for one term, richer with every term added); tuned bells (glockenspiel, bowed vibraphone, sine bells) for events; a soft synth bass with 2nd and 3rd harmonics.

Instrument foley: relay clacks for RUN/STOP and power, knob detent clicks, short blips for readouts and cursors, a tick per glyph as the beam writes, filtered-noise sweeps for morphs and camera dives, a falling zap for power-off; a faint electrical hum bed.
Silence: STOP cuts the music dead; the twist is heard over hum and a slow clock.
pitfalls_limits: Numbers that don't match the picture. Compute every readout from the drawn values; never type them.
Strobing afterglow. Frame-accumulated decay at 24 fps leaves doubled curves; draw ghosts sub-frame.
Thin features vanish when sampled. Sample curves at screen resolution and add dense samples around edges and spikes, or a 0.1 px spike disappears.
Crowded chains. Small circles pile up at the tip; push in, or draw only the circles larger than about a pixel and limit ghosts to the first few.
Out of frame. Size the chain so its full reach stays inside the graticule (a sum of radii can exceed the radius you expect).
Text in the glow. Keep glow on beams, not on type; no outlines or drop shadows on text.
Readouts that flicker. A value meant to be read is shown at a precision that holds still.
Facts. Mathematical claims shown as numbers come with their source (FACTS.md).
styles.engine_section: - `demo/film.py`: `frame(t)` returns the Manim mobjects for second `t` (world, camera `cam(t)`, `chain(t)`, `trace(s, t)`, `peak(N)`, titles via `WorldGlyphs`, HUD, amber layer, subtitles, end card); `render`, `events`, `subs`, `texts` commands. `tex/formulas.json`: MathJax SVG templates for the formula with any upper limit. - `demo/post.py`: the phosphor pass (channels → colour, bloom, shoulder, vignette, dither, CRT power-off). - `demo/mix.py`: voice, the Fourier plucks, signal tone, foley and score from `events.json`. - Minimal example of something new: a single phasor and its projection. `

styles.name: Paper Pop-up Book
styles.official_demo_line: A pop-up book opens on a desk; a sprite named Pip adventures through paper worlds and jumps out into ours.
styles.principles: Two worlds in one frame. The real world at human scale: a photoreal surface lit by an HDRI room, a few real objects, a macro lens (shallow focus, warm practical light, soft contact shadows). The paper world: a hardcover book in that room; when it opens, one board stands up as the backdrop and the lower page is the ground. Every set piece is a flat cut-paper card that lies on the page and pops up around its bottom edge. Characters are cut paper too: a few centimetres tall, flat, with a thick off-white border, a grey cardboard edge and grain.
construction: Real units (metres): page 0.3–0.5 m wide, actors 3–5 cm, near plane a few mm, so HDRI, shadows and depth of field behave like a real macro shot.

Cut-paper finish: Canvas2D art with a dark ink outline; its silhouette dilated (drawn at many angles on several rings, recoloured `source-in`) into a grey cardboard edge offset slightly down (thickness) and a wide off-white border; a shared paper grain on top

Drawing: one dark-brown ink (never black), thick outline + thinner detail line, round joins; shading = one hard crescent (fill with shade, refill shifted with base); wobbly shapes (low-harmonic noise), never perfect geometry; simple faces.

Pop-up pieces: planes with art on the front and plain paper on the back (same alpha); `alphaTest` + `alphaToCoverage`; a custom depth material with the alpha map so the shadow is the cut-out silhouette. Anything "3D" is several flat cards (front/back layers, t
The book is modelled: cloth cover with foil title (roughness/metalness map), page block with edge lines, a curling leaf.
Real world: HDRI environment and softly blurred background, real wood or fabric, a few CC0 props. Neutral tone mapping (ACES shifts paper colours).
colour_logic: Saturated children's-book colour, never neon; the real world stays natural and slightly warm so paper pops against it.
One dominant hue family per spread, so a page turn is also a colour change; a few accents (a red, a yellow, a gold) recur across spreads to stitch the book together.
Ink dark brown, border off-white, card backs plain paper.
Unfinished or "outside the story" pages lose colour: graphite on cream. Night is a change of the paper art; the real lamp keeps its warmth.
motion: On ones (60 fps suits the smooth macro camera), all a pure function of `t`. Paper moves stiffly; life comes from easing: `back()` overshoot for pop-ups, springs for things on strings, squash and stretch on characters.
Pop-ups rise back to front (delay grows with distance from the reader), far pieces lying back, near ones folding forward face-down; they fold down in the same order.
Plants and light props sway a few hundredths of a radian around their base.
Characters are flat cards redrawn per quantized pose (walk phase, arms, eyes, mouth, look, blink); walk phase follows distance walked, so feet don't slide.
Turning around = a `scale.x` flip between front and back drawings; never `rotation.y`. Jumps: parabolic arcs, squash at both ends, a paper puff on landing.
Page turn: a many-segment strip whose bend is integrated along its length, so it curls like paper.
camera_grammar: Pull up to a 3/4 view of the spread
Reverse shot from inside the book to the blurred room
Rising crane leaving the book small
sound_palette: Paper foley is the signature: page swish, cardboard thump, pop-up snap (short sine sweep + crinkle), fold and crease, pull-tab slide, footsteps as tiny taps with crinkle, slat flaps, string-drop tinks; the book's spine creak and closing thump. All synthesizabl
Character voices as typing blips: one waveform and pitch range per character, a blip every other letter.
Narration: one warm storyteller, picture-book sentences; pronunciations kept apart from displayed text.

Music: whimsical, acoustic or toy-like: music box, pizzicato strings, clarinet, glockenspiel, ukulele, toy piano, brushes. Options: a warmer cue for anything in the real room; a bar-aligned internal edit of a library track so its ending lands on a picture even
native_moves: The real object plays a part
pitfalls_limits: `rotation.y` shows a card edge-on, then its blank back → `scale.x` flip. Negative scale also swaps front/back materials → draw mirrored props instead.
A one-plane container hides its contents → back card + front card, contents between.
Near-lens foreground pop-ups fill the frame with blur → move them or close the aperture.
Rectangle shadows kill the illusion → alpha-mapped depth material on every card; tight shadow bias and a big shadow map against acne on thin cards.
A turning page goes black facing away from lights → emissive map = colour map.
ACES shifts paper colours → Neutral.
Headless Chrome falls back to software WebGL → GPU ANGLE flags; ES modules need HTTP.
Redrawing character canvases each frame → redraw only on pose change.

styles.name: Glass Product Render
styles.official_demo_line: Unboxing and close-ups of Aura, fictional glass earbuds, in strip-light sweeps and caustics.
styles.principles: A single hero object of glass, metal and light floating in an infinite black studio. Long strips *behind and beside* it turn clear glass into a thin white outline with rainbow edges; the internals show through as in a display case. Everything moves slowly and precisely; every cut, sweep and pulse lands on the beat.
construction: Studio = a strip-light scene, not an HDRI. Photo-studio HDRIs contain windows and clutter that print as messy streaks on glass. Build a tiny black scene of emissive planes and bake it to PMREM every frame (`pmrem.fromScene(env, 0, 1, 1000)`, dispose the previo

Clear glass: `MeshPhysicalMaterial`, transmission 1, roughness ≈ 0.015, IOR ≈ 1.5, thickness sets lensing (thicker = stronger), dispersion on (three r163+), near-neutral attenuation, `side: DoubleSide` so other glass sees its back faces.

Frosted glass: transmission ~0.85, roughness ~0.4, milky tint, thick. On black it reads as dark grey plastic unless something bright is behind or inside it: an opaque emissive shape inside (blurred into a soft internal glow) and/or a bright gradient behind.

Metals make transparency worth looking at: satin bands, chrome (roughness ≥ ~0.14), brushed surfaces via a roughness map, boards with gold traces. Anything inside transmissive glass must be opaque (only opaque objects reach the transmission buffer).

Light guides: dark polished opaque acrylic, clearcoat, emissive comet pulses along a UV axis via `onBeforeCompile` (Gaussian head, exponential tail, white-hot core, hue drifting with age). Idle emission ≈ 0.

Background: black with an optional dark-grey radial sweep that separates glass edges; the floor fades into it, no horizon line. Floor: black gloss, blurred mirror, radial fade, procedural caustics (lens ring with R/G/B radii offset, warped Voronoi filaments, r
colour_logic: The world is neutral: black, greys, the white of strip reflections, the metals' own tints.

One accent colour family, reserved for light (emission, caustic rings, the dispersion line on UI), optionally drifting between two neighbouring hues with age or energy. Examples: ice blue → soft violet; amber → rose; green → cyan. Pick it from what the product
Emitters that only illuminate (inside frosted glass) stay cool-white and dim.
Dispersion rainbows are allowed only at thick glass edges and in the caustic, never as a gradient on surfaces or type.
motion: Everything moves on ones (24 fps), eased: ease-in-out for camera orbits, ease-out for parts decelerating into a float, ease-in for a snap back.
The camera always drifts: slow orbits or push-ins; never a locked-off frame, never handheld, except a couple of frames of micro-shake on an impact.

Exploded view: parts spread along the axis (~2× product size), each with a small deterministic tilt and a spin proportional to its offset; long ease-out apart → short drifting hover → very short ease-in snap on a downbeat.
Objects lift out of cradles tilted toward camera and settle upright; lids hinge at the back and stand behind the object as a backlit halo.
Light pulses and sweeps are events on the beat grid, not free animation.
camera_grammar: Sweep over a dark object, slow push
Macro, rack focus surface → part inside
Exploded view, axis ~40° to view, orbit
sound_palette: Minimal electronic, never piano-and-strings. Timbres, as options: bowed-glass or wet-finger tones, granular crystal clouds, glass bells and FM glass plucks, a filtered tick grid for precision, a warm pad, sub drone, soft short kicks and claps, 808 bass (sine w
Lock every pulse, sweep and snap to the score: write the cue map first and share one hit list between the score and the renderer; light pulses may follow a syncopated bass pattern exactly.
Silence as a tool: a short stretch of total silence (reverb tails cut too) before a release, at most a reverse whoosh inside it.

Foley follows the material: glass shimmer for sweeps (band-passed noise + inharmonic partials, panned with the strip); glass-metal friction for moving covers; magnetic clicks (sub-2 ms transient + 3–5 kHz metal resonances + low thump); air puffs for moving par
pitfalls_limits: A manually updated mirror uses last frame's camera → call `scene.updateMatrixWorld(); camera.updateMatrixWorld()` first; the transmission pre-pass re-renders it → no-op its `onBeforeRender`, update once per frame.

A coloured emitter inside frosted glass tints the whole object; idle glow under a lens dome becomes a pale blob; AgX turns accents white; frosted glass on black is black; mirror chrome becomes a white disc → the rules in §2–§3.
An exploded view seen perpendicular to its axis is edge-on lines → axis ~40° to camera.
Pure profiles read as simple shapes (mushrooms, pot lids) → 3/4 views, lids upright behind.
Bass peaks without headroom push loudnorm into dynamic mode → limit them in the mix.
Concave glass facing camera prints the front card as a grey rectangle → card off.
styles.engine_section: In `demo/`: `studio.js` (strip env baked per frame, sweep, background, floor mirror + caustics + rings), `product.js` (glass / frosted / metal / guide materials, comet-pulse shader, `explode()`), `main.js` (staging, cameras, frosted subtitle bar, title glint), `story.js` (beat-grid timeline shared with the score), `music/score.py`, `mix.py` (foley + voice + ducking). New object: replace the geometry in `product.js` (e.g. a glass cylinder with a coiled light guide), keep materials and `studio.js`.

styles.name: Memphis Diorama
styles.official_demo_line: One river bend, four seasons, one take; each turns when the big tree squats and springs back.
styles.principles: - Paper and a grainy frame. A warm white ground; the picture lives in a rounded, organic frame whose edge dissolves into grain. It grows open from the centre at the start and draws back in at the end. - Memphis flat colour. Saturated primaries plus pastels, flat fills, no gradients; a deep-indigo ink outline; small patterns tiled on surfaces (dots, stripes, zigzags, terrazzo flecks, halftone). - The eye of a model-maker. High three-quarter, top-down or cutaway views. The film always looks at a *place*, never at a person. - Small motions everywhere. Water, wind in trees, cloud shadows, birds, b
construction: Three tones only: the top face is the brightest, sun-facing sides keep the base colour, the faces turned away drop to about ×0.5–0.95. Hard edges between faces, never smooth shading.
Hard shadows, never blurred, tinted cool purple (shadow ≈ base × (0.70, 0.58, 0.90)); the sun direction never changes within a film.
Halftone in the shade: inside shadows, a staggered grid of lighter dots in world space, like a print. It turns dark areas into texture instead of dirt.

Outline as a post pass from normals and depth: about 2 px deep indigo `#25214A` at 1080p. Light cones, decals, particles (rain, snow, petals, smoke) and thin stems carry no outline; a thin object that is all outline reads as an ink scribble.
Patterns belong to the world: dots and stripes are computed from world coordinates and stay on the object as it moves. Pattern scale grows with distance so far surfaces do not buzz.

Detail is built, not textured: a house is a plinth, plank-striped walls, white corner trims, two roof slabs and a ridge, a gable with a round window, framed windows with shutters and flower boxes, a door with a step, awning and lamp. A tree is a trunk with a b
colour_logic: The ground outside the frame is always warm white `#FFFCF6`; nothing else is drawn there.
5–7 saturated hues + 2–3 pastels carry the picture. Ink `#25214A` is only for outlines, type, tyres and window frames.

Cluster colour by area: neighbouring blocks differ in hue; one colour's share is controlled (a field type at about a third of the ground, not sprinkled at random). Leave large calm areas of one colour (water, a field, a square) so the picture can breathe.
Day is bright and warm. When it gets dark, darken by the scene: a night scene may be dark, but never grey all over.
motion: 60 fps, every frame moves; no stepping, no jitter. The frame's grain boils at 12 fps, which is the only thing on twos.
Shapes may be simple; motion may not. Everything eases. Vehicles accelerate, brake and nod; turns follow smooth curves, never polylines.
All natural motion is procedural and looping: water, trees, cloud shadows, leaves, snow, smoke, flocks. Every object has its own phase; nothing marches in step.
People are distant decoration: small, walking a cycle, flying a kite, rowing. No close-ups, no acting, no hand business.
Things never pop into being: they grow from nothing or bounce in with a back-ease; a change of state is announced by an object squashing down and springing back (anticipation, then overshoot).
What never moves: the frame's position, the type's position, the paper, the sun direction.
sound_palette: Warm, gentle and continuous: piano, Rhodes-like electric piano, marimba, celesta, music box, soft synth bass, a warm pad, brushes and shaker. A quiet stretch can be piano and pad alone.

One piece, not a medley: when the place changes (a season, day to night), keep the same harmony and tempo and change only how thick the accompaniment is. A section that stops and a new one that starts sounds broken.

Foley is the sound of small things, kept under the music: birds, ducks, water, a bicycle bell, raindrops, leaves, geese, wind, snow, the click or *ting* of a light coming on. Tuned foley (a light coming on) uses notes of the current chord or its pentatonic sca
The same event always makes the same sound: if every change of state starts with a squash, every squash gets the same thump, spring and rising harp.
styles.engine_section: `demo/memphis.js` (three.js r170): `Diorama(glCanvas, ctx2d)` renders at 2× with a normal-and-depth outline pass, composites the grainy organic frame (`grow` opens it) and draws the bottom type (`drawText`). `flat(hex, o)` is the flat material: `pat` (1 dots, 2 diagonal stripes, 3 zigzag, 4 vertical stripes, 5 hatch, 6 horizontal stripes), `patCol`, `patScale`, `lit` (no face tones), `emit`, `win` (facade windows), `nightCol`, `col2` / `patCol2` (the next state for a wave). Globals: `setSeason(x, z, r)` (wave), `setHalftone(1)`, `setNight`, `setDusk`, `setLamps([[x, y, z, r]…])`, `setWave` / `

styles.name: Satellite Briefing
styles.official_demo_line: A satellite follows the map to the Aral Sea and finds a desert; only the part someone dammed came back.
styles.principles: - The ground is a photograph: real, licence-clean, georeferenced satellite or aerial imagery of the actual place. Nothing on the ground is drawn, stylised or generated. - Two layers, two truths: the imagery is what the satellite saw; the hairlines are what the analyst measured. Marks are thin, white, sparse, and sit on real coordinates. - The grade moves with the story: orbit in true colour, the analysis layer in grey, colour back only where the story turns. - Scale is the camera: one zoom from orbit to the ground built from nested plates, with an altitude readout and a scale bar from the same
construction: Plates: georeferenced rasters with a lon/lat box, sampled in a shader where the camera ray hits the ground, nested by resolution (world → region → detail) with feathered edges so finer plates dissolve in as the camera descends.
Globe: ray–sphere from a perspective camera, a thin atmosphere rim, limb shading at orbit only; compute |C|² − R² in double precision (float32 fails below a few tens of km).

Time: dated plates share one grid. A soft scan front (a satellite pass, never a hairline) swaps them: north → south forward, south → north for a rewind. Growth can run outward from the old edge, ordered by a distance map.

The analyst's grade (one uniform from colour to grey): luminance with local contrast and clarity, a shoulder so salt, snow and cloud stay below white, toned blue-black → cool silver up to ~65 % grey, a fifth of the chroma. White belongs to the marks.

Marks: a 2D overlay through the same world → screen function: hairlines 1.2–2.6 px with a dark halo, dashes for history and claims, brackets, ticks, leader lines. Lines draw on; outlines print behind the scan.
Screen space only for instruments (altitude, scale bar, imagery credit) and the transcript strip. Everything else is anchored to the ground.
colour_logic: Neutral ground: grey, roughly 3–65 % in value. White means *measured*.
One accent (warm, e.g. amber) for the single reading on screen, never decoration.
A second hue may mark the claim the imagery tests (a map, a plan, a promise): flat, cartographic, never used for anything measured.
True colour is evidence: at orbit, and again only where the story turns (the field that greened, the water that returned).
motion: The camera never stops: distance interpolates in log space, segments ease, holds keep a 2–5 % creep or a slow rotation. No frozen frame longer than a second.
Marks arrive by being made: a line grows, an outline prints behind the scan, a counter rolls and lands with a small pop, a reticle snaps with overshoot.
Time changes are scans, never dissolves; their spacing tells the speed, and the camera moves with them (accelerating as the steps shorten, braking on the last).
Never moves: the ground under its annotations, the instrument positions.
sound_palette: Telemetry: FM pings (a lock-on ping worth bringing back), dry ticks on the grid that divide to accelerate, noise scans (rising for a rewind, falling forward), servo whines, a ratchet for a range line.
Weight: timpani, bass drum, gran cassa, bowed cymbal, a tam-tam reversed when time runs backwards. Measurements land on a pitched hit.
Synthesis: a pulse bass with audible 2nd and 3rd harmonics, detuned-saw pads under a low-pass, risers for dives.
Beds: orbit hum, radio hiss, data chatter; the place's own ambience (wind, water, a far horn), sparingly, often as J- or L-cuts.
native_moves: Time rings in a locked frame.
Colour returns where the story turns.
pitfalls_limits: Licences: not usable: Google Earth/Maps, Bing, Esri World Imagery, Mapbox Satellite, Planet, Maxar, news photos, AI-generated imagery. EOX Sentinel-2 cloudless is CC BY 4.0 only for 2016 (2018 onward is NC). Raw Copernicus Sentinel data need "Contains modified

Finding imagery for a new place: search by bounding box and date in the Planetary Computer STAC (Landsat C2, Sentinel-2 L2A; no account) or USGS EarthExplorer; MODIS/VIIRS and Blue Marble from NASA GIBS; coastlines, lakes and rivers from Natural Earth (borders
Seams: paths imaged on other days disagree. One date per path, each scene gain-matched on stable land, feathered overlaps, holes filled from the same year only.

Old sensors: Landsat MSS (to 1992) has no blue or SWIR and drops scan lines: nearest-neighbour resampling, near-zero rows as nodata filled from same-year scenes, scan-angle streaks cleaned on land only. Inspect every year at full contrast.
Plumes and haze cross water as bright diagonal bands: swap the scene for another date of the same year rather than painting it out.
Edges: resampling against nodata darkens scene rims (erode the mask); drop contour pieces along a plate border. Real straight edges (dikes, polders) can read as seams: frame them out or label them.
Grey mush at close range: raise local contrast for that altitude only and dim outside the measured corridor.
Water and cloud: MNDWI where shortwave infrared exists, only the basin you measure; clouds read as features in grey, so use the dry season.
styles.engine_section: - `demo/engine.js`: `makeCamera({lat, lon, d, tilt, heading, sx, sy})`, `project()` / `unproject()`, the WebGL2 plate shader (nested plates, time scans, growth map, analyst grade, printed-map layer, whip blur). - `demo/overlay.js`: hairlines, brackets, `readout`, the measured single-line `subtitle` strip, `text` with a registry for `window.TEXTS`. - `demo/tools/`: `fetch_landsat.py` (STAC, one date per path, same-year gap fill), `plates.py` (normalisation, streak cleaning, water masks, areas), `vectors.py` (shorelines, distances), `mapfield.py` (the printed map), `growth.py`. - Extra packages

styles.name: Engineering Briefing Board
styles.official_demo_line: Four bridge types are tested on one briefing wall, and the ship that must pass under picks the winner.
styles.principles: 1. A physical board in a room: enamel, window falloff, a sliding reflection, ghosts of earlier work, frame and tray. 2. Real things on it: cut-out photographs of the real objects, a few millimetres off the board, shadowed by one window, parallaxing. They are evidence: never a generated image presented as a real object. 3. Ink that means something: graphite for names and rules, blue for water and measurement, red only for the decision; rejected ideas erased to ghosts. 4. One continuous wall: no pages; the camera travels along lines, projections and leaders. 5. The whole wall, once: every shot i
construction: Board (z 0): procedural enamel, wiped ghost strokes, smudges, a window falloff, a sliding diagonal reflection; the frame shadows a warm grey wall.

Ink (multiply): flat colour at about 90 %, lighter core, round caps, a wet-tip glint on the stroke being drawn. Lettering: a marker font revealed glyph by glyph with seeded tilt and baseline jitter. Erasing leaves a blurred ghost (about 7 %).

Prints (z ≈ 6–14): photographs cut out at full resolution (a matting model, or a hand polygon / mask), clean edges, one shared grade (lower saturation, a touch warmer, lifted blacks). Thin structure (cables, wires, masts, railings) is measured in the photo and

Secondary layer (only where the camera never goes before the end): the photos as pinned prints, a source card, sums on sticky notes, a small sketch. Texture and proof for the final wall, lighter than the main line.
Props (z ≈ 8–26): magnetic tags, magnets, a steel ruler, printed cards, a pitted stamp impression; the tray (z 70) nearest the lens.
Camera: parallax by height, sub-frame motion blur (180° shutter), light grain. Only subtitles are screen-space.
colour_logic: Ground: the enamel and its light falloff; the wall around is neutral warm grey.

Ink: graphite = names, rules, facts; blue = water and measurement (dimensions, projection lines, measured numbers); red = the decision (a rejection, the key word of a verdict, the one mark to notice); grey for drafting only (extension lines, hatching).
Red is rare: two or three red marks per frame at most, never on a red object. Full colour belongs to the photographs; props stay neutral; a red magnet is a verdict.
motion: 24 fps on ones; nothing is stepped.
Camera: overlapping eased moves, velocity ∝ u^a (1−u)^b (a, b ≈ 1.5–4), so speed and acceleration never jump; b > a gives inertia. A hand-held breath (≤ 3 px) underneath; shake only on an impact.

Weight: prints are lowered from the camera side, land, bounce and settle as the shadow tightens; magnets clack on to pin them; tags swing; removed magnets pop toward the lens; struck things jolt and spring back. The camera may meet a landing close, briefly, on
Blurred in motion, sharp where words are read. Every 1–2 beats something lands, draws or swings; only silences and judgement holds go still.
Ink draws at the speed of a hand; dimension lines land with an arrowhead tap.
Never: dissolves, scale-pops on text, bouncy UI easing, text fading in by itself.
camera_grammar: Ride a line (with the pen or a dimension)
Whip with the line, overshoot, settle
Staircase framing (each new item with the previous result)
Judgement frame: the whole item, the limit and the verdict, held ≥ 2.5 s
Long pull-back to the whole wall
sound_palette: Room: an air-conditioning bed and traffic through the window, about 20 dB under the voice — audible, not a hiss; silences keep only this.

Foley: felt-tip squeaks scaled to stroke length, nib taps, magnet clacks (a pitch per magnet in a row), suction pops, print landings (board thump, paper slap), a ruler's ring, eraser felt, a stamp's thud.
The subject's own sound arrives early as a J-cut; the first sound after a silence is an impact or the subject's sound.

Music: a small rhythmic ensemble, walking to brisk — bass, a light kit, wooden percussion, low brass stabs for verdicts (or mallets); no piano-and-strings pad. Landings, stamps and arrows sit on the beat. Voice calm, briefing-room confident, about 8–10 dB over
native_moves: The subject passes through the answer.
pitfalls_limits: Text glimpsed in passing fails the reading time. Fix: words where the camera rests; frame each new item with the last result.
Only close-ups. The viewer never sees the whole object against the limit. Fix: detail → judgement frame → hold → verdict → move on.
Photos that don't belong together. Fix: one grade, one light vector, one viewpoint family.
Thin parts lost or stair-stepped by the matte. Fix: key them against the clean background, redraw clean lines at the measured positions.
Upsampled photos go soft in close-ups. Fix: full-resolution cuts, large sources, a per-frame check.
Lettering in photos (signs, names, logos). Fix: paint out, cut, or choose another photo.

The wall seen too early spends the ending; a sparse or tiny final wall wastes it. Fix: measure every frame's visible share; size the hierarchy for the poster; a quiet secondary layer, no empty middle.
styles.engine_section: - Photos: Wikimedia Commons (read each file page's licence and author), national libraries and archives (e.g. the Library of Congress: check each item's rights statement), agency media pages, Flickr Commons. Fine: CC0, public domain, CC BY (credit it). CC BY-SA, "no known restrictions" (≠ CC0) or other terms: name them to the user and ask first. For the user's own product, site or people, ask for their photos. No licensable photo of a real thing → draw it in marker as a sketch; never a generated image presented as the real object. - Facts: keep a `FACTS.md` in the project folder (each claim on

styles.name: LiDAR Survey
styles.official_demo_line: A laser survey strips the canopy off a Connecticut forest and finds 3.4 km of old farm walls.
styles.principles: - The cloud is the data: every point is a real return at its measured position; points appear, glow, lift away or give way to a surface, but are never moved into a shape. - Points become a surface: a front (scan line, cutting plane) behind which the cloud condenses into a solid model of the same place. - Classification is a lever: ground, vegetation, buildings, water are layers to peel, isolate and recolour. - Measurement in hairlines: one reading at a time, in the accent, attached to what it measures; numbers from the points or an official source. - Dark, quiet, exact: near-black ground, rest
construction: Points: GL points sized in world units (0.12–0.3 m), floor of one output pixel, soft discs, opaque and depth-tested (additive only for a ghost layer); colour from height or class, value from intensity; distance fog.
Quantise for the browser: uint16 positions (2 cm / 1 cm) plus a byte each for height above ground, class, intensity, seed.
Height above ground for every return (minus a ground model triangulated from class-2 returns) drives the colour ramp, the cutting plane and the ruler.

The solid surface: a 0.5–1 m mesh of the ground or surface model, smooth normals, baked short-radius AO, a low raking sun (20–35°), faint contours, crests lightened. Display exaggeration of micro relief (×2–3) only with an on-screen note; measure on undistorte
The front: one world-space plane (one uniform) shared by the point and surface shaders; points ahead of it brighten, a thin seam glows behind it and the surface fills in over tens of metres.
The cutting plane (by height above ground): returns above it lift away and fade, a ring glows where it meets the trees, a ruler on the frame edge tracks it.
colour_logic: Background near-black with a cold tint; never pure black, never a gradient sky.
Points: one ramp by height or class, desaturated (deep green-teal → pale; or grey → white); intensity modulates value, not hue. No rainbow elevation ramps.
The front and seams: one cool near-white; it is light, not a colour.
The solid surface: warm neutral (stone, clay, plaster), lit; its colour never competes with the accent.
motion: On ones, 24 fps; the camera never stops; keys as a C1 spline in target / distance / heading / pitch (no `lookAt` from nadir).
The front moves on an ease, slowest where the subject is; a cutting plane steps on the beat (eased steps, short holds) so the layers read.
Points appear behind a front or by height, never by random fade-in across the whole frame.
Readings land with a small pop; traced features light up along their length in order.
Never moves: the points relative to each other (no wobble, no noise displacement), the instruments' positions.
camera_grammar: Crane down with tilt to oblique
Low oblique close to the cloud (10–20° pitch, 90–150 m)
sound_palette: Instrument sounds: FM pings, fine crackle as points arrive, noise sweeps tied to a front, ticks that divide (8ths → 16ths → 32nds) to accelerate, a descending pitched blip per peeled layer, a ratchet while a counter rolls, a ping when a reading lands.
Weight and synthesis: timpani, bass drum, gran cassa for condensations and cuts, a reversed swell into the main impact; low-passed detuned-saw pads; a pulse bass with audible 2nd/3rd harmonics.
Dry and wet: one option is electronics while the subject is still points, and a single organic, wooden or bowed timbre (marimba, bowed vibraphone) for the found features once the surface exists.
Beds: the place's own ambience (wind in leaves, water, traffic) at the start and the end as J- and L-cuts; a thin air bed in between.
pitfalls_limits: Finding data for a new place: USGS 3DEP (US) as Entwine Point Tiles per project at `https://s3-us-west-2.amazonaws.com/usgs-lidar-public/<project>/ept.json`, projects and footprints in `boundaries/resources.geojson` of github.com/hobuinc/usgs-lidar; bare-earth

Licences: public domain, CC0, CC BY and attribution-only government licences are fine, with credit in `CREDITS`. ODbL, CC BY-SA, "no known restrictions" (not CC0) or non-commercial terms: name them to the user and ask first. Never commercial scans or Google 3D
Facts: keep a FACTS.md in the project folder (claim, source URL, quoted wording, or the measurement method) and deliver it with the film.
Coordinates: EPT copies are often Web Mercator: convert to a local east/north/up frame first; check the vertical datum against known ground.
Leaf-off vs leaf-on: leaf-off lidar reaches the ground but its canopy is sparse; say which season each layer is.
Classification is the provider's: class 1 mixes vegetation, buildings and noise; drop 7 and 18; finish a cut below 0 m or low vegetation stays as stripes.
A dense cloud reads as a flat carpet from afar: go close and low for volume; let the distance fog out.
Scan striping is real texture; don't frame a reveal on it at grazing angles.
