styles.name: Under the Microscope
styles.official_demo_line: One continuous move from a liver slide to a single nucleus; two circles, counted pixel by pixel, differ 2.4 times in blue.
styles.principles: - The specimen is a photograph: a real micrograph or whole-slide scan of the actual sample, CC0, public domain or CC BY. Nothing on the specimen is drawn, retouched or generated. A whole-slide image (WSI) is the ideal source: one sample, one registered pyramid from millimetres to microns, with the pixel size in its metadata. - Scale is the camera: one log-space dive (and, when the story wants it, the climb back) through nested plates of the same sample. The scale bar shortens and jumps in a 1-2-5 sequence, the field-of-view readout rolls, the magnification steps. - Focus has a grammar: a rack-
construction: Plates: the WSI pyramid levels as plates in one world frame (level-0 pixels), the coarse levels whole and alpha-feathered at the scan edge, the fine levels as crops around where the camera lands. Each frame draws the finest plate that is downsampled no more th

The naked-eye plate: the scanner's own photo of the whole slide (many WSI files carry one), registered through the scan's area-of-interest metadata and checked against the tissue's centroid. Cut the glass out of the scanner tray, remove the line-sensor streaks
One grade for every plate: glass normalised to a warm white, a little density and chroma in the stain, nothing else. No false colour, no film emulation.
The bench: graphite under a slow pool of light; a soft shadow under the slide.

Focus: screen-space Gaussian blur on a frame rendered with a margin (so edges never go dark); the focal sweep is a tilted sharp front crossing a softened frame. A light illumination vignette, nothing more.

Marks in screen space but anchored to the specimen through one world → screen function: hairlines 1.5–2.5 px with a dark or light halo, circles drawn on as arcs with cardinal ticks, dimension lines with end ticks, leader lines with one elbow. Counted pixels ar
colour_logic: Glass: warm paper white. Bench: graphite. The stain is evidence and keeps its true colour (e.g. trichrome red and blue, H&E pink and purple).
One accent, cool and away from the stain's hues (mint against red and blue; amber against a green or purple stain), only for the measured reading and the counted pixels.
Ink on glass is near-black; type on stain sits on a frosted panel in warm white.
motion: The camera is a similarity transform (zoom, roll, position) interpolated as a log spiral between keys (M^u about the fixed point of the two frames), so every push is a true dive towards one point and the roll is part of it. Ease the moves, creep 2–5 % during h
Magnification changes happen where the plates actually change, each with a breath of focus, a turret click and the new magnification said once, large.
Marks arrive by being made: a dimension line grows from its centre, a circle is drawn as an arc, a scan front counts pixels while the reading rolls, the reading lands with a small spring.
Never moves: the specimen under its marks, the instrument positions.
camera_grammar: Pull back to frame two marks
The climb (reverse dive, scale bar jumping back)
sound_palette: Instrument foley: the objective turret (a click, a detent, a small metal ring), a focus servo, pen on glass for each line drawn, a band-passed scan travelling left to right with counter ticks that speed up, a soft filtered sweep for the focal plane.

Music: hard-mallet vibraphone in 8ths and 16ths, marimba ticks, bowed vibraphone and water glasses for pads and the motif, glockenspiel for each reading that lands, a pulse bass with 2nd/3rd harmonics, timpani and bass drum under the landings. Harmony stays op
Beds: a quiet lab room (fan, a little mains hum).
Silence before the verdict and before the climb; the first sound after it is the reading or the turn.
native_moves: The focal sweep and the ring.
pitfalls_limits: Licences: most microscopy on the web is CC BY-NC or all rights reserved. Usable: CC0 whole-slide scans (e.g. the OpenSlide test data: check each file's licence line), public-domain government micrographs (NIH, CDC PHIL, NASA, USGS), CC BY collections (Cell Ima

Finding material for a new topic: search by organ, stain or material plus "whole slide" in the OpenSlide test data, NCI Imaging Data Commons (TCGA/CPTAC slides, licence per collection), the Cell Image Library, Wellcome Collection, Wikimedia Commons (filter by
Different samples never zoom into each other: two micrographs of "the same thing" at two scales are two specimens. Use one pyramid; if you must join sources, cut on a focus breath and say so.
Pixel size: read it from the file (XMP `ScanRes`, TIFF resolution, OME `PhysicalSizeX`); a slide-photo's resolution tag can be trusted only after checking against the scan.
Upsampling shows as mush beyond ~1.6×: end the dive at the scan's real resolution.
Tile seams: some scanners overlap tiles; check the joint info, frame out visible seams.
Labels and logos on the slide: barcodes and IDs are part of the object; manufacturer logos are not — fill or crop them.
Claims: a stain's colour means what the stain protocol says, nothing more; measured shares are of the drawn region and the stated threshold, never a clinical score.

styles.name: Archive Light Table
styles.official_demo_line: The telegram said 57 seconds; under a loupe, the Wrights' glass negatives and the archive say 59.
styles.principles: - The objects are real: scans of public-domain or licensed archive items, at their true proportions, with their real damage (broken corners, emulsion edges, folds, pencil marks). Nothing in them is drawn or generated. - Light comes from below: the table glows a near-white cool grey; film and glass transmit it, paper glows warm at its edges, opaque things read darker than the table. - The loupe is the camera's door: every dive into an object goes through a loupe that lands on it. The inside of the lens is where the object changes state. - Catalogue truth: every object carries its real identifie
construction: One world, one camera: every object is a textured quad on the table with a centre, rotation and scale (texture px → world units at true size). The camera is a 2D centre, zoom and roll; the table and every mark go through the same world → screen function.
The light table: an emissive surface (≈ 0.97 white, slightly cool), soft falloff, diffuser noise, an aluminium frame and a dark desk beyond. It can be switched off (ambient ≈ 0.04) and flicker on.

Glass negatives: transmission from the scan's positive, `T = 0.035 + 0.9 · (1 − pos)^1.25`, with a warm silver-gelatin tint; the emulsion mask comes from the scan (white margin touching the border = no glass), so broken corners show the table. Dust and scratch
Paper: backlit, its colour is transmission (paper tone × light); lit lines get darker ink and brighter paper; unlit text can dim to bring one line forward.

The loupe: inside the lens each pixel maps back to the table through the magnification (≈ 2.5×) with a pincushion term (k ≈ 0.16 at the rim), slightly different per RGB channel for colour fringes. Around it: a black ring with a bevel highlight and a clear acry

The photograph space: after the push the lens stops being a lens. A photo gains depth from a ground-plane nearness map (zero at the horizon, linear in the row below it), cut-out layers for upright subjects and a filled background; a dolly and a lateral shift d
colour_logic: Neutral ground: the light table (near-white, cool) and the archive's own tones (silver greys, paper tans). Do not regrade the archive into a colour scheme.
One signal colour (e.g. a signal orange) for marks, readings, anchors and the verdict; never as a fill behind pictures, never for decoration.
Text is ink (near-black) on light areas and paper-white on dark caption plates; choose the contrast by the ground, never colour on colour.
Positives inside the lens may be gently levelled (black and white points) so a weak scan reads; negatives stay as the glass gives them.
motion: 24 fps on ones; every camera parameter on smooth monotone curves through keys (no overshoot, no stepping).
The camera glides across the table, slows to let the loupe land, then pushes. Speed lives in the glides and pushes; holds are for reading.
The loupe lands with a fast ease-out (≈ 0.4 s), lifts the same way. Lines draw on in 0.3–0.6 s; text wipes in from its leader side; numbers count up and land with the voice.
What never moves: the archive's own content outside a photograph space, and the table itself.
camera_grammar: loupe landing + push into the lens
inside the lens: tracking along a line
pull back to the whole table
sound_palette: Ambience: the light table's ballast hum (100 Hz and harmonics), starter clicks, room tone. Inside a photograph the hum gives way to that place's air.
Foley: the loupe on glass (a clack with a high ring), paper sweeps for glides and lit lines, ticks for scales and counters, a pen stroke for a verdict, soft clicks as labels land.

Music: restrained and small: a felt piano, a few strings, glass or bowed metal for the moments of seeing. Build by subdivision and register, not by drums. Leave real silences before a reveal or a verdict; the first sound after them should be the loupe, the pla
Voice: a calm narrator, short sentences that state what the object says. Music about 10 dB under the voice, ducked while it speaks; −14 LUFS.
native_moves: Negative to positive under the loupe.
Two records, held side by side.
pitfalls_limits: Over-magnifying a weak scan: keep the lens interior under about 1.5 screen px per scan px; choose items by scan size.
The loupe sweeping over empty table: lay objects close together, land the loupe straight onto the object (drop in, don't slide in), and glide the camera over objects, not gaps.

Shear in the photograph space: one depth map for a photo with people or machines in it tears them apart. Cut upright subjects into layers, fill behind them, and keep 2.5D moves small enough that the fill is barely seen.
Labels that scroll away: a label on a moving table leaves the frame before it is read; hold the camera, or fix the caption on screen.
Vintage creep: no sepia, no halftone, no paper-ageing overlay. The age is in the objects, not the grade.
styles.engine_section: - `demo/film.js`: `IT` (objects: centre, rotation, scale), `toW()` / `toT()` (texture ↔ world), `CAM` keys and `w2s()`, `dive()` (loupe point, land/lift times, lens interior as tracks), `shot(t)`, `int2s()` (photograph → screen for marks), the shader (`lightTable`, `paper`, `negative`, `parallax`, rim and skirt), the overlay (`annot`, `measure`, `compare`, `indexPanel`). - `demo/tools/prep.py`: emulsion masks from scans, difference matting of a subject against a smooth sky, ground-only cuts, push-pull fill. - Minimal example, not in the demo: put one 35 mm slide (`IT.slide = {c, r, k, size}`),

styles.name: Security X-ray
styles.official_demo_line: One night at an airport screening console: a power bank, a bottle of water, and six live crabs that move in the CT.
styles.principles: - Transmission, not rendering. Every pixel is the path length of the X-ray through matter, split by material class. Overlaps change the colour (a cable over clothes turns green), walls glow at their edges, solid metal goes dark. - The colour code is the language. Orange = organic (Zeff < 10), green = mixed or light inorganic (Zeff 10–18), blue = metal (Zeff > 18), black = nothing got through. The legend sits on screen; the audience learns it within seconds. - A machine with a person behind it. The console chrome (lane, belt speed, clock, bag counter, material legend, function keys, status) is
construction: Thickness pass (three.js): every mesh double-sided, depth test off, additive blending into a float target. A fragment writes `±distance × density × class`, minus for front faces, plus for back faces, so each pixel holds the path length through organic (R), ino

Every solid must be closed. An open tube or a missing cap leaves a hole that reads as a dark or bright fleck; cap tube ends, keep winding outward, never mirror with a negative scale (it flips the sign).

Dual-energy colouriser (one full-screen shader): high and low energy attenuation from the three channels; their ratio picks the hue (orange → green → blue), the total sets brightness. Brightness rises with thickness, peaks, then falls towards black, so thick s

Two displays. The screening image is opaque on a navy belt background (so black can read as black); the CT volume is additive glow on the dark reconstruction field. Both use the same material classes.

The scan. A fixed curtain line; the bag moves through it; columns that have passed are in colour, the rest a pale grey preview. Material filters (organic strip, metal strip, high penetration) are wipes across the image.
Textures in object space: weave for fabric, lumps for food, paper and foam, anchored to the object and measured in millimetres so they stay put when the camera zooms.
colour_logic: The four material colours are reserved for X-ray matter. UI and annotations never use pure organic orange or metal blue as decoration.
Neutral ground: near-black navy for the console, a slightly lighter navy for the empty belt.
Operator colours, one meaning each: amber = flagged / under review, red = refused, green = cleared, pale blue = machine state (scanning, curtain, CT). One verdict colour per screen.
Text is near-white on dark plates; dim blue-grey for secondary machine text.
motion: The belt moves at constant speed with short decelerations to a stop (a real belt has inertia), and a small settle.
Operator actions are fast and precise: boxes are dragged open from a corner in 0.25–0.3 s, zoom eases in/out, measurement lines grow and tick.
Counters and clocks jump on cuts to compress hours; within a shot they run in real time.
Material filters and rescans are wipes; the CT appears through a short digital tear.
CT orbits are slow and continuous, ease in and out, with a push and a near-stop where the detail is.
Never moves: the console chrome, the legend, the view frames. Judged frames are locked.
camera_grammar: Push from booth into the screen
Tight crop on part of the console
sound_palette: One family of console tones (sine with a little second harmonic, soft edges): scan chirp, two-tone alarm, single clear tone, low buzzing refusal, rising beeps for list rows. Keep the same family for the whole film.

Machine foley: belt motor and rollers, X-ray tunnel buzz (120 Hz + filtered noise) while a bag passes, servo whine for zoom, relay clicks for keys, a CT gantry whir, a thump when the belt stops, a pitch-falling power-down.

Score: plucked and short-bowed strings (pizzicato, spiccato) for the flow, tremolo strings and timpani for a held judgment, harp and sustained strings for release; tuned percussion (vibraphone, marimba, glockenspiel, xylophone) for small comic or tender moment
Silence: drop the groove under a judgment, leave the hum.
pitfalls_limits: Wrong colours for the material. Aluminium is green-blue, steel blue, lithium cells blue-green, glass and bone green, water and food orange. Check every prop's class; a black area must be a genuinely thick, dense object.
Clutter. Too many overlapping objects turn into mud. Keep 4–8 readable objects per bag, iconic shapes (keyboard grid, coil spring, J-hook) and vary the classes.
Thin things vanish (a strap seen flat, a 1 mm plate): raise density or thickness until it reads at the shot's scale.
Open meshes and mirrored meshes produce flecks and negative thickness (see §2).
Text over the image. Panels go beside the object; dim the image outside the operator's box rather than covering it.
Flat side view. Low objects look like a strip in the side view; use it for tall or layered things, not for crops.
Facts. Screening rules differ between domestic and international flights and between airlines; quote the exact rule for the route you show, keep FACTS.md with source URLs and wording.
Render state. Set a render target's viewport and scissor before binding it; a stale viewport squashes the image and makes frames depend on render order.

styles.name: Radar Sweep Documentary
styles.official_demo_line: A storm at Parkes, 21 July 1969: a 64-metre dish tipped to its limit holds on and catches the moonwalk for the world.
styles.principles: - Existence is scanned. Nothing is lit by ambient light. A subject appears only when a scan reaches it: a bright front line, a short glow, then echoes that persist and decay. Black means "not yet seen", not "shadow". - Echoes are the material. Surfaces resolve into contour lines, range rings around the subject, a survey grid and ghost copies of the scan front, each fading at its own rate. A moving subject leaves wireframe after-images: the echo records time. - The subject keeps a cold rim. Once scanned, the hero object carries a thin cold rim light so its silhouette never sinks into the ground
construction: One scan function shared by every material in a space: `d = S − dot(p, D)` for a plane moving along `D`; `d < 0` is unseen (black), the front `exp(−d²/w²)` is the bright line, behind it a glow `exp(−d/L₁)` and a slow trail `exp(−d/L₂)` with `L₂ ≫ L₁`. Ghost co
Two scans can overlap: behind the new front the new scan applies, ahead of it the previous one keeps ageing. This is how a scan rewrites a scene into another time.

Echo geometry: contour lines from height, range rings around the subject, a coarse survey grid, all line-antialiased with `fwidth` and faded out where they would alias. Structure edges (EdgesGeometry) and panel seams follow the same scan.

Surfaces: near-black base, lit only by the scan terms, a small daylight term when the scene is a grey day, and a rim term `(1 − n·v)³` in cold blue for the subject. Additive lines for wireframe, opaque surfaces for silhouettes.

Hard light when there is a real light source (a low sun): flat-shaded facets, one strong direction, long planar shadows cast onto the ground. Crinkled foil or rough metal take a noise-perturbed normal and a narrow specular.

Sky: either deep night (a dim Milky Way and stars that never flicker) or an overcast day (a layered, slowly rolling cloud deck, brighter at the horizon, with slanted rain). The two must be told apart at a glance: day is a lit grey, never night.
colour_logic: Black is the ground. Brightness belongs to what the scan has just touched.
Echo colour: a cold blue-white (example `#B3DBFF`); the scan front is white.
One warm accent (example `#F2C48D`) reserved for the target and the signal path; at most one warm element per frame.
A warning red (example `#FF8C78`) only for a value over a limit, and only on the readout.
motion: The scan advances in surges on the beat (an ease-out push per beat, mixed with a steady drift so it never stops dead). Its speed is the film's pulse.
Echoes decay smoothly; nothing blinks.
Machines move with weight: anticipation, a long ease, a bounce against the stop, and a wireframe after-image trail while moving.
Weather, when a film has it (wind, rain, dust), moves continuously and slants with the gusts; the camera shakes only with the weather, more in close-ups.
Stars never move on screen: on a star shot the camera only translates (no rotation) and the sky rides with it.
Frame rate and grain: 24 fps.
camera_grammar: Low camera near the ground, slow push
Side medium with a slow orbit
Overhead or space view drifting around a globe
Interior hold, then a fast lateral track
sound_palette: Ambience first: wind (low, slow gusts), rain hiss, room tone; it drops away in space.
Scan foley: an air surge per push and a clean sonar ping (with two quieter echoes), panned with the scan; a struck metallic ring when the scan meets the subject.
Machines: drive motors, gear teeth, a heavy clank on the stop, metal groan under load, an electric bell behind glass.
Signal: a short quindar-like beep, a low carrier, TV hiss and line buzz that clean up when the source improves.
pitfalls_limits: Night everywhere: a day scene left as black as night tells the wrong time. Lift the sky and the ground into a grey day.
Too dark to read: subject and labels sinking into black. Give the subject a rim and lift the exposure of reading shots.
A scan front passing right in front of the lens blows out the frame; fade the front near the camera.
Star flicker: sub-pixel stars and a rotating camera. Keep stars ≥ ~1.5 output px, below the bloom threshold, and the camera unrotated.
Dark patches behind text show as smudges on a grey sky; use them only on night frames, or use a proper plate.
Floating models: a camera below the terrain or an object without ground contact; keep ground, horizon and base in frame, add contact shadows.
Blocky stand-ins: a recognisable machine needs its recognisable parts (legs, pads, facets, windows, antennas), not two boxes.
Fake data: a trace or gauge with invented numbers. Label only the sourced value; leave the rest unscaled.
styles.engine_section: three.js (WebGL2), one `render(t)`; per space a scene with its own scan uniforms; EffectComposer with bloom and a grade pass; a 2D canvas overlay for all type, gauges, tags and subtitles, positioned through the camera's projection. Scan wipes use a second renderer with a CSS clip. Everything is closed-form in `t`.

styles.name: Thermal Camera
styles.official_demo: A Building on a Winter Night
styles.official_demo_line: A thermal camera circles an old apartment block on a snowy night: a leaking window, pipes inside the walls, a cat asleep on a warm bonnet, and the same block a year after its retrofit.
styles.principles: - Temperature is the picture. Every pixel is an apparent temperature mapped through one palette and one scale; brighter means warmer, always. Nothing is coloured for drama. - It looks like a sensor. A coarse grid (320×240 or 640×480 class, cropped to 16:9) blown up to the frame, optical softness, temporal noise, column stripes, lens shading. Never a clean gradient. - Physics decides what glows. Surfaces get temperatures from heat flow (indoor vs outdoor, thermal bridges, leaks, bodies, engines), then emissivity and reflection decide what the camera reads: glass and bare metal look cold because
construction: Two passes, one camera. A picture pass (PBR, real lights, night or day) and a thermal pass in which every material writes °C into a float target. The composite chooses per pixel: picture, thermal, or a split.

Thermal materials: a surface temperature model (steady-state wall: T_out + ΔT·U·R_se; bridges as bands; local sources as Gaussians; plumes as animated noise), then `apparent = ε(θ)·T + (1−ε(θ))·T_reflected`, with emissivity falling off at grazing angles and th

Sensor simulation in screen space: render the thermal pass at ~3× the sensor grid, integrate with an optics blur into the sensor resolution, add temporal noise (~0.1 °C), fixed column/row patterns and corner shading, read the sensor back for all measurements,
Transparent heat (exhaust, breath, steam) blends in temperature space: alpha-composite °C, not colour.
The picture pass must hold up on its own (real light sources, believable materials); the thermal reveal is only as strong as the baseline.
colour_logic: One palette per film (iron: black → indigo → purple → magenta → orange → yellow → white).

The scale (level and span) is part of the story: wide span for overview, narrow span to reveal faint structure, the same scale when two images are compared. Out-of-range values clip to the palette ends.
The isotherm owns one colour outside the palette (a saturated green) and means only "above the threshold".
Overlay graphics are white with a dark halo; a single accent (pale green) is reserved for a verdict.
motion: 30 fps; sensor noise is new every frame, meter readouts refresh at ~6 Hz, overlays snap in with a short ease (crosshairs collapse onto their point, numbers roll up from the ambient value and land).
Heat moves the way heat moves: plumes rise and waver, breath and turbulence flicker, cooling is slow. Bodies breathe.
A scan line travels at a steady, mechanical pace (1–3 s across the frame) with a thin white edge and a faint warm glow on the thermal side.
Never moves: the scale bar and time stamp positions; a locked comparison frame.
Frame rate and grain: mux grain 1, a light film grain.
camera_grammar: Scan line across a locked or slowly pushing frame
Fixed split with the camera trucking past
Crane or tilt over an edge
Low push onto a living thing
sound_palette: The instrument: a faint fan hum whenever the camera is on; scan = electric hum + filtered noise sweep; lock-on beep with a quick roll of ticks; a two-tone alarm for the isotherm; a soft mechanical clack for the detector's flat-field shutter (NUC); a click for
The world's heat as sound: wind and cold air, water moving in pipes, an engine ticking as it cools, the sounds of the living subject (breath, a rustle, a footstep) kept close and dry.

Music: sparse and cold (bowed vibraphone, glass, harp, celesta-like glockenspiel, strings in a low register); a pulse that can turn into a heartbeat when the subject is circulation; one warm chord for the verdict.
Mix: tones and foley over the music; music ducks under readouts and living sounds; low end under control (high-pass ~40 Hz); about −16 LUFS before mastering, true peak ≤ −3 dBTP.
pitfalls_limits: Glass is not transparent. Infrared does not see through windows; lit rooms look no warmer. Never show interiors through glass in the thermal pass.
Reflections lie. Shiny metal and glass show the sky's cold or a lamp's heat, not their own temperature. Measure on matte, high-emissivity surfaces, or say what is reflected.
Too clean reads as CG. Without noise, optics blur and a coarse grid, the image looks like a gradient render. Simulate the sensor, then upsample.
Moiré from fine geometry (railings, grilles, branches): supersample the thermal pass and blur before decimating to the sensor grid.
Numbers must match colours. Read every value from the same temperature buffer that is coloured; register the measured median for reading time; keep the scale range visible whenever a value is shown.
Comparisons on different scales are meaningless. Lock level and span before judging.

Trackers must not chatter. The per-frame hottest pixel is noisy: two equally warm spots (two eyes, two bulbs) swap places from frame to frame and the marker jitters by whole sensor pixels. Find the hot point once from the buffer, pin the marker to that point o
Thin hot features vanish at distance. A crack or a gap one sensor pixel wide reads cooler from far away; frame closer or use a box maximum.
styles.engine_section: - `demo/src/thermal.js`: `TM()` (generic thermal material: base, gradient, hot spots, noise, emissivity) and `TMC(body)` (custom GLSL body writing `T`, `eps`); `apparent()` and `envT()` in `glsl.js`; `setPass()` swaps every mesh between its picture and thermal material. - `demo/src/post.js`: render targets, the sensor pass (optics, noise, fixed pattern, shading, read-back), bloom, and the composite (split line, isotherm, depth-edge overlay, palette). - `demo/src/hud.js`: colour scale, spot meter, box stats (`boxStat` → avg/max/max position), labels with leaders, the `window.TEXTS` registry. -

styles.name: Data Storytelling
styles.official_demo_line: A hundred years of summer temperatures, where the chart itself tells the story.
styles.principles: The chart is the film. Every mark is a real number and every movement is a meaningful chart operation (a mark lands, an axis grows, the scale changes, a series morphs, a note is pinned). The data is real, openly licensed and traceable. You change the framing, never the numbers.
construction: Paper: warm cream, fixed-seed fibre noise and a faint dot grid in world space. Ink: dark warm ink for axes and series, pale warm grey for grid and zero line, IBM Plex Mono ticks.
Marks: data dots carry a thin ink ring so pale values stay visible on cream. A mark lands with a short pop and a thin ripple; suppress ripples when marks arrive closer than ~0.1 s.
Handwriting (Caveat) in pencil, per-glyph jitter, graphite grain, written on as the tip dances over the x-height. Leaders are wobbly curves ending in an un-closed ring around the mark.
The red–blue pencil: hex body, blue half / red half, sharpened wood cone. Only the tip end shows, from the lower right; its shadow drifts farther and softer with lift; sharp tip, soft body.
Layout: a plot box fixed in world space, a memory zone for early notes, every note pinned in data space (value + pixel offset) so rescales keep the layout, a bottom band for the caption.
colour_logic: Colour encodes one thing: the value. Diverging data uses a ramp (ColorBrewer RdBu family) centred on the mean of a meaningful reference period, with a symmetric span; data with no natural centre uses one sequential ramp. Everything else is ink on cream.
Honesty beats drama: pale values stay pale; never stretch a ramp to make a change look bigger.
The two pencil leads have meanings: blue for memories and human notes, red for records and warnings. A change of lead marks a turn.
One `accent` colour may bypass the ramp for a mark that is not data (a logo, a highlight).
motion: The rhythm of the data is the rhythm of the film. Map the marks to a musical grid; to accelerate, one option is to divide the beat instead of changing tempo. Pick a tempo whose finest subdivision lands on whole frames (at 24 fps a minute has 1440 frames; the c

Pencil acting: lift before each tap, land with the shadow meeting the tip, a tiny rebound; hurry as data densifies, tremble like a seismograph needle at a peak. It can flinch (recoil and freeze), hesitate (hover before a mark) and exit (hand the story to the v
Rescale reads as ratchet clicks (stepped, each step eased); a calm rescale is smooth.
Morph: a staggered sweep, each mark easing into its new form; notes fade as it passes and return as tiny marks.
No fades to blank or dissolves. Transitions are chart operations: axis growth, pull-backs, rescales, morphs, a cell widening into the next frame.
camera_grammar: Extreme close-up on one mark, following its leader
Full view first, then dive to one mark
Pull back as axes grow out of the marks
Track the pencil, newest mark at ~60 % of width
Pedestal with rising data, a Dutch angle creeping in
Punch-in over 2 frames, decaying shake, jolt on rescale
Fast pull-out, roll, small constant tremor
Hold on one mark, then pull back
Pull and pan to add more real data
Lateral pan across notes in the memory zone
sound_palette: Ambience follows the places the notes evoke (J-cuts in, L-cuts out). Foley is graphite, paper and wood: tick-and-paper taps, scratches for handwriting, a ruler hiss for axes, a paper puncture for a broken frame, a wooden click for the pencil flip, ratchet teet

Sonification is the music: pitch = value, rhythm = time density. Low values snap to a pentatonic scale, middle ones to semitones, extreme ones unquantized, with detune growing away from the reference. Timbre: a low-pass-gate "plonk" (sine + FM whose index rise
Bed: detuned-saw pad, soft kick, noise shaker, low-passed hats, sine sub, sample-and-hold blips, drones; harmony can darken or brighten with the data.
Silence is a tool: true digital silence (all layers) where the data should be heard alone, before a key mark, a morph or a verdict; the first sound after it matters most.
pitfalls_limits: Select data columns by header name, never by index; print every fact the narration claims.
Notes collide with later data → data-space pins, a memory zone.
A frame break rescaled too fast is invisible → hold the pierced state ≥ half a beat.
Right-aligned notes are still written left to right → the pencil hops to the first letter.
Helpers that set `globalAlpha` must multiply the incoming alpha, or fades skip them.
Tails leak across a hard silence → render before/after in separate buffers; verify on decoded samples.
In dense passages the pencil body lies across fresh marks → steepen its angle.
Synthesized human sounds (a laugh) are uncanny → use a soft non-human sound.
styles.engine_section: `demo/engine.js` (Canvas 2D, world units = chart pixels at zoom 1) is the style: paper, camera, value ramps, `pencilStroke` (any polyline in pencil), `inkShape` (any closed shape: bars, areas, map shapes), `plotShape`, `handText`, `dataDot`, `morphMark`, annotation geometry, `drawPencil`, `caption`. `demo/music/score.py` holds the sonification. The function table and a minimal example are in [DEMO.md](DEMO.md#engine-reference).

styles.name: Projection-Mapped Model
styles.official_demo: How a Flattened City Grew Back
styles.official_demo_line: A projector paints Rotterdam's white model layer by layer, from the 1940 gap to today's towers.
styles.principles: - The model is real geometry of a real place: building footprints and heights from open data (§2), extruded at a stated scale (1:1000, 1:2000…). Nothing on the model is invented or "representative", and no generated image ever stands in for the place. - The model is white; data is light. Colour is never painted into the material: it is projected, so it brightens surfaces that face the projector, fades on walls turned away, stops at the edge of the throw and reaches a little onto the plinth. - Layers arrive one at a time, each with its own gesture of light (a wash, a pop-on, a rising level, a m
construction: Model: matte white (≈ #F3F3F1, roughness ≈ 0.9), crisp edges; water a darker satin inlay in the base plate; bridges low white slabs; a thin base plate on a dark satin plinth.

Light model: house light = one soft key + a neutral studio environment + AO on close shots. Projection = a term added to the lit surface in the shader: `colour × (0.42 + 0.58 · max(N·toProjector, 0)) × throw mask`, scaled by albedo, reduced on water. Never a t

Building data is the material. First look for the place's own open 3D or footprint-with-height data: 3DBAG (Netherlands, CC BY 4.0), PLATEAU (Japan, CC BY 4.0-compatible), city open-data portals (footprints with heights or floors, zoning, plans). Fine: CC0, pu

Layers depend on what exists. Construction years per building are a Dutch luxury (BAG); elsewhere they are often missing. Substitute what the data does hold and the medium can still project: heights or floor counts, footprint area, zoning or plan status, a bou
A layer is state, not a picture: per-building attributes (year, height, rank, flags) live in vertex data; the shader decides each frame what colour the projector gives them.

The sun is a real directional light with shadow maps, computed from the place's latitude and a real date and time (NOAA/Meeus solar position). The projector can trace what the sun does (a shadow footprint) but never fakes a shadow.
colour_logic: Neutral ground: white model, dark room (near black), dark plinth. Projector black level is a cool near-black on the plate.

One hue family per layer, chosen for the data: a single categorical accent for "the old/the exception" (e.g. warm amber), a sequential ramp for continuous data (blue → cyan → white for time, violet → magenta → peach for height).
A colour may return only with the same meaning (the "before" colour reused later marks the same set of buildings).
The sun is warm, its shade is a projected deep blue; data colours are put away when the sun arrives.
motion: The camera moves continuously and slowly; it changes speed with the layers, never stops dead.

Light is the actor. Each layer arrives by a soft-edged gesture of light: a wash spreading from the projector axis, buildings switching on one by one with a short flash, a level climbing every facade, the sun's clock running. No hard line sweeping the table.
House lights cut fast (a relay, 0.25 s) and return slowly (1 s); the projector strikes with a brief flicker.
Counters roll while the light moves and land when it lands; measured lines grow from A to B with ticks.
What never moves: the model, the plinth, the pins' anchors on the model.
camera_grammar: Macro glide at rooftop height, shallow focus
Boom down to a low angle against black
Pull back as the house lights return
sound_palette: The room: room tone, the projector fan (hum + filtered air) rising when the lamp strikes, relays for the house lights, a lamp strike (zap + thump), the air of a light wash (sliding band-passed noise).
Light as sound: mallets and glass for things switching on, bowed vibraphone for held light, a rising mallet line and air riser for a climbing level, one glass note per highlighted building.
Weight: timpani, gran cassa, gong, low brass for a heavy fact; warm low brass for a turn.
Floor: contrabass and cellos only as a floor under the chords; no generic piano and strings melody.
pitfalls_limits: Wall normals wound the wrong way show inside faces (walls look hollow): derive the outward normal from ring orientation. Shared walls between parts z-fight: skip the overlap below the lower neighbour.
Warm HDRIs turn the white model beige: use a neutral studio environment.
GTAO on wide grazing views produces wedge-shaped dark bands; keep it on close shots only.
A low sun lights facades, not roofs: shoot from the sunlit side or side-on. Narrow shadows vanish among all the others: trace the one that matters (fill + edge) and measure it.
Hairline scan lines read as laser scanning: give every projection front a wide soft edge or switch buildings individually.
Floating labels: anchor pins on the tallest part of a building, not on its footprint centroid.
Numbers from mixed sources (official height vs measured roof): say which on screen ("roof", "measured").
styles.engine_section: - `demo/studio.js` — `makeStudio(W, H, model)`: renderer, post, room, the projection material (`projMaterial(kind)` injects `projLight()` / `roofGlow()` into MeshStandardMaterial), the city mesh (`buildCity`: outward normals, shared walls removed), plate, plinth, house light (index 0) and sun (index 1). Uniforms `U` drive every layer. - `demo/tools/prep.py` — 3DBAG + BGT only: it reads 3DBAG fields (`b3_h_70p`, `b3_h_maaiveld`, `oorspronkelijkbouwjaar`) and Dutch RD coordinates (`tools/rd.py`). Another source needs its own adapter that writes the same `model.json`: `{size:[w,d] model metres, b

styles.name: Data Physicalization
styles.official_demo_line: Twelve years of wind and solar stacked as real plates, spiralling round a walnut dial until solar overtakes.
styles.principles: - The unit is an object. One plate, block or coin equals one stated quantity, and the rule is said on screen once ("1 plate = 10 GW"). A heavier material marks every tenth unit, so the stack is its own ruler. - Scale is exact. Heights, counts and areas are computed from the data; rounding is one unit at most and written in the facts. Two series compared on the same base use the same unit. - Studio light, real matter. Metal reflects an HDRI, wood shows grain, acrylic transmits; nothing glows, nothing is outlined, no fake UI. - Growth is assembly. Data increases by pieces being placed, one after
construction: Pieces: thin boxes or cylinders instanced in the thousands, each with a few-millimetre random offset and yaw, a ±7 % value change and a hairline gap: that is what makes a stack read as stacked, not as a bar.

Material per series, chosen so two series separate in one glance at thumbnail size: brushed metal against tinted acrylic, pale wood against dark stone, copper coins against paper. A third material (e.g. brass) only for the ruler pieces, shared by every series.
Base: a real-texture slab (wood veneer, stone) with inlaid marks: a tick ring, the series' paths, the labels of categories or years, cut into the surface at the base's own scale, lit with the scene.

Rendering: PBR (transmission for acrylic), an HDRI at low intensity for reflections only, a warm key at 20–35° with long soft shadows, one or two cool rims so metal and acrylic separate from wood at distance; GTAO, physical depth of field, 2× supersampling, a
Screen space only for type: readings, verdicts, the source line, subtitles, the title card. Every reading is pinned to its object through the same world → screen function as the camera.
Post: grain light (the background is pale), no lens flares, no chromatic aberration.
colour_logic: The set is warm and neutral: a seamless greige sweep, the base in a natural material, the series in material colours (silver, pale teal, brass, oak). Material, not paint, separates series.
One accent (e.g. signal orange) for the reading or verdict that matters on this screen; nothing else is accent-coloured.
Ink is near-black at two strengths (value, then labels at ~60 %).
No rainbow series palettes, no colour ramps on the objects, no dark mode.
motion: On ones, 24 fps; the camera never stops (2–5 % creep on holds).
Cascade: a stack assembles bottom-to-top in 0.5–1.0 s, each piece dropping a few centimetres with an ease-out.

Feed: one period's increase arrives piece by piece from out of frame, quintic ease-out, a yaw that unwinds ("placed", not "dropped"), 8–16 pieces per second, the counter rolling with the pieces landed.
A single heavy object falls with gravity, lands with one small damped bounce, its shadow tightening.
Readings fade in with a 16 px rise and draw their leader; they leave by fading, never by sliding.
Never moves: the base, a piece once landed, the ruler pieces.
camera_grammar: Macro dolly along a stack's edge, rack focus
Low lateral track along the series
Locked three-quarter frame on two subjects
sound_palette: The material's own sound is the foley: metal plates tick bright and short (inharmonic partials 3–8 kHz), acrylic toks duller (1–3 kHz), wood knocks, coins ring. A cascade is a burst of these at the landing times, scaled down as density rises.

The ruler sings: every ruler piece (each 10th) rings a pitched mallet note, one timbre per series (e.g. glockenspiel for metal, glass harp for acrylic), climbing a pentatonic scale with the count — the chart becomes an arpeggio.

Score: mallets and air — marimba ostinato, bowed and struck vibraphone, harp, glass, a soft synth pad and a pulse bass with audible 2nd/3rd harmonics; horns for a turn. Accelerate by subdivision (8ths → 16ths), not tempo.
Impacts: a turn or a last object lands on punch (60–120 Hz) + bass drum + timpani + a bell; the two or three designed impacts are the loudest moments.
pitfalls_limits: Two materials too alike (bright aluminium vs clear acrylic) read as one series: give one a tint or a finish change, and check at thumbnail size.
Long shadows and warm reflections turn metal brown at distance: add a cool rim light and keep the base darker than the pieces.
Thin pieces moiré at 2–3 px per layer: random per-piece value and offset, 2× supersampling.
A reading pinned to a moving object can leave the frame: clamp it to a safe box.
Counters that roll by time instead of by landed pieces lie; tie them to the object count.
Rounding to whole pieces can invert close values; when two values are within one unit, say so on screen or choose a finer unit.
Transmission streaks at low angles: acrylic roughness ≥ 0.2, tinted attenuation.
styles.engine_section: - `demo/set.js` — `buildSet(scene)` (HDRI, warm key + cool rims, base with inlay canvas, instanced pieces per material, the last object) and the landing schedule (`SHEETS`, `EVENTS`, `landed(stack, t)`); change `PAIRS`, the unit and the materials for any single or paired series. - `demo/film.js` — cylindrical camera keys (`track`, `core/lib.js`) with focus on a target point, the reading kit (`pairLabels`, `verdict`, `plate`, `swatch`), counter, subtitles (`SUBCHECK`), `TEXTS`, `EV`. `demo/mix.py` — material foley (`tick_alu`, `tok_acr`), ruler notes, suck-outs, master. - Extra packages and pac

styles.name: Transit Map
styles.official_demo_line: A printed metro map grows from one 6 km line in 1993 to 21 lines and 906 km.
styles.principles: - Eight directions only. Every line segment, river edge and coastline is horizontal, vertical or at 45°; every corner is one fillet radius. A line never wiggles. - Growth is drawing. A line exists as far as its pen tip has travelled; stops light when the tip passes; an interchange appears only when the second line actually arrives, and it lands with weight. - Ink on a sheet. The map is printed on paper with tooth and fibres, lit by one raking light, and the sheet lies on a dark table. The camera sees it as an object: in perspective, with depth of field, and with its edge in wide or low shots.
construction: Interchange shape follows the station. Points side by side make a horizontal stadium, stacked points a vertical one; lines that cross at one point make a circle r 0.13 with the ink outline, which reads as an interchange next to the 0.085 stop because of its bl

Two passes. A 2D canvas inks only the region the camera sees into a texture (about 1.35× the screen density at the focus, capped at 4096², mipmapped, anisotropic filtering), limited in depth to a few camera distances so low views don't starve; a WebGL pass int

Paper: warm off-white, procedural and tileable, sampled in world coordinates so it never slides. Three layers: a cloud of value at about 9 G period with detail down to 0.04 G, a tooth at about 2.4 G period, and short fibres 0.02–0.1 G long. Paper value varies

Light: one raking light from one corner of the sheet (north-west in our demo), about 33° above the paper, neutral in colour and fixed for the whole film; it lifts that corner about 7 % above the opposite one. A specular sheen (up to +10 %, narrow lobe) appears
The sheet edge sits on a near-black warm table (about #1B1918) with a contact shadow that fades over about 0.2 G. Far away the table goes into a warm dark haze so the horizon never aliases.
Grade: a light vignette (up to −24 % in the corners), a 1.02 gamma, a light film grain at the master; no colour cast, no bloom except the pen-tip halo.
colour_logic: Neutral ground: warm off-white paper; ink near-black for text and interchange outlines; secondary text in warm grey; water one pale blue with a darker edge, its labels in a mid blue.
Line colours carry identity and nothing else. A real network uses its published colours; an invented one picks hues spaced around the wheel at similar weight, never two neighbours alike.
Mode is carried by line form, never by hue. Each line keeps its colour whatever kind of vehicle runs on it:

Paper inside a line is never painted. The paper of a bus core or a ferry lane is erased out of the ink layer (canvas `destination-out`), so the procedural paper of the print pass shows through with its own tooth and light; a paper-coloured stroke never matches
motion: 30 fps. Pen tips move on monotone keyframes; a tip may slow on a station and accelerate between them, never stop dead mid-segment.
Stops pop from 0.6× with a small overshoot in about 0.28 s and a ring in the line colour that spreads from 0.10 to 0.42 G and fades in 0.6 s. Minor stops pop the same way at a smaller size.

Interchanges scale down from 2× in 0.22 s with an ink ring spreading to 0.64 G. A major interchange falls from above in about 0.4 s (from 3.4× its size, its shadow offset and blurred, sharpening as it lands), then rings in ink and in the colours of the lines t
Line bullets spring in with a back ease and carry the opening year; they fade when the story moves past their chapter.
Vehicles (§2): white capsules at a constant speed, one per 4 G of track in each direction, only on finished track; boats slower than trains and buses.

A line that starts from a station already on the map makes it an interchange the moment its tip leaves; start that tip at least 0.5 s after the first line has reached the station, so the capsule's fall reads as an arrival.
camera_grammar: ride the pen tip, aim about 1.5 G ahead of it
drop low where a line meets water
low oblique sweep with shallow focus
glide across the sheet to another panel
rise until the sheet edge and the table show
push in to one segment under a paper veil
sound_palette: Tuned percussion for drawing and stops: glockenspiel, marimba, vibraphone; a stop is a pluck, an interchange a pop with a low thump.
A two-note station chime as the motif, returning at the turns of the story.

Layering by line: each new line adds one voice to a running ostinato (flute, spiccato strings, xylophone, horn staccato, harp, trumpet, oboe…), so the arrangement grows with the network. Accelerate by adding voices, not by changing tempo; a groove written in f

Matter: a felt-tip glide under every drawing tip; rail clacks in pairs for trains; ratchet ticks for the counter; a filtered, submerged mix while a line runs under water; a descending whistle and a low hit for a capsule that falls.
pitfalls_limits: Off-grid geometry: any segment not at 0/45/90° breaks the style. Route between points with an automatic bend (straight then diagonal, or the reverse) and validate every segment.

Labels over lines, or labels that jump: give labels a paper halo and place them once against the finished network, before the first frame. Placing against what is drawn so far makes labels hop as lines arrive.
Parallel lines sharing a corridor collide: offset each line by ±0.10 G and let one capsule enclose all points of the station.
Too much text in wide shots: hide minor names by zoom, not by time.

A flat map: a top view all the way through reads as a slideshow. Tilt, focus and the sheet edge are what make it an object; a still of the style should show at least one tilted view with depth of field.
Paper too loud: tooth and fibres stronger than a few percent turn the sheet into plaster or canvas.
Mode by colour: a ferry or bus line in a "ferry blue" breaks colour as identity. Use the line forms in §3.

Real networks: published colours and station names are facts, logos and branded bullets are not; the film is an unofficial tribute and says so on screen. Check every date and length against official sources; encyclopaedia figures for opening sections are often
styles.engine_section: The pipeline, independent of any code: (1) the network as data: stations with native and second-language names and a tier, lines as lists of stations, offsets and bends on the G lattice, water as bands and areas; (2) expand each route into an octilinear polyline, fillet the corners, measure arc length; (3) precompute everything time-dependent once: when each tip passes each station (by bisection on its keyframes), when a station becomes an interchange, label placement on the finished network; (4) per frame: camera → the region of the sheet it sees → ink that region into a texture (water, surfa

styles.name: 3D Map Explainer
styles.official_demo_line: From the globe down into the strait a fifth of the world's oil squeezes through: two lanes, a cut through the sea floor, and pipelines that can carry only a fraction of it around.
styles.principles: - The ground is real data. Elevation and bathymetry from public tiles, imagery from licence-clean satellite mosaics, coastlines and place names where they really are. Nothing on the ground is invented or traced; whatever is drawn (a route, a pipeline path) is labelled schematic. - Two layers. The terrain says *what this place is like*; the glowing layer says *what happens here*. The data layer is the only thing that glows. - Relief stands up. Heights are exaggerated (about ×3 for land, stated on screen) and lit by a low sun, so mountains read even from orbit. - The data layer advances. Each ti
construction: Terrain: one mesh per level of detail (a detailed grid for the place, a coarser one for the region; the coarse one discards itself under the fine one with a small overlap and is lowered a few tens of metres so the seam never fights). Imagery as albedo, graded

The sea: not the imagery's colour. Shade it by real depth: coastal shallows keep a little of the imagery's texture toned teal, deep water goes to navy. Distances along the coast are measured in kilometres, so every zoom level shades alike.

Sun and shadows: one directional sun about 20° high, a weak sky/ground hemisphere fill. Shadows are baked into textures (march toward the sun over the height grid, penumbra widening with distance to the occluder) and multiplied into the direct light; shadow ma

The glowing layer: additive ribbons, not tone-mapped, so only they trigger bloom. Width = the larger of a real width and a minimum in pixels (computed per vertex from the distance to the camera): routes stay 2–3 px from orbit, a lane or a road keeps its true w
Lines on land (pipelines, borders): the glowing line sits on a dark casing in normal blending, the way charts print a cased line; on bright desert a glow alone washes out.

Traffic (ships, trains, trucks, planes): flat warm-white glyphs with a short fading wake or trail, scaled to stay about the same size on screen at any height; offset a little inside their lane so they never sit on the bright centre line.
colour_logic: Neutral ground: the place's own colours, warmed. No colour ramps over the terrain.

Amber is data (routes, lanes, the main quantity). Cool white is boundaries (lane edges, limits). Warm white is what moves and what measures (traffic, rulers, the measured line). A second data hue (a teal) appears only when a quantity is compared against the ma
Type on land is dark brown ink, type on water pale sea blue, type on dark shadowed mountains warm white. No outlines, no drop shadows.
The sea's navy and the night side of the globe are the only large dark areas.
motion: The camera never stops dead: distance interpolates in log space, keys are monotone cubic, holds keep a slow drift.

The glowing layer arrives by being drawn: lines grow from their source, a lane ignites with a bright head running along its real course, pulses flow in the direction of travel, pillars grow slab by slab on the beat.
Depth of field, fog and bloom change continuously with height; nothing pops.
Traffic moves at a time-lapse speed that reads (a few km per film second), all in its lanes.
Frame rate and grain: 24 fps; mux grain 1, a light film grain.
camera_grammar: Dive and level out (log distance, pitch from ~80° to ~45°)
Orbit + crane down to the cut
Low tracking shot along a line
Big pull-out over the whole region
sound_palette: Score: low plucked strings for a pulse, cello spiccato when things move, bowed vibraphone and harp for light and air, hand chimes or glockenspiel for each thing that lights up, frame drum on downbeats, a horn swell under a quantity; a low sine pedal with 2nd a

Foley: thin high-altitude air that thickens as the camera comes down, a whoosh for each dive, small data ticks for terminals and rulers, a sub thump and an electric shimmer when a lane ignites, a low tearing sweep for the cut, a muffled undersea hush inside a
Silence: under the cross-section the music thins to a pedal; before a verdict, half a bar of nothing.
Mix: narration compressed and ~10 dB (RMS) over the music; the music bus dips 300 Hz–4 kHz and ducks under each line; −14 LUFS, true peak ≤ −1 dB.
native_moves: A line ignites along its true course.
pitfalls_limits: Licences: Sentinel-2 cloudless by EOX is CC BY 4.0 only for the 2016 release (later releases are CC BY-NC-SA); AWS Terrain Tiles (SRTM, GMTED, ETOPO1, GEBCO) are free with attribution; OSM data is ODbL (credit and share-alike for the database): name the terms

Facts: every number on screen and in the narration needs a named source and a stated basis (whose estimate, which year, what is counted); when sources disagree, show both and say whose is whose. Keep them in `FACTS.md`. Schematic things (routes, simplified pip

Resolution: z10 terrain is ~150 m per cell; very close flights look soft, small islands are missing (mark them with a dot, do not invent them). Fetch finer data only for the area the camera will really approach.
Mercator vs sphere: the flat map is Web Mercator, the globe is a sphere; matching a dissolve needs the camera converted, not hand-placed, and the dissolve kept short (≈ 0.8 s).
Shimmer: no real-time shadow maps over large flights; no lines under ~2 px; no thin dashes from orbit (fade dashes out with distance).
Sun glint: a camera that looks toward a low sun over water gets a large specular blob that blooms; keep the sea's roughness high enough, or look away from the sun.
Glow close to the lens: a pillar or a lane right in front of the camera blooms into a blob; start growth after the camera has risen, or lower bloom with distance.

Comparisons: a small quantity in a pale colour on bright terrain disappears; use a solid contrasting hue, the same scale, a clean background and number labels as large as the main one, and hold ≥ 2.5 s.
styles.engine_section: - `demo/index.html`: the demo's whole film on one timeline (its strait, ships and pipelines are the demo's subject; your film maps its own): terrain meshes with baked shadows, the ribbon shader, ships, the cross-section wall, pillars, pipelines, the globe and its routes, both camera tracks and the globe ↔ map conversion, the 2D overlay (labels, measurements, rulers, subtitles, end card). - `demo/post.js`: physical depth of field, bloom, grade (a copy of `core/three/post.js`). - `demo/tools/`: `fetch.py`, `fetch_wide.py`, `fetch_world.py` (tiles), `prep.py`, `prep_wide.py` (height grids, graded

styles.name: Blob Simulation
styles.official_demo_line: 160 flocked Pips race for beans: the fast ones eat first and run dry first, and after 20 generations the board turns blue.
styles.principles: - The simulation is real. Positions, headings, what each Pip eats, its energy, whether it survives and whether it has children all come from a deterministic run with a fixed seed; the picture interpolates the record. Nothing is placed by hand to make a point. Changing a rule changes the film. - One Pip = one individual. Counts are Pips, distributions are Pips standing in printed bars, a population is a board full of Pips. - A character you can follow. The camera can always drop to one Pip, see its face and its state, and rise again to the whole board. The story of a rule is told through one or
construction: Pip (three.js, instanced: one InstancedMesh per part, hundreds per frame):

Body: a lathe profile, a wide-based, round-bellied, domed "mochi" about 0.9 tall and 1.07 wide, flat bottom sitting firmly on the board. A soft curled tuft on top (thick root, thin tip, round end). Two flat oval feet in front, body colour × 0.8.
Face: ink only. Eyes are tall glossy beads with one large and one small white glint; a pale blush on each cheek (body colour mixed 30% towards `#FF9A8F`); the mouth is a matte arc.

Expressions change only eyes, mouth and brows (geometric parts): neutral, happy / fed, eating (open mouth), sleepy / tired, surprised, determined (brows low inside), sad (brows high inside). Expressions change through a blink (closed for about 0.15 s), never i
Traits on the body: the trait being studied is the body colour (a ramp, §3); size = scale; perception = bigger eyes.

Flock, opaque: MeshPhysicalMaterial, roughness 0.9, specular 0.1, sheen 1 tinted by each Pip's colour, sheen roughness 0.35; an extra fibre edge glow (`pow(1 − N·V, 2.6) × 0.6`, towards a paler shade of the same colour) that separates outlines in a dense crowd
colour_logic: Up to five team colours in a frame, taken in the order of the table.
For a continuous trait the five team colours are the stops of a ramp (OKLab interpolation, lightness rising along it), so the colour of the whole board reads as the state of the population.
Type is ink; secondary type is ink at reduced opacity (0.75 / 0.55), never another grey.

Derived colours follow the rules and are never picked on their own: feet = body × 0.8; cheeks = body towards `#FF9A8F` 30%; kicked-up fluff `#FFF7EA`; printed bar grounds = team colour towards `#F4EEE3` 78%; glints white.
motion: Hop by distance: the hop phase is distance travelled ÷ stride (stride grows with speed); when a Pip stops, the hop amplitude fades with a smoothed "moving" factor, so feet never slide and no Pip freezes in mid-air. Lean forward 0.12–0.22 rad, squash and stretc

Anticipation, action, follow-through: turn and crouch before a run; the body bulges as it eats and the bean flies into the mouth; a Pip that runs out of energy slumps and fades to spent grey; at a verdict the ones that go stretch up once and shrink away (never
Breathing: idle Pips breathe (±2% squash, each with its own phase), until the final hold, which is perfectly still.

Bodies never interpenetrate: in the simulation Pips are points; every frame the drawn positions are relaxed apart (three passes by body radius) so neighbours touch but never merge. This changes only the drawing.
Time is a tool: the simulation clock can run at any rate against the film clock (monotone, continuous); slow motion is kept for the one moment a rule bites.
Frame rate and grain: 24 fps.
sound_palette: Warm mallets and plucks: marimba, kalimba, hang, glockenspiel, xylophone, vibraphone (struck and bowed), harp, pizzicato and sustained cellos, woodblock; a synthesized shaker. No piano-and-strings pad, no drum kit.

Foley from the simulation: one soft felt step per hop (gain by distance to the camera, pan by screen position), a pitched pop per bean appearing, a two-note "nom" per bean eaten, a falling sigh when a Pip runs dry, a soft poof when one goes.
Data as pitch: births, generations and Pips landing in a chart are pitched by their value (a higher value, a higher note), so the score follows the numbers.
Narration, when used, sits about 10 dB above the bed; the music leaves 300 Hz–4 kHz to it.
native_moves: The cast on a number line
pitfalls_limits: Translucent, jelly, glass or clear-coated Pips look cheap and refract each other; keep them opaque flock.
Fibre normals shimmer in motion without mipmaps and anisotropy; supersample.
Shadow cameras that follow the camera make shadows swim; fix the sun.
Screen-space AO on hundreds of small bodies flickers and halos; use contact blobs.
Charts as floating cards with shadows break the bench: print them, or let the Pips be the chart.
More than one main chart plus one small chart in a frame turns into a slide.
Type over the crowd is unreadable; find or make clean ground first.
The food colour must never fall inside the trait ramp.
styles.engine_section: three.js r170 with instanced parts; a deterministic simulation module that records every step; post from `core/three/post.js`; the 2D canvas layer for type; sound events exported from the page (`window.EV`) and mixed with `core/audio/sampler.py` and `sfx.py`. See the demo's code entry points in DEMO.md.
